I: § April 8
My priceless Varvara Alexeyevna!

Yesterday I was happy, excessively happy, as happy as can be! For once in your life, you stubborn girl, you listened to me. In the evening, at about eight o'clock, I woke up (you know, my dearest, that I like to sleep an hour or two after the office), got out a candle, laid out my papers, mended my pen, and suddenly, quite by chance, I raised my eyes — and truly, my heart simply leaped like this! So you did understand what I wanted, what my little heart wanted! I see the corner of the curtain at your window turned back and pinned to the pot of balsam, exactly as I hinted to you then; and just then it seemed to me that your little face flashed at the window, that you too were looking at me from your little room, that you too were thinking of me. And how vexed I was, my dear, that I could not make out your sweet little face properly! There was a time, my dearest, when we too saw clearly. Old age is no joy, my own! Even now everything somehow swims before my eyes; work a little in the evening, write something, and by morning the eyes are red and the tears run so that one is ashamed before strangers. Yet in my imagination your little smile shone out, my little angel, your kind, friendly little smile; and in my heart I felt exactly what I felt then, when I kissed you, Varenka — do you remember, my little angel? Do you know, my dear, it even seemed to me that you shook your little finger at me there? Was it so, you rogue? You must certainly describe all this more fully in your letter.

Well, and how do you like our little invention about your curtain, Varenka? Charming, isn't it? Whether I am sitting at my work, or going to bed, or waking up, I already know that you too are thinking of me there, remembering me, and that you yourself are well and cheerful. Lower the curtain — it means, goodbye, Makar Alexeyevich, it is time to sleep! Raise it — it means, good morning, Makar Alexeyevich, how did you sleep? or: how is your health, Makar Alexeyevich? As for me, thank the Creator, I am well and all is well with me! You see, my darling, how cleverly it is devised; and no letters needed! Cunning, isn't it? And the invention is mine! Well, what do you say, Varvara Alexeyevna, how am I at such things?

I must tell you, my dearest Varvara Alexeyevna, that I slept well last night, contrary to expectation, with which I am very pleased; although in new lodgings, after moving in, one always somehow cannot sleep; everything is somehow this way and not quite right! I got up today like a bright falcon — what a delight! What a fine morning it is today, my dearest! They opened our window; the sun is shining, the little birds are chirping, the air breathes of spring scents, and all nature is coming to life — well, and everything else there was likewise fitting; all in order, in the spring manner. I even dreamed quite pleasantly today, and all my dreams, Varenka, were about you. I compared you to a bird of heaven, created for the delight of people and the adornment of nature. Then I thought, Varenka, that we too, people living in care and turmoil, must envy the carefree and innocent happiness of the birds of heaven — well, and the rest all of the same kind, like unto it; that is, I kept making such far-fetched comparisons. I have a little book there, Varenka, in which the very same thing is described, all of it quite in detail. I write this because, my dearest, there are all sorts of dreams. And now it is spring, and the thoughts are all so pleasant, sharp, ingenious, and the dreams that come are tender; everything is in rose colour. That is why I wrote all this; though, to tell the truth, I took it all from the book. There the author expresses the same wish in verse, and writes —
Why am I not a bird, a bird of prey!

And so on, and so forth. There are other thoughts there too, but never mind them! But where did you go this morning, Varvara Alexeyevna? I was not yet getting ready for the office, and you, like a true spring bird, fluttered out of your room and crossed the yard, looking so cheerful. How glad I was, looking at you! Ah, Varenka, Varenka! Do not be sad; tears cannot cure grief; this I know, my dearest, I know it from experience. Now you are so peaceful, and your health has improved a little too. Well, how is your Fedora? Ah, what a kind woman she is! Write and tell me, Varenka, how you live with her now and whether you are content with everything. Fedora is a little grumbling; but don't pay attention to that, Varenka. God bless her! She is so kind.

I have already written you of our Teresa here — also a kind and faithful woman. And how anxious I was about our letters! How would they be passed along? And then the Lord sent Teresa, for our good fortune. She is a kind, gentle, silent woman. But our landlady is simply merciless. She works her to death, like some rag.

Well, what a hole I have landed in, Varvara Alexeyevna! What lodgings! Before, you know, I lived like a hermit, quietly, peacefully; if a fly flew by in my room, one could hear the fly. But here it is noise, shouting, uproar! And you don't yet know how it is all arranged here. Imagine, for example, a long corridor, completely dark and dirty. On its right hand there is a blank wall, and on the left it is all doors and doors, like hotel rooms, stretching all in a row. Well, and these rooms are let, and there is one little room in each; one person lives in a room, sometimes two or three. Do not ask for order — it is Noah's ark! However, the people seem good, all so educated, learned. There is one clerk (he is in the literary line somewhere), a well-read man: he talks of Homer, and of Brambeus, and of various authors of theirs, talks of everything — a clever man! Two officers live here and are always playing cards. A midshipman lives here; an English tutor lives here. Wait, I shall amuse you, my dearest; I shall describe them in my next letter satirically, that is, how they are in themselves, with every detail. Our landlady — a very small and dirty old woman — goes about all day in slippers and a dressing gown and shouts all day at Teresa. I live in the kitchen, or, more correctly, I should put it this way: next to the kitchen there is a room (and our kitchen, I must tell you, is clean, light, very nice), a small room, a modest little corner... that is, or rather better to say, the kitchen is large, with three windows, and along its cross wall I have a partition, so that it comes out as though another room, a supernumerary one; everything spacious, convenient, and there is a window, and everything — in a word, everything convenient. Well, this is my little corner. So don't you think, my dearest, that there is anything else in it or some mysterious meaning; that it is, you see, a kitchen! — that is, I do, perhaps, live in that very room behind the partition, but that is nothing; I keep apart from everyone, I live quietly, little by little, I live on the sly. I have put in a bed, a table, a chest of drawers, a couple of chairs, and hung up an icon. True, there are better lodgings — perhaps even much better — but the convenience is the main thing; it is all for the convenience, and don't you think it is for anything else. Your window is opposite, across the yard; and the yard is narrow, one can catch sight of you in passing — all the merrier for me, poor wretch, and cheaper too. Here the very last room, with board, costs thirty-five roubles in paper money. Beyond my means! And my lodging costs me seven roubles in paper money, and board five silver roubles: that makes twenty-four and a half, and before I paid exactly thirty, but then I denied myself in many things; I did not always drink tea, and now I have saved on both tea and sugar. It is, you know, my own, somehow shameful not to drink tea; here all the people are well-off, so it is shameful. One drinks it for the sake of others, Varenka, for show, for tone; but for me it is all the same, I am not fastidious. Reckon it so, for pocket money — something is always needed — well, some boots, a bit of clothing — how much is left? That is all my salary. I do not grumble and am content. It is enough. It has been enough for several years; there are rewards too. Well, goodbye, my little angel. I have bought a couple of pots with balsam, and a geranium — not expensive. And perhaps you like mignonette too? There is mignonette, then, only write me; and you know, write everything as fully as possible. Do not, however, think anything, and do not doubt about me, my dearest, that I have taken such a room. No, it was convenience that compelled me, and convenience alone tempted me. I, my dearest, am saving money, putting it aside; I have a kopeck or two. Do not look at the fact that I am so quiet that it seems a fly could knock me down with its wing. No, my dearest, I am no fool where I myself am concerned, and my character is exactly such as befits a man of firm and untroubled soul. Goodbye, my little angel! I have scribbled you almost two sheets, and it is long past time for the office. I kiss your little fingers, my dearest, and remain
Your humblest servant
and most faithful friend
Makar Devushkin.

P. S. I ask for one thing: answer me, my little angel, as fully as possible. I am sending you herewith, Varenka, a pound of sweets; eat them in good health, and for God's sake do not worry about me and do not take offence. Well, goodbye then, my dearest.
§ April 8
Dear Sir, Makar Alexeyevich!

Do you know that we shall have to quarrel with each other altogether in the end? I swear to you, good Makar Alexeyevich, that it is even painful for me to accept your presents. I know what they cost you, what privations and denials of the most necessary things to yourself. How many times have I told you that I need nothing, absolutely nothing; that I am not able to repay even the kindnesses with which you have so far showered me. And why do I need these pots? Well, the balsams are all right, but why the geranium? One need only carelessly say a little word, as for example about this geranium, and you buy it at once; it must have been expensive? What a charm its flowers have! Crimson, in little crosses. Where did you get such a pretty little geranium? I have put it in the middle of the window, in the most conspicuous place; and on the floor I shall put a bench, and on the bench more flowers; only just let me grow rich myself! Fedora is delighted; our room is like paradise now — clean, light! Well, and why the sweets? And really, I guessed at once from your letter that something was not quite right with you — paradise, and spring, and fragrances flying about, and little birds chirping. What is this, I thought, is there not perhaps some poetry here too? Indeed, nothing but verses is lacking in your letter, Makar Alexeyevich! Tender feelings and dreams in rose colour — everything is here! About the curtain I never thought; it must have caught by itself when I moved the pots; so there you are!

Ah, Makar Alexeyevich! Whatever you say there, however you reckon your income to deceive me, to show that it all goes entirely on yourself alone, you will not hide or conceal anything from me. It is clear that you are depriving yourself of necessities because of me. What came into your head, for example, to take such lodgings? You are disturbed there, troubled; it is cramped and inconvenient for you. You love solitude, and there is everything imaginable around you! You could live much better, judging by your salary. Fedora says that you used to live incomparably better than now. Can it be that you have spent your whole life like this, alone, in privation, without joy, without a friendly, kind word, renting corners from strangers? Ah, good friend, how sorry I am for you! Spare your health at least, Makar Alexeyevich! You say that your eyes are growing weak, so do not write by candlelight; why write? Your zeal for the service is probably known to your superiors without that.

Once more I beg you, do not spend so much money on me. I know that you love me, but you yourself are not rich... Today I too got up cheerful. I felt so well; Fedora had been working a long time already, and got me some work too. I was so glad; I only went out to buy some silk, and set to work. The whole morning my heart was so light, I was so merry! And now again it is all black thoughts, sadness; my whole heart aches.

Ah, what will become of me, what will my fate be! The hard thing is that I am in such uncertainty, that I have no future, that I cannot even guess what will become of me. To look back is frightening. There it is all such grief that my heart is torn in two at the mere memory. Forever shall I lament the wicked people who ruined me!

It is growing dusk. Time to work. I should like to write you of many things, but there is no time, the work is due. I must hurry. Of course, letters are a good thing; it is not so dull. But why do you yourself never come to see us? Why is that, Makar Alexeyevich? Now you are near, and sometimes you have free time too. Do come, please! I saw your Teresa. She seems so ill; I felt sorry for her; I gave her twenty kopecks. Yes! I almost forgot: be sure to write everything, as fully as possible, about your way of life. What sort of people are around you, and do you get on well with them? I very much want to know all this. Mind, be sure to write! Today I shall turn back the corner of the curtain on purpose. Go to bed earlier; yesterday I saw your light until midnight. Well, goodbye. Today it is anguish, and boredom, and sadness! It must be that sort of day! Goodbye.
Yours
Varvara Dobroselova.
§ April 8
Dear Madam, Varvara Alexeyevna!

Yes, my dearest, yes, my own, it seems a day like that has fallen to my wretched lot! Yes; you have made fun of me, an old man, Varvara Alexeyevna! However, I am to blame myself, wholly to blame! I should not, at my age, with a wisp of hair left on my head, have launched into amours and innuendoes... And I will say further, my dearest: man is sometimes strange, very strange. And, my holy saints! What he begins to talk of, where he sometimes gets carried away! And what comes of it, what follows from it? Why, absolutely nothing follows, and such rubbish comes out that Lord preserve me! I, my dearest, I am not angry, but it is only very vexing to remember it all, vexing that I wrote to you so floridly and so foolishly. And I went to the office today so jauntily, like a dandy; there was such a radiance in my heart. For no reason at all it was a holiday in my soul; I was merry! I took up the papers diligently — and what came of it afterwards! Only afterwards, when I looked about me, everything was as before — grey and dim. The same ink stains, the same tables and papers, and I too the same; just as I was, so I remained, exactly the same — so what was the use of riding Pegasus? And what did it all come from? That the sun peeped out and the sky turned azure! From that, was it? And what scents are there, when in our yard under the windows all sorts of things happen! It must have all seemed so to me out of foolishness. And yet it happens sometimes that a man gets so lost in his own feelings and talks nonsense. This comes from nothing else than excessive, foolish warmth of the heart. I did not come home, I dragged myself; for no reason my head began to ache; that, I suppose, is all of a piece. (A draught on my back, perhaps.) I rejoiced at the spring like a fool of fools, and went out in my cold overcoat. And you mistook my feelings, my own! Their outpouring took quite another direction. Fatherly affection inspired me, solely pure fatherly affection, Varvara Alexeyevna; for I take the place of your own father, because of your bitter orphanhood; I say this from the soul, from a pure heart, as a kinsman. Be that as it may, I am to you at least a distant relation, at least, as the proverb says, a relation at the seventh remove, but still a relative, and now your nearest relative and protector; for where you had most right to seek protection and defence, you found betrayal and insult. And as to verses, I will tell you, my dearest, that it does not become me at my age to practise composing verses. Verses are nonsense! For verses they flog little boys in schools nowadays... that is the thing, my own.

What is this you write to me, Varvara Alexeyevna, about comforts, and peace, and all sorts of things? My dearest, I am not peevish and not demanding, I have never lived better than now; so why be fussy at my age? I am fed, clothed, shod; and where should we go in for fancies! We are not of count's blood! My father was not of noble rank, and with his whole family was poorer than I in income. I am no pampered fellow! However, if it comes to the truth, in my old lodgings everything was incomparably better; it was more free and easy, my dearest. Of course, my present lodging is good too, even in some respects merrier and, if you like, more varied; I say nothing against that, but all the same I am sorry for the old one. We old, that is, elderly people grow used to old things as to something of our own kin. The little lodging was, you know, so small; the walls were... well, what is there to say! — the walls were like all walls, it is not about them, but the memories of all my past bring a melancholy over me... A strange thing — it is hard, and yet the memories seem pleasant. Even what was bad, what I was sometimes vexed at, even that in memory is somehow cleansed of the bad and appears to my imagination in an attractive light. We lived quietly, Varenka; I and my landlady, the old woman, now departed. And I recall my old woman now with a sad feeling! She was a good woman and did not charge much for the lodging. She used to knit blankets from various scraps on needles an arshin long; that was all she did. We kept one light together, so we worked at one table. She had a granddaughter, Masha — I remember her still a child — she will be a girl of thirteen now. Such a rogue she was, cheerful, always making us laugh; so we lived, the three of us. On a long winter evening we would sit down at the round table, drink a little tea, and then set to work. And the old woman, so that Masha should not be bored and that the rogue should not be naughty, would begin telling fairy tales. And what tales they were! Not only a child, but a sensible and clever man would listen spellbound. Why! I myself would light my little pipe and listen so that I forgot my work. And the child, our little rogue, would grow thoughtful; she would prop her rosy cheek on her little hand, open her pretty little mouth, and at a frightening tale would press, press herself to the old woman. And we loved to look at her; and one did not notice the candle burning down, nor hear how outside sometimes the blizzard raged and the snowstorm swept. It was good for us to live, Varenka; and so we lived together almost twenty years. But why have I rattled on! Perhaps such a subject does not please you, and it is not so easy for me to recall, especially now: it is twilight. Teresa is busy with something, my head aches, and my back aches a little too, and my thoughts are so strange, as though they ache too; I am sad today, Varenka! What is this you write, my own? How can I come to you? My dear, what will people say? One would have to cross the yard, our people would notice, would start asking — talk would begin, gossip would begin, they would give the matter another meaning. No, my little angel, I had better see you tomorrow at vespers; that will be more prudent and less harmful to us both. And do not hold it against me, my dearest, that I have written you such a letter; when I read it over, I see it is all so disjointed. I, Varenka, am an old, unlearned man; I did not learn in my youth, and now nothing will enter my head if I start learning again. I confess, my dearest, that I am no master of description, and I know, without anyone else's pointing out and laughing, that if I try to write anything a little more ornate, I shall pile up nonsense. I saw you at the window today, saw how you lowered the blind. Goodbye, goodbye, God keep you! Goodbye, Varvara Alexeyevna.
Your disinterested friend
Makar Devushkin.

P. S. I, my own, write satires about no one now. I have grown old, my dear Varvara Alexeyevna, to bare my teeth for nothing! And they would laugh at me too, as the Russian proverb says: he who digs a pit for another... will fall into it himself.
§ April 9
Dear Sir, Makar Alexeyevich!

Well, aren't you ashamed, my friend and benefactor, Makar Alexeyevich, to be so melancholy and capricious? Surely you were not offended! Ah, I am often careless, but I did not think you would take my words for a cutting jest. Be assured that I would never dare to jest at your years or your character. It all happened through my giddiness, and still more because it is terribly dull, and out of boredom one takes up anything. And I supposed that you yourself in your letter wanted to laugh. I felt terribly sad when I saw that you were displeased with me. No, my good friend and benefactor, you will be mistaken if you suspect me of insensibility and ingratitude. I know how to value in my heart all that you have done for me, in defending me from wicked people, from their persecution and hatred. I shall pray to God for you forever, and if my prayer reaches God and heaven hears it, you will be happy.

I feel very unwell today. Fever and chill alternately. Fedora is very anxious about me. You are wrong to be ashamed to come to us, Makar Alexeyevich. What is it to others! You are acquainted with us, and that is the end of it!.. Goodbye, Makar Alexeyevich. There is nothing more to write about now, and I cannot: I am terribly unwell. I beg you once more not to be angry with me and to be assured of that constant respect and that attachment with which I have the honour to remain your most devoted
and most obedient servant
Varvara Dobroselova.
§ April 12
Dear Madam, Varvara Alexeyevna!

Ah, my dearest, what is this with you! Every time you frighten me so. I write to you in every letter that you should take care, that you should wrap up, not go out in bad weather, observe caution in everything — and you, my little angel, do not listen to me. Ah, my dear, you are just like some child! You are weak, weak as a blade of straw, I know. The least breeze and you are ill. So you must take care, look after yourself, avoid dangers, and not plunge your friends into grief and dejection.

You express a wish, my dearest, to learn in detail about my way of life and all that surrounds me. I hasten with joy to fulfil your wish, my own. I shall begin from the beginning, my dearest: there will be more order. First, in our house, at the clean entrance, the stairs are really quite decent; the front stairs especially are clean, light, wide, all cast iron and mahogany. But the back stairs — do not even ask: winding, damp, dirty, the steps broken, and the walls so greasy that your hand sticks when you lean on them. On every landing stand broken trunks, chairs and cupboards, rags hang about, windows are smashed; tubs stand with all sorts of filth, with dirt, with rubbish, with eggshells and fish bladders; a bad smell... in a word, not nice.

I have already described to you the arrangement of the rooms; it is, there is no denying, convenient, that is true, but somehow it is stuffy in them, that is, not that it smells bad, but, if one can put it so, a rather rotten, sharply sweetish smell of some kind. At first the impression is unfavourable, but that is nothing; you need only be with us two minutes and it passes, and you do not notice how everything passes, because you yourself somehow smell bad, and your clothes smell, and your hands smell, and everything smells — well, and you get used to it. Our siskins simply die. The midshipman is buying his fifth already — they do not live in our air, and that is all. Our kitchen is large, spacious, light. True, in the mornings it is a little smoky when they fry fish or beef, and they pour and wet everything about, but in the evening it is paradise. In our kitchen old linen always hangs on ropes; and since my room is not far, that is, almost adjoins the kitchen, the smell of the linen troubles me a little; but never mind: you live and get used to it.

From very early morning, Varenka, the bustle begins with us, people get up, walk about, knock — everyone rises who has to, who is in service or just on his own account; everyone begins to drink tea. The samovars are mostly the landlady's, there are few of them, so we all keep to a turn; and whoever turns up out of turn with his teapot gets his head washed at once. I did just that the first time, and... but why write it! It was then that I became acquainted with everyone. With the midshipman I became acquainted first; he is so open, told me everything: about his father, his mother, his sister who is married to an assessor in Tula, and about the town of Kronstadt. He promised to protect me in everything, and at once invited me to tea. I found him in that very room where they usually play cards. There they gave me tea and were determined that I should play a game of chance with them. Whether they were laughing at me or not I do not know; only they themselves had been playing the whole night through, and when I came in they were playing too. Chalk, cards, and such smoke went about the whole room that it stung the eyes. I did not play, and they at once remarked that I talk philosophy. After that no one spoke to me the whole time; and I, to tell the truth, was glad of it. I shall not go to them now; they have the gambling fever, sheer gambling fever! At the clerk's of the literary line there are also gatherings in the evenings. Well, with him it is nice, modest, innocent and delicate; all on a refined footing.

Well, Varenka, let me remark to you in passing that our landlady is a most vile woman, and a real witch besides. You have seen Teresa. Well, what is she really? Thin as a plucked, sickly chicken. In the house there are only two servants altogether: Teresa and Faldoni, the landlady's man. I do not know, perhaps he has some other name, only he answers to this one; everyone calls him so. He is red-haired, some sort of Finn, blind in one eye, snub-nosed, a boor: he is always quarrelling with Teresa, they all but fight. In general, to live here is not altogether good... For everyone to fall asleep at night all at once and be at peace — that never happens. Somewhere or other they are always sitting and playing, and sometimes things are done that it is shameful to tell. Now I have got used to it somewhat, but I wonder how family people get on in such a Sodom. A whole family of some poor people rents a room from our landlady, only not next to the other numbered rooms, but on the other side, in a corner, apart. Quiet people! No one hears anything of them. They live in one little room, partitioned off by a screen. He is some clerk without a post, dismissed from the service seven years ago for something. His surname is Gorshkov; a grey-haired, small man; he goes about in such greasy, such worn clothes that it hurts to look at him; far worse than mine! Pitiful, feeble (we meet sometimes in the corridor); his knees tremble, his hands tremble, his head trembles, from some illness perhaps, God knows; timid, afraid of everyone, he walks along the wall; I am bashful at times, but this man is worse still. His family is a wife and three children. The eldest, a boy, is the image of his father, just as sickly. The wife was once quite good-looking, and it is still noticeable; she goes about, poor thing, in such pitiful rags. They are in debt to the landlady, I have heard; she is not very kind to them. I have heard too that Gorshkov himself has some unpleasantness, for which he lost his post... a lawsuit, not a lawsuit, under trial, not under trial, under some investigation perhaps — truly I cannot tell you. Poor they are, poor — Lord, my God! It is always quiet and still in their room, as if no one lived there. One does not even hear the children. And it never happens that the children frolic or play, and that is a bad sign. Once, in the evening, it happened that I passed by their door; at that moment the house had gone unusually quiet; I heard sobbing, then whispering, then sobbing again, as though they were weeping, so softly, so pitifully, that my heart was wrung, and afterwards the thought of these poor people did not leave me all night, so that I could not even sleep properly.

Well, goodbye, my priceless little friend, Varenka! I have described everything to you as best I could. Today I have thought all day only of you. My heart has ached for you, my own. You see, my darling, I know that you have no warm cloak. These Petersburg springs, the winds and the rains with a little snow — these are the death of me, Varenka! Such a blessed temperature of the air that Lord preserve me! Do not blame me, darling, for my writing; I have no style, Varenka, no style at all. If only I had some! I write whatever comes into my head, only to cheer you up with something. You see, if I had studied somehow, that would be another matter; but how did I study? Not even for a copper's worth.
Your constant and faithful friend
Makar Devushkin.
§ April 25
Dear Sir, Makar Alexeyevich!

Today I met my cousin Sasha! Horror! She too will be ruined, poor girl! I have also heard from others that Anna Fyodorovna is asking about me everywhere. She seems never to stop persecuting me. She says that she wants to forgive me, to forget all the past, and that she will certainly come to see me herself. She says that you are not a relative of mine at all, that she is a nearer relative to me, that you have no right whatever to interfere in our family relations, and that it is shameful and improper for me to live on your charity and at your expense... she says that I have forgotten her bread and salt, that she perhaps saved my mother and me from death by hunger, that she fed and watered us and was out of pocket on us for over two and a half years, that she forgave us a debt besides all this. And she would not spare even my mother! And if my poor mother knew what they did to me! God sees!.. Anna Fyodorovna says that in my foolishness I did not know how to keep my happiness, that she herself led me to happiness, that she is not guilty in anything else, and that I myself did not know how, or perhaps did not wish, to stand up for my honour. And who is to blame here, great God! She says that Mr. Bykov is quite right and that one cannot marry every woman who... but why write it! It is cruel to hear such an untruth, Makar Alexeyevich! I do not know what is happening to me now. I tremble, weep, sob; I have been writing you this letter for two hours. I thought that she at least acknowledged her guilt towards me; and now see how she is! For God's sake, do not be alarmed, my friend, my only well-wisher! Fedora exaggerates everything: I am not ill. I only caught a little cold yesterday when I went to Volkovo to have a requiem said for my mother. Why did you not go with me; I asked you so. Ah, my poor, poor mother, if you rose from the grave, if you knew, if you saw what they did to me!..
V. D.
II: I am sending you a few grapes, my darling; for a convalescent they are said to be good, and the doctor recommends them to quench thirst, only for thirst alone. The other day you wanted some little rolls, my dearest; so I am sending them to you now. Have you an appetite, my darling? — that is what matters. However, thank God that it has all passed and ended and that our misfortunes too are coming wholly to an end. Let us give thanks to heaven! As for books, I cannot get any anywhere for the time being. There is a good book here, they say, written in very lofty style; they say it is good, I have not read it myself, but here they praise it much. I have asked for it for myself; they promised to forward it. Only will you read it? You are fastidious with me in this respect; it is hard to suit your taste, I know you, my dear; you surely want nothing but poetry, sighs, amours — well, I shall get verses, I shall get everything; there is a copied notebook there.

I live well. You, my dearest, please do not worry about me. As for what Fedora told you about me, it is all nonsense; tell her she lied, be sure to tell her, the gossip!.. I did not sell my new uniform coat at all. And why, judge for yourself, why sell it? They say forty silver roubles of reward are coming to me, so why sell? Do not worry, my dearest; she is suspicious, Fedora is, she is suspicious. We shall live well, my dear! Only you, my little angel, get well, for God's sake get well, do not distress an old man. Who tells you that I have grown thin? Slander, again slander! I am perfectly healthy and have grown so stout that I am ashamed again myself, fed and content to the full; if only you would get well! Well, goodbye, my little angel; I kiss all your little fingers and remain your eternal, unchanging friend

P. S. Ah, my darling, what is this, you have started writing again in earnest?.. What nonsense are you spouting! And how can I come to you so often, my dearest, how? I ask you. Only by taking advantage of the darkness of night; and now there are almost no nights: it is that season. And I, my dearest, my little angel, hardly left you at all during the whole of your illness, during your delirium; but even then I do not know myself how I managed all that; and afterwards I stopped coming, because they began to be curious and ask questions. Here already, without that, some gossip has been woven. I rely on Teresa; she is not talkative; but all the same, judge for yourself, my dearest, how it will be when they all learn about us? What will they think and what will they say then? So brace your little heart, my dearest, and wait until you are well; and afterwards we shall arrange a rendezvous somewhere outside the house.
III: § June 1
Dear Makar Alexeyevich!

I so want to do something to please you, something agreeable, in return for all your trouble and care on my behalf and for all your affection for me, that I have at last brought myself to the tedious task of rummaging through my chest of drawers and finding my notebook, which I am now sending to you. I began it in the happy time of my life. You have often asked me with curiosity about my former life, about my mother, about Pokrovsky, about my stay with Anna Fyodorovna, and finally about my recent misfortunes, and you have so impatiently wished to read this notebook, in which I took it into my head, God knows why, to set down some moments of my life, that I have no doubt I shall give you great pleasure by sending it. As for me, it made me somehow sad to read it over again. It seems to me that I have grown twice as old since I wrote the last line of these notes. All of it was written at different times. Goodbye, Makar Alexeyevich! I am dreadfully bored now, and I am often tormented by sleeplessness. What a tiresome thing convalescence is!
V. D.
§ I

I was only fourteen when my father died. My childhood was the happiest time of my life. It began not here, but far from here, in the provinces, in the back of beyond. Father was the steward of the vast estate of Prince P—, in the province of T—. We lived in one of the prince's villages, and we lived quietly, unnoticed, happily... I was such a lively little thing; all I did, as I remember, was run about the fields, the groves, the garden, and nobody troubled about me at all. Father was ceaselessly taken up with business, Mother was occupied with the household; I was taught nothing, and I was glad of it. From the very early morning I would run off to the pond, or to the grove, or to the hayfield, or to the reapers — and never mind that the sun was scorching, that I had strayed I did not know where from the village, that I scratched myself on the bushes and tore my dress — I would be scolded at home afterwards, but I did not care.

And I think I should have been so happy if I could have spent my whole life without leaving the country and living in one place. Yet I was forced, while still a child, to leave my native parts. I was only twelve years old when we moved to Petersburg. Ah, how sadly I remember our mournful preparations! How I cried when I said goodbye to everything that was so dear to me. I remember throwing myself on Father's neck and begging him with tears to stay in the country at least a little longer. Father shouted at me, Mother wept; she said it had to be, that business required it. The old Prince P— had died. The heirs dismissed Father from his post. Father had some money out at interest in the hands of private persons in Petersburg. Hoping to mend his circumstances, he thought his own presence here necessary. All this I learned afterwards from Mother. We settled here on the Petersburg Side and lived in the same place until Father's death.

How hard it was for me to get used to the new life! We arrived in Petersburg in the autumn. When we left the country the day was so bright, warm and sunny; the farm work was coming to an end; on the threshing floors huge stacks of grain were already piled up and noisy flocks of birds crowded about; everything was so clear and cheerful, while here, as we entered the city, there was rain, a rotten autumn drizzle, foul weather, slush, and a crowd of new, unfamiliar faces, inhospitable, discontented, angry! Somehow we got settled. I remember how everyone in our house bustled about, all of them busy, setting up a new household. Father was never at home, Mother had not a quiet moment — I was quite forgotten. It was sad for me to get up in the morning after our first night in the new place. Our windows looked out on some yellow fence. The street was constantly muddy. Passers-by were few, and they all wrapped themselves up so tightly, and all of them looked so cold.

And at home we had terrible gloom and boredom all day long. We had almost no relatives or close acquaintances. Father was on bad terms with Anna Fyodorovna. (He owed her something.) People came to see us quite often on business. They usually argued, made a noise, shouted. After every visit Father became so discontented and angry; for hours he would walk from corner to corner, frowning, and not say a word to anyone. Mother did not dare then even to speak to him and kept silent. I would sit down in some corner with a book — quiet and still, not daring to stir.

Three months after our arrival in Petersburg I was sent to a boarding school. How sad it was for me at first among strangers! Everything was so dry and unfriendly — the governesses were such shouters, the girls such mockers, and I such a little savage. Strict, exacting! Hours fixed for everything, a common table, tedious teachers — all this at first tore me to pieces and wore me out. I could not even sleep there. I would cry all night, that long, dull, cold night. In the evenings everyone would be repeating or learning their lessons; I would sit over my dialogues or vocabulary, not daring to move, and all the while I thought of our home corner, of Father, of Mother, of my old nurse, of the nurse's fairy tales... ah, how sad it was! Even the most trifling thing in the house is remembered with pleasure. You think and think: how good it would be at home now! I should be sitting in our little room by the samovar with my own people; it would be so warm, so good, so familiar. How I should embrace Mother now, tightly, tightly, warmly, warmly! You think and think, and then you cry quietly from longing, pressing the tears down in your breast, and the vocabulary will not go into your head. If you have not learned your lesson for the morrow, all night you dream of the teacher, of Madame, of the girls; all night in your sleep you repeat your lessons, and the next day you know nothing. They put you on your knees and give you only one dish. I was so unhappy, so dull. At first all the girls laughed at me, teased me, put me off when I recited my lessons, pinched me when we went in rows to dinner or tea, and complained of me to the governess for nothing at all. But what a paradise it was when Nurse would come for me on Saturday evening. I would embrace my old woman in a transport of joy. She would dress me and wrap me up, she could not keep up with me on the way, and I chattered and chattered to her, telling her everything. I would come home gay and joyful and hug my own people tightly, as if after a ten years' parting. Then would begin the talk, the conversations, the stories; you greet everyone, laugh, shriek with laughter, run about, jump. With Father there would be serious conversations, about the sciences, about our teachers, about the French language, about Lhomond's grammar — and we were all so merry, so content. Even now it is cheering to remember those moments. I tried with all my strength to learn and to please Father. I saw that he was giving me his last farthing while he himself struggled God knows how. With every day he grew gloomier, more discontented, angrier; his character was quite spoiled: his affairs did not go well, and there were debts without end. Mother was afraid even to cry, afraid to say a word, lest she should anger Father; she became so ill; she grew thinner and thinner and began to have a bad cough. I would come home from the school and find only sad faces; Mother quietly weeping, Father angry. Reproaches and rebukes would begin. Father would begin saying that I gave him no joy, no comfort; that they were depriving themselves of their last bit for my sake, and that I still could not speak French; in a word, all the failures, all the misfortunes, everything, everything was taken out on me and on Mother. And how could one torment poor Mother? Looking at her, one's heart broke: her cheeks were sunken, her eyes hollow, her face had such a consumptive colour. I got the worst of it. It always began over trifles, and then God knows where it would end; often I did not even understand what the matter was. What was not laid at my door!.. The French language, and that I was a great fool, and that the headmistress of our school was a negligent, stupid woman; that she did not look after our morals; that Father could not find himself a post to this day, and that Lhomond's grammar was a wretched grammar and Zapolsky's much better; that a great deal of money had been thrown away on me for nothing; that I was evidently insensible, made of stone — in a word, I, poor child, struggled with all my might, repeating dialogues and vocabulary, and was to blame for everything, answerable for everything! And this was not at all because Father did not love me: he doted on Mother and me. But so it was; that was his character.

Cares, vexations and failures wore poor Father out to the last extreme: he became distrustful, bilious; he was often close to despair, began to neglect his health, caught a cold and suddenly fell ill, suffered a short time, and died so suddenly, so unexpectedly, that for several days we were all beside ourselves from the blow. Mother was in a sort of stupor; I was even afraid for her reason. As soon as Father died, the creditors appeared as if out of the earth and descended on us in a crowd. Everything we had we gave up. Our little house on the Petersburg Side, which Father had bought half a year after our move to Petersburg, was sold as well. I do not know how the rest was settled, but we ourselves were left without a roof, without shelter, without food. Mother suffered from a wasting illness, we could not feed ourselves, there was nothing to live on, ruin lay ahead. I had only just turned fourteen. It was then that Anna Fyodorovna visited us. She always says that she is some kind of landowner and that she is some sort of relation of ours. Mother also said that she was a relation, only a very distant one. In Father's lifetime she never came to see us. She appeared with tears in her eyes, said she took a great interest in us; condoled with us on our loss and on our wretched situation, and added that Father himself had been to blame: that he had lived beyond his means, reached too high, and relied too much on his own strength. She showed a wish to become closer to us and proposed that we forget our mutual unpleasantness; and when Mother declared that she had never felt any ill will toward her, she shed tears, took Mother to church and ordered a requiem for "the dear soul" (so she expressed it of Father). After this she solemnly made peace with Mother.

After long preambles and warnings, Anna Fyodorovna, having painted in bright colours our wretched situation, our orphanhood, hopelessness and helplessness, invited us, as she herself put it, to take shelter with her. Mother thanked her, but for a long time could not decide; but since there was nothing else to be done and no other arrangement was possible, she announced at last to Anna Fyodorovna that we accepted her offer with gratitude. I remember as if it were now the morning when we moved from the Petersburg Side to Vasilyevsky Island. The morning was an autumn one, clear, dry, frosty. Mother wept; I was dreadfully sad; my breast was bursting, my soul was oppressed by some inexpressible, terrible longing... It was a hard time.
§ II

At first, while we — that is, Mother and I — had not yet got used to our new home, we both felt somehow uneasy and strange at Anna Fyodorovna's. Anna Fyodorovna lived in her own house, in the Sixth Line. The house had only five clean rooms. In three of them lived Anna Fyodorovna and my cousin Sasha, who was being brought up by her — a child, an orphan, with neither father nor mother. Then in one room lived we, and finally in the last room, next to ours, lodged a poor student, Pokrovsky, a lodger of Anna Fyodorovna's. Anna Fyodorovna lived very well, more richly than one might have supposed; but her fortune was a mystery, as were her occupations. She was always bustling about, always preoccupied, going out and driving out several times a day; but what she did, what she was busy about and why, I could never guess. She had a large and varied acquaintance. Guests were forever coming to her, and God knows what sort of people, always on some business and only for a minute. Mother always used to take me off to our room as soon as the bell rang. Anna Fyodorovna was terribly angry with Mother for this and kept repeating that we were too proud, proud beyond our means, that we should have something to be proud of, and she would not stop for hours. I did not understand then these reproaches of pride; in just the same way it is only now that I have learned, or at least guess, why Mother had been unwilling to live at Anna Fyodorovna's. Anna Fyodorovna was a wicked woman; she tormented us without ceasing. To this day it is a mystery to me why she invited us to her house at all. At first she was quite kind to us — and then she showed her true character completely, as soon as she saw that we were utterly helpless and had nowhere to go. Later she became very kind to me, even somehow coarsely kind, to the point of flattery, but at first I suffered together with Mother. She reproached us at every turn; all she did was talk about her benefactions. To outsiders she introduced us as her poor relations, a helpless widow and orphan, whom she had taken in out of charity, for the love of Christ. At table she followed with her eyes every piece we took, and if we did not eat, the same story began again: that we despised her food; not to take it amiss, that she was glad of what she had; that perhaps we ourselves had been better off. She abused Father at every turn: said he had wanted to be better than others and it had turned out badly; that he had left his wife and daughter to beg; and that if a benevolent relation, a Christian, compassionate soul had not been found, God knows we might have had to rot from hunger in the middle of the street. What did she not say! It was not so much bitter as disgusting to listen to her. Mother wept at every moment; her health grew worse from day to day, she visibly wasted away, and meanwhile we worked from morning till night, got orders for work, sewed, which Anna Fyodorovna did not like at all; she kept saying that she did not keep a fashionable shop in her house. But we had to be clothed, we had to put something aside for unforeseen expenses, we had to have money of our own at all costs. We saved against any emergency, hoping that in time we might move somewhere. But Mother lost the last of her health at work: she grew weaker every day. The illness, like a worm, visibly gnawed at her life and brought her closer to the grave. I saw everything, felt everything, suffered everything; it all happened before my eyes!

Day followed day, and each day was like the one before. We lived quietly, as if not in a city at all. Anna Fyodorovna gradually grew calmer, in proportion as she herself came fully to feel her dominion. No one, however, ever thought of contradicting her. In our room we were separated from her half by a corridor, and next to us, as I have already mentioned, lived Pokrovsky. He taught Sasha French and German, history, geography — all the sciences, as Anna Fyodorovna said,

and for that he received from her lodging and board; Sasha was a very quick girl, though lively and mischievous; she was about thirteen then. Anna Fyodorovna remarked to Mother that it would not be a bad thing if I too began to study, since at boarding school I had been poorly taught. Mother agreed with joy, and for a whole year I studied with Pokrovsky together with Sasha.

Pokrovsky was a poor, very poor young man; his health did not allow him to attend classes regularly, and he was called a student with us only out of habit. He lived modestly, meekly, quietly, so that he could not even be heard from our room. He looked so strange; he walked so awkwardly, bowed so awkwardly, spoke so oddly, that at first I could not look at him without laughing. Sasha played tricks on him incessantly, especially when he gave us our lessons. And on top of that he was of an irritable character, constantly getting angry, flying out at every trifle, shouting at us, complaining of us, and often went off to his room in a temper without finishing the lesson. In his room he sat over his books all day. He had many books, and all of them expensive, rare books. He taught somewhere else too and received some small pay, so that whenever he had a little money, he would at once go off to buy books.

In time I came to know him better, more closely. He was the kindest, most worthy of men, the best of all I have ever happened to meet. Mother respected him greatly. Afterwards he was for me too the best of friends — after Mother, of course.
Continuation

At first I, such a big girl, played pranks together with Sasha, and we would rack our brains for hours over how to tease him and drive him out of patience. He grew angry in a most comical way, and we found it extremely amusing. (I am ashamed even to remember it.) Once we teased him about something almost to tears, and I distinctly heard him whisper: "Wicked children." I was suddenly confused; I felt ashamed and bitter and sorry for him. I remember that I blushed to my ears and, almost in tears, began to beg him to calm himself and not to be offended by our foolish pranks, but he closed his book, did not finish our lesson, and went off to his room. All day I was torn by remorse. The thought that we, children, had by our cruelties brought him to tears was unbearable to me. So we had been waiting for his tears. So we had wanted them; so we had succeeded in driving him to his last patience; so we had forced him, unhappy, poor man, to remember his cruel lot! I did not sleep all night from vexation, from sorrow, from remorse. They say that remorse eases the soul — on the contrary. I do not know how self-love came to mingle with my grief. I did not want him to take me for a child. I was already fifteen then.

From that day I began to torment my imagination, devising a thousand plans for how I might suddenly make Pokrovsky change his opinion of me. But I was at times timid and shy; in my present position I could not decide on anything and confined myself to mere dreams (and God knows what dreams!). I only stopped playing pranks together with Sasha; he stopped being angry with us; but for my self-love that was not enough.

Now I shall say a few words about one of the strangest, most curious and most pitiable people I have ever happened to meet. I speak of him now, in this very place in my notes, because until this very time I had paid almost no attention to him — so interesting did everything that concerned Pokrovsky suddenly become to me!

There used to appear at our house sometimes a little old man, dirty, badly dressed, small, grey-haired, shapeless, clumsy, in a word, strange to the last degree. At first glance one might think that he was somehow ashamed of something, as if he felt shy of himself. For this reason he was always somehow cringing, somehow grimacing; he had such mannerisms and contortions that one could conclude, almost without mistake, that he was not in his right mind. He would come to us and stand in the hall at the glass doors, not daring to enter the house. If any of us passed by — I, or Sasha, or one of the servants whom he knew to be kind to him — he would at once wave, beckon to us, make various signs, and only when you nodded to him and called him — the agreed sign that there was no stranger in the house and that he might come in when he pleased — only then would the old man quietly open the door, smile joyfully, rub his hands with pleasure, and go on tiptoe straight to Pokrovsky's room. This was his father.

Afterwards I learned in detail the whole history of this poor old man. He had once served somewhere, was without the slightest abilities, and held the very lowest, most insignificant post in the service. When his first wife (the mother of the student Pokrovsky) died, he took it into his head to marry a second time, and married a townswoman. With the new wife everything in the house went upside down; nobody had any peace from her; she took everyone in hand. The student Pokrovsky was then still a child, about ten years old. His stepmother hated him. But fate favoured little Pokrovsky. The landowner Bykov, who knew the clerk Pokrovsky and had once been his benefactor, took the child under his protection and placed him in some school. He took an interest in him because he had known his late mother, who, while still a girl, had been befriended by Anna Fyodorovna and given in marriage by her to the clerk Pokrovsky. Mr. Bykov, a friend and close acquaintance of Anna Fyodorovna's, moved by generosity, gave five thousand roubles as the bride's dowry. Where this money went is unknown. So Anna Fyodorovna told me all this; the student Pokrovsky himself never liked to speak of his family circumstances. They say his mother was very pretty, and it seems strange to me why she made so unfortunate a marriage, to such an insignificant man... She died while still young, some four years after her marriage.

From the school young Pokrovsky went to some gymnasium and then to the university. Mr. Bykov, who came very often to Petersburg, did not leave him without his protection here either. On account of his poor health Pokrovsky could not continue his studies at the university. Mr. Bykov introduced him to Anna Fyodorovna, recommended him himself, and in this way young Pokrovsky was taken in for his board, on the understanding that he should teach Sasha whatever was required.

As for old Pokrovsky, from grief at his wife's cruelties he gave himself up to the worst of vices and was almost always in a state of drunkenness. His wife beat him, sent him to live in the kitchen, and brought him to such a pass that he finally grew used to blows and bad treatment and did not complain. He was not a very old man, but through his bad habits he had almost lost his mind. The only sign of human, noble feeling in him was his unbounded love for his son. They said that young Pokrovsky was as like his late mother as two drops of water. Could it be that memories of his former good wife gave birth in the heart of the ruined old man to such a boundless love for him? The old man could talk of nothing but his son and regularly visited him twice a week. He did not dare to come more often, because young Pokrovsky could not bear his father's visits. Of all his faults, the first and most important, beyond question, was disrespect for his father. Yet the old man too was at times the most tiresome creature in the world. First, he was terribly curious; second, with conversations and questions, the emptiest and most senseless, he continually kept his son from his work; and finally he sometimes came in a drunken state. The son little by little weaned the old man from his vices, from his curiosity and from his incessant chatter, and at last brought him to the point where he listened to him in everything as to an oracle and did not dare to open his mouth without his permission.

The poor old man could not wonder at and rejoice enough in his Petenka (so he called his son). When he came to visit him, he almost always had an anxious, timid air, probably from uncertainty about how his son would receive him; he usually could not make up his mind to go in for a long time, and if I happened to be there, he would question me for twenty minutes or so — how was Petenka? was he well? in what particular frame of mind, and was he not busy with something important? What exactly was he doing? Was he writing, or occupied with some reflections? When I had encouraged and calmed him sufficiently, the old man would at last venture in and open the door very softly, very carefully, thrust in his head first, and if he saw that his son was not angry and nodded to him, would quietly enter the room, take off his little overcoat and his hat, which was always crumpled, full of holes, with the brim torn off — hang everything on a hook, doing it all softly, noiselessly; then he would carefully sit down somewhere on a chair and never take his eyes from his son, catching all his movements, wishing to guess the mood of his Petenka. If the son was the least bit out of sorts and the old man noticed it, he would at once get up from his place and explain "that, you see, Petenka, I am only here for a minute. I walked a long way, was passing by and stopped in to rest." And then silently, meekly, he would take his little coat and little hat, softly open the door again and go away, smiling with an effort in order to keep in his soul the grief that had welled up and not show it to his son.

But when the son received his father well, the old man was beside himself with joy. Pleasure shone in his face, in his gestures, in his movements. If the son spoke to him, the old man always rose a little from his chair and answered quietly, obsequiously, almost with reverence, and always trying to use the choicest, that is, the most ridiculous expressions. But the gift of speech was not given to him: he would always become confused and timid, so that he did not know what to do with his hands or with himself, and afterwards for a long time would whisper his answer over to himself, as if wishing to correct it. And if he managed to answer well, the old man would preen himself, straighten his waistcoat, his cravat, his coat, and assume an air of dignity. And sometimes he grew so bold, he carried his daring so far, that he would quietly get up from his chair, go to the shelf of books, take some book, and even read something right there, whatever the book might be. All this he did with an air of feigned indifference and coolness, as if he could always make himself at home like this with his son's books, as if his son's kindness were no marvel to him. But once I happened to see how the poor fellow was frightened when Pokrovsky asked him not to touch the books. He became confused, hurried, put the book back upside down, then wanted to set it right, turned it over and put it with the edges outward, smiled, blushed, and did not know how to make up for his crime. Pokrovsky by his advice weaned the old man little by little from his bad habits, and as soon as he saw him sober three times in a row, he gave him on parting, at the first visit, a quarter-rouble or a half-rouble or more. Sometimes he bought him boots, a cravat or a waistcoat. And then the old man in his new things was as proud as a cock. Sometimes he came in to see us. He brought Sasha and me gingerbread cocks and apples, and would always talk with us about Petenka. He asked us to study attentively, to obey, said that Petenka was a good son, a model son, and on top of that a learned son. Here he would wink at us so comically with his left eye, make such amusing faces, that we could not help laughing and laughed at him heartily. Mother liked him very much. But the old man hated Anna Fyodorovna, although in front of her he was as quiet as water and lower than the grass.

Soon I stopped studying with Pokrovsky. He still considered me a child, a lively little girl, on a level with Sasha. This hurt me very much, because I was trying with all my strength to make up for my former behaviour. But I was not noticed. This irritated me more and more. I almost never spoke with Pokrovsky outside lessons, and indeed could not speak. I blushed, grew confused, and then cried somewhere in a corner from vexation.

I do not know how it would all have ended if one strange circumstance had not helped to bring us together. One evening, when Mother was sitting with Anna Fyodorovna, I quietly went into Pokrovsky's room. I knew he was not at home, and truly I do not know why it came into my head to go in. Until then I had never even looked in, although we had lived side by side for more than a year. This time my heart beat so hard, so hard, that it seemed as if it would leap out of my breast. I looked around with a kind of special curiosity. Pokrovsky's room was very poorly furnished; there was little order. Five long shelves of books were nailed to the walls. On the table and on the chairs lay papers. Books and papers! A strange thought visited me, and with it a sort of disagreeable feeling of vexation took possession of me. It seemed to me that my friendship, my loving heart, was not enough for him. He was learned, and I was stupid and knew nothing, had read nothing, not a single book... Here I looked enviously at the long shelves that were bending under their books. Vexation, anguish, a sort of fury seized me. I wanted to, and on the spot decided to, read his books, every one of them, and as soon as possible. I do not know, perhaps I thought that, having learned everything that he knew, I should be worthier of his friendship. I rushed to the first shelf; without thinking, without stopping, I seized the first dusty old volume that came to hand and, blushing, turning pale, trembling with agitation and fear, carried the stolen book off to my room, resolved to read it at night, by the night-light, when Mother was asleep.
Continuation

But how vexed I was when, having come to our room, I hurriedly opened the book and saw some old, half-rotten Latin work, all eaten by worms. I went back without losing time. I had only just wanted to put the book on the shelf when I heard a noise in the corridor and someone's footsteps close by. I hurried, I hastened, but the wretched book was so tightly placed in the row that when I took out one, all the others parted of themselves and pressed together so that there was no more room for their former comrade. I had not the strength to squeeze the book in. Yet I pushed the books as hard as I could. The rusty nail on which the shelf was fastened, and which seemed to have been waiting on purpose for this moment to break — broke. The shelf flew down at one end. The books poured noisily onto the floor. The door opened, and Pokrovsky came into the room.

I must remark that he could not bear anyone making free in his domain. Woe to him who touched his books! Judge then of my horror when books, small, large, of every possible format, size and thickness, rushed from the shelf, flew, bounced under the table, under the chairs, all over the room. I wanted to run, but it was too late. "It is over, I thought, it is over! I am lost, ruined! I am playing pranks, frolicking like a ten-year-old child; I am a stupid girl! I am a great fool!!" Pokrovsky was terribly angry. "Well, that was all that was wanting! — he cried. — Are you not ashamed to play such tricks!.. Will you ever be quiet?" And he rushed to pick up the books himself. I bent down to help him. "No need, no need, — he cried. — You would do better not to go where you are not asked." But then, somewhat softened by my submissive movement, he went on more quietly, in his recent teacherly tone, making use of his recent right as a teacher: "Well, when will you grow sensible, when will you think? Just look at yourself, you are not a child, not a little girl, you are already fifteen!" And here, probably wishing to verify whether it was true that I was no longer little, he glanced at me and blushed to his ears. I did not understand; I stood before him and looked at him with all my eyes in amazement. He rose, came up to me with an embarrassed air, became terribly confused, began to say something, apologising, it seemed, perhaps, for only now noticing that I was such a big girl. At last I understood. I do not remember what happened to me then; I was confused, lost, blushed even more than Pokrovsky, covered my face with my hands and ran out of the room.

I did not know what to do, where to hide from shame. The mere fact that he had found me in his room! For three whole days I could not look at him. I blushed to tears. The strangest thoughts, absurd thoughts, whirled in my head. One of them, the wildest, was that I wanted to go to him, have it out with him, confess everything, tell him everything frankly, and assure him that I had acted not as a silly girl but with a good intention. I had quite decided to go, but, thank God, my courage failed me. I can imagine what I should have done! Even now I am ashamed to remember all this.

A few days later Mother suddenly became dangerously ill. She had not risen from her bed for two days and on the third night was in a fever and delirious. I had already gone one night without sleep, tending Mother, sitting by her bed, bringing her drink and giving her medicine at the appointed hours. On the second night I was utterly worn out. At times sleep overcame me, my eyes swam green, my head went round, and every minute I was ready to fall from exhaustion, but Mother's faint moans woke me, I started, awoke for a moment, and then drowsiness overcame me again. I was in torment. I do not know — I cannot recall — but some terrible dream, some dreadful vision visited my disordered head in that agonising moment of the struggle between sleep and waking. I awoke in terror. The room was dark, the night-light was dying, bands of light now suddenly flooded the whole room, now barely flickered on the wall, now vanished altogether. I felt afraid for some reason, a kind of horror came over me; my imagination was stirred up by the terrible dream; anguish gripped my heart... I jumped up from my chair and involuntarily cried out from some tormenting, fearfully oppressive feeling. At that moment the door opened, and Pokrovsky came into our room.

I remember only that I came to myself in his arms. He carefully sat me down in an armchair, gave me a glass of water, and showered me with questions. I do not remember what I answered him. "You are ill, you are very ill yourself, — he said, taking me by the hand, — you have a fever, you are ruining yourself, you do not spare your health; calm yourself, lie down, go to sleep. I will wake you in two hours, calm yourself a little... Lie down, do lie down!" — he went on, not letting me utter a single word in objection. Weariness took from me my last strength; my eyes closed from weakness. I lay back in the armchair, resolved to sleep only half an hour, and slept till morning. Pokrovsky woke me only when it was time to give Mother her medicine.

The next day, when, having rested a little during the day, I prepared to sit again in the armchair by Mother's bed, firmly resolved this time not to fall asleep, Pokrovsky knocked at our door at about eleven o'clock. I opened. "It is dull for you to sit alone, — he said to me, — here is a book; take it; it will not be so dull." I took it; I do not remember what book it was; I hardly looked into it then, although I did not sleep all night. A strange inner excitement did not let me sleep; I could not stay in one place; several times I got up from the armchair and began to walk about the room. A sort of inner contentment spread through my whole being. I was so glad of Pokrovsky's attention. I was proud of his anxiety and care for me. I thought and dreamed all night. Pokrovsky did not come in again; and I knew he would not come, and I made guesses about the next evening.

The following evening, when everyone in the house had gone to bed, Pokrovsky opened his door and began to talk to me, standing on the threshold of his room. I do not now remember a single word of what we said to each other then; I remember only that I was shy, confused, vexed with myself, and waited impatiently for the end of the conversation, although I myself wished for it with all my strength, dreamed of it all day and composed my questions and answers... From that evening the first knot of our friendship was tied. Throughout Mother's illness we spent several hours together every night. Little by little I overcame my shyness, though after each of our conversations there was still something to be vexed with myself about. Yet I saw with secret joy and proud pleasure that for my sake he forgot his intolerable books. By chance, in jest, the talk once turned to the fall of the books from the shelf. It was a strange moment; I was somehow too frank and open-hearted; warmth and a strange rapture carried me away, and I confessed everything to him... that I wanted to learn, to know something, that it vexed me to be taken for a girl, a child... I repeat that I was in a very strange frame of mind; my heart was soft, there were tears in my eyes — I hid nothing and told everything, everything — about my friendship for him, about my wish to love him, to live with him at one in heart, to comfort him, to soothe him. He looked at me somehow strangely, with confusion, with amazement, and said not a word to me. I suddenly felt terribly hurt and sad. It seemed to me that he did not understand me, that perhaps he was laughing at me. I suddenly burst into tears like a child, sobbed, could not hold myself back; as if I were in some kind of fit. He seized my hands, kissed them, pressed them to his breast, entreated me, comforted me; he was deeply moved; I do not remember what he said to me, but I both wept and laughed and wept again, blushed, could not utter a word for joy. Yet, in spite of my agitation, I noticed that in Pokrovsky there still remained some embarrassment and constraint. It seemed he could not marvel enough at my transport, my rapture, so sudden, hot, ardent a friendship. Perhaps at first he was only curious; afterwards his hesitation vanished, and with a feeling as simple and direct as mine, he accepted my attachment to him, my friendly words, my attention, and answered all this with the same attention, as friendly and kind, as a sincere friend of mine, as my own brother. My heart was so warm, so happy!.. I did not hide, did not conceal anything; he saw it all, and with every day became more and more attached to me.

And truly I do not remember what we did not talk over together in those painful and yet sweet hours of our meetings, at night, by the trembling light of the little lamp and almost at the very bedside of my poor sick mother?.. About everything that came into our minds, that tore itself from our hearts, that begged to be spoken — and we were almost happy... Oh, it was a sad and a joyful time — both together; and it is both sad and joyful for me now to remember it. Memories, whether joyful or bitter, are always painful; at least so it is with me; but this pain too is sweet. And when the heart feels heavy, hurt, weary, sad, then memories refresh and revive it, as drops of dew on a damp evening, after a hot day, refresh and revive a poor, withered flower scorched by the heat of the day.

Mother was recovering, but I still went on sitting at her bedside at night. Pokrovsky often gave me books; I read, at first so as not to fall asleep, then more attentively, then greedily; a great deal that was new, until then unknown and unfamiliar to me, was suddenly opened before me. New thoughts, new impressions poured all at once in an abundant flood into my heart. And the more agitation, the more confusion and labour it cost me to take in these new impressions, the dearer they were to me, the more sweetly they shook my whole soul. All at once, suddenly, they crowded into my heart, giving it no rest. Some strange chaos began to disturb my whole being. But this spiritual violence could not, and had not the power to, unsettle me completely. I was too much of a dreamer, and that saved me.

When Mother's illness ended, our evening meetings and long conversations ceased; we sometimes managed to exchange words, often empty and of little meaning, but I loved to give everything its own meaning, its own special, understood value. My life was full, I was happy, quietly, peacefully happy. So several weeks passed...

One day old Pokrovsky came to see us. He chatted with us for a long time, was unusually merry, brisk, talkative; laughed, made jokes in his own way, and finally solved the riddle of his delight and announced to us that in exactly a week it would be Petenka's birthday and that on this occasion he would certainly come to his son; that he would put on a new waistcoat and that his wife had promised to buy him new boots. In a word, the old man was perfectly happy and chattered about everything that came into his head.

His birthday! This birthday gave me no peace by day or by night. I resolved without fail to remind Pokrovsky of my friendship and to give him something. But what? At last I thought of giving him books. I knew that he wanted to have the complete works of Pushkin, in the latest edition, and I decided to buy Pushkin. I had about thirty roubles of my own, earned by needlework. This money was put aside for a new dress. I at once sent our cook, the old woman Matryona, to find out what the whole of Pushkin cost. Trouble! The price of all eleven volumes, adding the cost of binding, was at least sixty roubles. Where to get the money? I thought and thought and did not know what to decide. I did not want to ask Mother. Of course Mother would certainly have helped me; but then everyone in the house would have learned of our gift; and besides, this gift would have turned into thanks, into payment for a whole year of Pokrovsky's labours. I wanted to give it alone, secretly from everyone. And for his labours with me I wanted to remain forever indebted to him without any payment whatever except my friendship. At last I thought of a way out of the difficulty.
Conclusion

I knew that at the second-hand booksellers' in the Gostiny Dvor one could sometimes buy a book for half the price if only one bargained, often a little-used and almost perfectly new one. I made up my mind to go to the Gostiny Dvor without fail. And so it happened; the very next day there came up some errand both for us and for Anna Fyodorovna. Mother felt unwell, Anna Fyodorovna very conveniently grew lazy, so that all the commissions had to be entrusted to me, and I set out together with Matryona.

To my good fortune I very soon found Pushkin, in a very handsome binding. I began to bargain. At first they asked more than in the shops; but then, though not without difficulty, going away several times, I brought the merchant to the point where he lowered his price and limited his demand to ten silver roubles. How cheerful I was, bargaining!.. Poor Matryona did not understand what was happening to me and why I had taken it into my head to buy so many books. But horror! All my capital was thirty roubles in paper money, and the merchant would on no account agree to take less. At last I began to plead, begged and begged him, and at last prevailed. He came down, but only two and a half roubles, and swore that even this reduction he made only for my sake, because I was such a nice young lady, and that for anyone else he would never have given way. Two and a half roubles were wanting! I was ready to cry from vexation. But a most unexpected circumstance helped me in my trouble.

Not far from me, at another table of books, I saw old Pokrovsky. Four or five booksellers had crowded around him; they had confused him completely and hustled him altogether. Each of them offered him his goods, and what did they not offer him, and what did he not want to buy! The poor old man stood in the midst of them as if beaten down, and did not know what to take up of all that was offered him. I went up to him and asked what he was doing here. The old man was very glad to see me; he loved me beyond measure, perhaps no less than Petenka. "Why, I am buying books, Varvara Alexeyevna, — he answered me, — I am buying books for Petenka. His birthday will soon be here, and he likes books, so I am buying them for him..." The old man always expressed himself comically, and now on top of that he was in the most dreadful confusion. Whatever he asked the price of was a silver rouble, two roubles, three silver roubles; he did not even ask the price of the big books, but only looked at them enviously, ran his fingers over the leaves, turned them in his hands and put them back in their place. "No, no, this is dear, — he said under his breath, — but perhaps something from over here," — and then he began to turn over thin little pamphlets, songbooks, almanacs; these were all very cheap. "But why are you buying all these, — I asked him, — they are all terrible trash." — "Oh, no, — he answered, — no, just look what good little books there are here; very, very good little books there are!" And the last words he drew out in such a plaintive sing-song that it seemed to me he was ready to cry from vexation that good books were dear, and that at any moment a tear would drop from his pale cheeks onto his red nose. I asked whether he had much money. "Why, here, — and the poor fellow took out all his money, wrapped in a greasy piece of newspaper, — here is a half-rouble, a twenty-kopeck piece, about twenty kopecks in copper." I at once dragged him to my bookseller. "Here are eleven whole books that cost only thirty-two roubles and a half; I have thirty; add two and a half, and we shall buy all these books and give them together." The old man went wild with joy, poured out all his money, and the bookseller loaded him with our whole common library. My old man stuffed books into all his pockets, gathered them up in both hands, under his arms, and carried it all off to his place, giving me his word to bring all the books to me secretly the next day.

The next day the old man came to his son, sat with him for an hour or so as usual, then came in to us and sat down beside me with an irresistibly comical air of mystery. At first, with a smile, rubbing his hands with proud pleasure at possessing some secret, he announced to me that the books had all been carried over to us quite unnoticed and were standing in a corner of the kitchen under Matryona's protection.
