Then the conversation naturally turned to the expected holiday; then the old man expanded on how we should give our present, and the deeper he went into his subject, the more he spoke of it, the more noticeable it became to me that he had something on his mind which he could not, dared not, was even afraid to express. I went on waiting and kept silent. The secret joy, the secret pleasure which I had so easily read until now in his strange manners, his grimacing, his winking with his left eye, vanished. He grew every moment more uneasy and sad; at last he could bear it no longer.

— Listen, — he began timidly, in an undertone, — listen, Varvara Alexeyevna... do you know what, Varvara Alexeyevna?.. — The old man was in dreadful confusion. — You see: when his birthday comes, you take ten books and give them to him yourself, that is, from yourself, on your own part; and I will then take the one eleventh and also give it from myself, that is, properly on my own part. So, you see — you will have something to give, and I will have something to give; we shall both have something to give. — Here the old man became confused and fell silent. I looked at him; he awaited my verdict with timid expectation. "But why do you want us not to give together, Zakhar Petrovich?" — "Why, Varvara Alexeyevna, it is just so... you see, it is, that is..." — in a word, the old man became confused, blushed, stuck fast in his sentence and could not budge.

— You see, — he explained at last. — I, Varvara Alexeyevna, am naughty at times... that is, I wish to tell you that I am almost always naughty, and always naughty... I keep to what is not good... that is, you know, when it is so cold outside, also when there are sometimes various unpleasantnesses, or somehow one feels sad, or something unpleasant happens, then I cannot hold back at times, and I go naughty, and drink sometimes too much. Petrusha dislikes this very much. He, you see, Varvara Alexeyevna, gets angry, scolds me and reads me various morals. So now I should like to prove to him with my gift that I am reforming and beginning to behave well. That I saved up to buy a book, saved a long time, because I almost never have any money, except that Petrusha sometimes gives me some. He knows that. Consequently he will see the use of my money and will know that I do it all for him alone.

I felt terribly sorry for the old man. I did not think long. The old man looked at me with anxiety. "But listen, Zakhar Petrovich, — I said, — you give them all to him!" — "How all? that is, all the books?.." — "Why yes, all the books." — "And from myself?" — "From yourself." — "From myself alone? that is, in my own name?" — "Why yes, in your own name..." I thought I explained very clearly, but the old man could not understand me for a very long time.

"Why yes, — he said, thinking, — yes! that would be very good, that would be most excellent, but how about you, Varvara Alexeyevna?" — "Well, I shall give nothing." — "What! — cried the old man, almost frightened, — so you will give Petenka nothing, so you do not want to give him anything?" The old man was frightened; at that moment he seemed ready to give up his proposal so that I too might give his son something. He was a good soul, this old man! I assured him that I should gladly give something, but only that I did not want to take the pleasure away from him. "If your son is pleased, — I added, — and you are glad, then I shall be glad too, because secretly, in my heart, I shall feel as if I had really given it." At this the old man was completely reassured. He stayed with us two hours more, but all this time could not sit still; he got up, fussed, made a noise, romped with Sasha, kissed me by stealth, pinched my hand, and made faces quietly at Anna Fyodorovna. Anna Fyodorovna finally drove him out of the house. In a word, the old man was so carried away with delight as perhaps had never happened to him before.

On the festive day he appeared at exactly eleven o'clock, straight from church, in a coat decently darned, and really in a new waistcoat and new boots. In both hands he had a bundle of books. We were all sitting then in the drawing room at Anna Fyodorovna's drinking coffee (it was Sunday). The old man began, it seems, by saying that Pushkin was a very good poet; then, stumbling and getting muddled, he passed suddenly to the point that one must behave well and that if a man does not behave well, it means that he is naughty; that bad inclinations ruin and destroy a man; he even enumerated several pernicious examples of intemperance and concluded by saying that for some time he had completely reformed and that now he was conducting himself exemplarily well. That he had felt the justice of his son's admonitions even before, that he had felt all this for a long time and laid it all up in his heart, but now had begun to restrain himself in deed as well. In proof of which he was giving the books, bought with money he had saved over a long time.

I could not keep from tears and laughter as I listened to the poor old man; so he knew how to tell a lie when need arose! The books were carried into Pokrovsky's room and put on the shelf. Pokrovsky guessed the truth at once. The old man was invited to dinner. That day we were all so merry. After dinner we played forfeits and cards; Sasha frolicked, and I kept up with her. Pokrovsky was attentive to me and kept seeking an opportunity to speak with me alone, but I would not let him. It was the best day in the whole four years of my life.

And now there will be only sad, heavy memories; the tale of my black days begins. That is perhaps why my pen begins to move more slowly and seems to refuse to write further. That is perhaps why I went over with such ardour and such love in my memory the smallest details of my little life in my happy days. Those days were so short; they were replaced by grief, black grief, which God alone knows when will end.
My misfortunes began with the illness and death of Pokrovsky.

He fell ill two months after the last events described here by me. During these two months he tirelessly busied himself about the means of living, for until now he had not yet had a settled position. Like all consumptives, he did not part to his last minute with the hope of living a very long time. A place as a teacher was coming up for him somewhere; but he had an aversion to that trade. To serve in some government office he could not because of his ill health. Besides, one would have had to wait a long time for the first salary. In short, Pokrovsky saw only failures everywhere; his character was spoiled. His health was giving way; he did not notice it. Autumn came on. Every day he went out in his light little overcoat to see about his affairs, to ask and beg for a place somewhere — which tormented him inwardly; he wetted his feet, got soaked in the rain, and at last took to his bed, from which he never rose again... He died in the depth of autumn, at the end of the month of October.

I scarcely left his room during the whole of his illness, nursed him and waited on him. Often I did not sleep whole nights. He was rarely conscious; he was often delirious; he spoke God knows of what: of his place, of his books, of me, of his father... and it was then that I heard a great deal about his circumstances that I had not known before and had not even guessed. In the first period of his illness everyone in our house looked at me somehow strangely; Anna Fyodorovna shook her head. But I looked everyone straight in the eye, and they no longer condemned me for my concern for Pokrovsky — at least Mother did not.

Sometimes Pokrovsky recognised me, but this was rare. He was almost all the time unconscious. Sometimes whole nights he talked with someone for a long, long time, in indistinct dark words, and his hoarse voice echoed dully in his narrow room, as in a coffin; I felt afraid then. On the last night especially he was like one frenzied; he suffered terribly, was racked with anguish; his groans tore my soul. Everyone in the house was in a kind of fright. Anna Fyodorovna kept praying that God might take him as soon as possible. A doctor was called. The doctor said that the patient would certainly die by morning.

Old Pokrovsky spent the whole night in the corridor, at the very door of his son's room; they had spread some matting for him there. He kept coming into the room; it was terrible to look at him. He was so crushed by grief that he seemed quite insensible and senseless. His head shook with fear. He trembled all over and kept whispering something to himself, reasoning about something with himself. It seemed to me that he would go out of his mind with grief.

Before dawn the old man, exhausted by the pain of his soul, fell asleep on his matting like one dead. At eight o'clock his son began to die; I woke the father. Pokrovsky was in full consciousness and took leave of all of us. Strange! I could not weep; but my soul was torn to pieces.

But most of all his last moments tormented and racked me. He kept asking for something for a long, long time with his stiffening tongue, and I could make out nothing of his words. My heart was breaking with pain! For a whole hour he was restless, grieving over something, trying to make some sign with his chilled hands, and then he would begin again to ask plaintively, in a hoarse, dull voice; but his words were only incoherent sounds, and again I could understand nothing. I brought all our people to him, gave him drink; but he sadly shook his head. At last I understood what he wanted. He was asking me to lift the curtain at the window and open the shutters. He surely wished to look for the last time at the day, at God's light, at the sun. I drew back the curtain; but the beginning day was mournful and sad, like the fading poor life of the dying man. There was no sun. Clouds covered the sky with a misty veil; it was so rainy, so gloomy, so sad. A fine rain beat on the panes and washed them with streams of cold, dirty water; it was dim and dark. The rays of the pale day barely entered the room and scarcely contended with the trembling light of the lamp lit before the icon. The dying man looked at me, very, very sadly, and shook his head. A minute later he died.

Anna Fyodorovna herself arranged the funeral. A coffin was bought, quite plain, and a carter was hired. To cover the expenses Anna Fyodorovna seized all the books and all the belongings of the deceased. The old man argued with her, made a noise, took from her as many books as he could, stuffed all his pockets with them, put them in his hat, wherever he could, carried them about with him all three days and did not part with them even when it was time to go to church. All these days he was like one without memory, like one stupefied, and with a kind of strange solicitude kept fussing about the coffin: now straightening the wreath on the dead man, now lighting and taking away the candles. It was plain that his thoughts could not settle properly on anything. Neither Mother nor Anna Fyodorovna was in church at the funeral service. Mother was ill, and Anna Fyodorovna had quite made ready, but quarrelled with old Pokrovsky and stayed behind. Only I was there, and the old man. During the service a kind of fear came over me — as if a foreboding of the future. I could scarcely stand it in the church. At last the coffin was closed, nailed down, set on a cart and driven away. I accompanied it only to the end of the street. The carter went off at a trot. The old man ran after it and wept aloud; his weeping shook and broke with his running. The poor fellow lost his hat and did not stop to pick it up. His head was wet with rain; a wind was rising; the sleet lashed and stung his face. The old man, it seemed, did not feel the bad weather and with tears ran from one side of the cart to the other. The skirts of his shabby coat fluttered in the wind like wings. From all his pockets books stuck out; in his hands was some huge book which he held tightly. Passers-by took off their caps and crossed themselves. Some stopped and wondered at the poor old man. The books kept falling out of his pockets into the mud. He was stopped, shown his loss; he picked them up and again set off in pursuit of the coffin. At the corner of the street some beggar woman attached herself to him to follow the coffin. The cart turned the corner at last and vanished from my sight. I went home. In terrible anguish I threw myself on Mother's breast. I clasped her tightly, tightly in my arms, kissed her and sobbed aloud, pressing fearfully against her, as if trying to hold in my embrace my last friend and not give her up to death... But death already stood over poor Mother!
IV: § June 11

How grateful I am to you for yesterday's walk to the islands, Makar Alexeyevich! How fresh it is there, how lovely, and what greenery! It is so long since I have seen anything green; when I was ill, it always seemed to me that I must die, that I should certainly die; judge, then, what I must have felt yesterday! Please do not be angry with me for being so sad yesterday; I felt very well, very light, but in my very best moments I am always sad for some reason. As for my crying, that is nothing; I do not know myself why I am always crying. I feel things painfully, irritably; my impressions are morbid. The cloudless, pale sky, the sunset, the evening stillness — all this, I do not know — but somehow I was disposed yesterday to take every impression heavily and painfully, so that my heart overflowed and my soul asked for tears. But why am I writing all this to you? It is hard for the heart to say such things, and harder still to tell them over. But perhaps you will understand me. Both sadness and laughter! What a kind man you are, really, Makar Alexeyevich! Yesterday you kept looking me straight in the eyes, to read in them what I felt, and you took such delight in my delight. Whether it was a little bush, or an avenue, or a strip of water — there you were; you stood before me, preening yourself and peering into my eyes, just as if you were showing me your own estates.

This proves that you have a kind heart, Makar Alexeyevich. That is why I love you. Well, goodbye. I am ill again today; yesterday I got my feet wet and caught a cold; Fedora is ill too, with something or other, so that we are both poorly now. Do not forget me, and come to see us often.
Yours,
V. D.
§ June 12
My dear Varvara Alexeyevna!

And I, my dearest, thought you would describe yesterday to me in real poetry, and what came out was only one plain little sheet. I say this because, although you wrote me little in your sheet, you described it all extraordinarily well and sweetly. Nature, and the various rural pictures, and everything else about your feelings — in a word, you described it all very well. Whereas I have no talent at all. I could scribble ten pages, and nothing comes of it; I cannot describe a thing. I have tried already. You write to me, my dear one, that I am a kind man, without malice, incapable of harming my neighbour, and one who understands the goodness of the Lord shown in nature, and you bestow various other praises on me. All this is true, my dearest, all this is perfectly true; I really am just as you say, and I know it myself; but when I read what you write, my heart is moved in spite of me, and then all sorts of heavy reflections come. So now listen to me, my dearest, and I will tell you something, my dear one.

I will begin by saying that I was only seventeen years old when I came into the service, and it will soon be thirty years since I began my career. Well, I cannot deny that I have worn out a good many uniform coats; I have grown to manhood, grown wiser, seen people; I have lived, I may say that I have lived in this world, so much so that they once even wished to put me forward for a decoration. Perhaps you do not believe it, but really, I am not lying to you. And what of it, my dearest — there turned out to be spiteful people over all this! And let me tell you, my dear one, that although I am an ignorant man, a stupid man, perhaps, my heart is just the same as anyone else's. So do you know, Varenka, what a spiteful man did to me? It is shameful to say what he did; ask me why he did it? Because I am meek, because I am quiet, because I am kind! I did not suit their taste, and so it started against me. At first it began with, "Well, Makar Alexeyevich, this and that"; and then it became, "As for Makar Alexeyevich, do not even ask"; and now they have concluded with, "Of course, it is Makar Alexeyevich, naturally!" There, my dearest, you see how it went: everything on Makar Alexeyevich; all they have managed to do is to make a proverb of Makar Alexeyevich in our whole department. And that is not all: they made a proverb of me, and almost a term of abuse, and they got at my boots, my uniform, my hair, my figure: nothing is to their liking, everything must be altered! And all this has been repeated from time immemorial, every blessed day. I am used to it, because I get used to everything, because I am a meek man, because I am a small man; but still, what is it all for? What harm have I done to anyone? Did I snatch someone's rank? Did I blacken anyone before the higher-ups? Did I beg for a reward I should not have had? Was I cooking up some intrigue? Why, it is a sin even to think such a thing, my dearest! Well, what would I do with all that? Just consider, my dear one, whether I have abilities sufficient for cunning and ambition! Then why such misfortunes upon me, Lord forgive me? You find me a worthy man, and you are incomparably better than all of them, my dearest. For what is the greatest civic virtue? Yevstafy Ivanovich remarked the other day in private conversation that the most important civic virtue is knowing how to make money. He said it as a joke (I know it was a joke), but the moral is that one must not be a burden to anyone; and I am a burden to no one! I have my own crust of bread; true, it is a plain crust of bread, at times even a stale one; but it is there, earned by labour, and used lawfully and irreproachably. Well, what can one do! I know myself that I do little by copying; but all the same I am proud of it: I work, I sweat. Well, what is there in it, really, that I copy! Is it a sin to copy? "He copies, you see!" "That rat of a clerk copies, you see!" But what is dishonourable in that? The handwriting is so clear and good, pleasant to look at, and his Excellency is pleased; I copy the most important papers for him. Well, I have no style, I know that myself, the accursed thing; that is why I did not get on in the service,

and even to you now, my dear one, I write simply, without frills, just as the thought lies on my heart... I know all this; but still, if everyone took to composing, who would copy? That is the question I put, and I beg you to answer it, my dearest. Well, so I am now aware that I am needed, that I am indispensable, and that there is no reason to confuse a man with nonsense. Very well, let him be a rat, if they have found a likeness! But this rat is needed, this rat brings benefit, they hold on to this rat, this rat gets a reward — that is the kind of rat he is! However, enough of this matter, my dear one; I did not mean to speak of that at all, but I got a little heated. Still, it is pleasant now and then to do oneself justice. Goodbye, my dear one, my dear, my good little comforter! I will come, I will certainly come to see you, to look in on you, my bright one. And meanwhile do not be dull. I will bring you a book. Well, goodbye then, Varenka.
Your heartfelt well-wisher,
Makar Devushkin.
§ June 20
Dear Sir, Makar Alexeyevich!

I am writing to you in haste, in a hurry, finishing my work by the deadline. You see, here is the matter: a good purchase can be made. Fedora says that an acquaintance of hers is selling a uniform coat, quite brand new, with trousers, a waistcoat and a cap, and they say it is all very cheap; so you should buy it. You are not in need now, and you have money; you say yourself that you have. Come, please, do not be miserly; all this is necessary. Just look at yourself, in what old clothes you go about. It is a disgrace! All in patches. You have nothing new, I know it, though you assure me that you have. God knows where you disposed of it. So listen to me, please, and buy it. Do it for me; if you love me, buy it.

You sent me linen as a gift; but listen, Makar Alexeyevich, you are ruining yourself. It is no joke, how much you have spent on me — it is dreadful how much money! Ah, how you love to squander! I do not need it; all this was quite superfluous. I know, I am sure, that you love me; really, there is no need to remind me of it by presents; and it is hard for me to accept them from you; I know what they cost you. Once and for all, enough; do you hear? I ask you, I beg you. You ask me, Makar Alexeyevich, to send the continuation of my notes; you wish me to finish them. I do not know how I managed to write even what I have written! But I have not the strength now to speak of my past; I do not even wish to think of it; these memories frighten me. And to speak of my poor mother, who left her poor child as prey to those monsters, is hardest of all for me. My heart bleeds at the mere recollection. It is all still so fresh; I have not had time to collect myself, let alone to grow calm, although more than a year has already passed since all that. But you know everything.

I told you of Anna Fyodorovna's present thoughts; she blames me for ingratitude and denies every accusation of her complicity with Mr. Bykov! She calls me back to her; says that I am begging alms, that I have taken a bad road. She says that if I return to her, she will undertake to settle the whole affair with Mr. Bykov and make him atone for all his guilt toward me. She says that Mr. Bykov wants to give me a dowry. God be with them! I am well here with you, with my good Fedora, who by her attachment to me reminds me of my late nurse. You are only a distant relation of mine, yet you protect me with your name. And them I do not know; I shall forget them, if I can. What more do they want from me? Fedora says that it is all gossip, and that they will leave me alone at last. God grant it!
V. D.
§ June 21
My dear little dove, my dearest!

I want to write, but I do not know where to begin. How strange it is, my dearest, that we now live as we do. I say this because I have never spent my days in such joy. Why, it is as though the Lord had blessed me with a home and a family! My darling, my pretty child! What is this you are saying there about the four little shirts that I sent you? You needed them, after all — I learned it from Fedora. And for me, my dearest, it is a special happiness to satisfy your needs; that is my own pleasure, so leave me be, my dearest; do not touch me and do not contradict me. Nothing like this has ever happened to me, my dearest. I have gone out into society now. In the first place, I live twice over, because you too live very near me, to my comfort; and in the second place, a lodger, my neighbour Ratazyayev, the very clerk who holds the literary evenings, has invited me to tea today. There is a gathering today; we are going to read literature. That is how we are now, my dearest — there! Well, goodbye. I have written all this just so, with no apparent purpose, and only to inform you of my well-being. You told me, my dear, through Teresa, that you need some coloured silk for your embroidery; I will buy it, my dearest, I will buy it, I will buy the silk. Tomorrow I shall have the pleasure of satisfying you completely. I even know where to buy it. And meanwhile I remain
your sincere friend,
Makar Devushkin.
§ June 22
Dear Madam, Varvara Alexeyevna!

I inform you, my dear one, that a most pitiful event has happened in our flat, truly, truly deserving of pity! Today, at five in the morning, Gorshkov's little boy died. I only do not know of what, some scarlet fever, perhaps; the Lord knows! I visited these Gorshkovs. Well, my dearest, how poor they are! And what disorder! And no wonder: the whole family lives in one room, divided only by a little screen for decency's sake. They already have the coffin standing there — a simple one, but rather a pretty coffin; they bought it ready-made; the boy was nine years old; he showed promise, they say. And it is pitiful to look at them, Varenka! The mother does not weep, but she is so sad, poor thing. Perhaps it is even easier for them, now that one is off their shoulders; but they have two left, a baby at the breast and a little girl of six or a little more. What pleasure is there, really, in seeing a child suffer, and your own child too, and having nothing even to help him with! The father sits in an old, greasy frock coat on a broken chair. Tears are running down his face, though perhaps not from grief, but only from habit, because his eyes are running. He is such an odd man! He blushes all the time when you speak to him, gets confused and does not know what to answer. The little girl, the daughter, stands leaning against the coffin, so dull, poor little thing, so thoughtful! And I do not like it, my dearest Varenka, when a child grows thoughtful; it is unpleasant to look at! Some rag doll lies on the floor beside her — she is not playing with it; she holds her little finger to her lips; she stands there and does not stir. The landlady gave her a sweet; she took it, but did not eat it. It is sad, Varenka — is it not?
Makar Devushkin.
§ June 25

Dearest Makar Alexeyevich! I am sending your book back to you. It is a perfectly worthless little book! — one cannot even pick it up. Where did you dig up such a treasure? Joking aside, can you really like such books, Makar Alexeyevich? Now, I have been promised that they will get me something to read in a few days. I will share it with you, if you like. And now, goodbye. Really, I have no time to write more.
V. D.
§ June 26

Dear Varenka! The thing is that I really did not read that little book, my dearest. True, I read a few pages, and saw that it was nonsense, written just for the sake of silliness, to make people laugh; well, I thought, it must really be amusing; perhaps Varenka will like it; so I took it and sent it to you.

But Ratazyayev has promised to give me something truly literary to read, and then you will have books, my dearest. Ratazyayev knows what he is about — he is an expert; he writes himself, oh, how he writes! Such a lively pen and style in abundance; that is, in every word — whatever you like — even in the emptiest, the very commonest, the lowest word, such as I myself might say sometimes to Faldoni or Teresa, even there he has style. I go to his evenings too. We smoke tobacco, and he reads to us, sometimes for five hours on end, and we keep listening. It is a feast, not literature! Such a delight, flowers, simply flowers; from every page you could tie a bouquet! And he is so courteous, kind and gentle. Well, what am I beside him, what? Nothing. He is a man with a reputation, and what am I? Simply — I do not exist; and yet he is gracious to me. I copy a few things for him. Only do not think, Varenka, that there is some trick in it, that he is gracious to me precisely because I copy. Do not believe the gossip, my dearest, do not believe that vile gossip! No, I do it of my own accord, of my own will, for his pleasure, and that he is gracious to me is his doing for my pleasure. I understand the delicacy of the gesture, my dearest. He is a good, a very good man, and an incomparable writer.

And literature is a fine thing, Varenka, a very fine thing; I learned this from them the day before yesterday. A profound thing! It strengthens people's hearts, it instructs, and — there is much else about all this written in their book. Very well written! Literature is a picture, that is, in a certain way a picture and a mirror; an expression of passions, criticism of the subtlest kind, instruction for edification, and a document. I have picked all this up from them. I will tell you frankly, my dearest, that when you sit among them, listening (smoking a pipe too, as they do, perhaps) — and when they begin to contend and argue about various subjects, then I simply give up, and there, my dearest, you and I would have to give up altogether. Then I turn out a perfect blockhead, I am ashamed of myself, so that the whole evening you search for some way to put even half a little word into the general subject, and as if on purpose this half a little word is not to be found! And you feel sorry for yourself, Varenka, that you yourself are not this and not that; that, as the proverb says, you grew up but did not bring back any sense. For what do I do now in my free time? I sleep, like a fool of fools. Whereas instead of useless sleeping I could occupy myself with something pleasant; sit down, for instance, and write a little. It would be useful to myself and good for others. And, my dearest, just look how much they get, may the Lord forgive them! Take Ratazyayev, for instance — how he gets it! What is it to him to write a sheet? Some days he has written as many as five, and he says he gets three hundred roubles a sheet. Some little anecdote or something curious — five hundred, give it or not, burst if you must, but give it! And if not — well, we sometimes put a thousand or two into our pocket! How is that, Varvara Alexeyevna? And that is not all! He has a notebook of little verses there, and every verse quite small — seven thousand, my dearest, he asks seven thousand, just think. Why, that is landed property, a solid house! He says they offer him five thousand, but he will not take it. I reason with him, I say — take the five thousand from them, my good sir, and spit on them, for five thousand is money! No, he says, they will give seven, the rogues. Such a slippery fellow, really!

And now, my dearest, since it has come to this, I will copy out for you, so be it, a passage from "Italian Passions." That is the name of one of his works. Here, read it, Varenka, and judge for yourself.
"...Vladimir shuddered, passions seethed madly within him, and his blood boiled...

"Countess," he cried, "Countess! Do you know how terrible this passion is, how boundless this madness? No, my dreams did not deceive me! I love, I love rapturously, furiously, insanely! All your husband's blood will not drown the furious, seething rapture of my soul! Paltry obstacles will not stop the all-rending, infernal fire that furrows my exhausted breast. Oh Zinaida, Zinaida!...
"Vladimir!..." whispered the countess, beside herself, bowing to his shoulder...
"Zinaida!" cried the enraptured Smelsky. A sigh escaped from his breast. A conflagration flared in bright flame upon the altar of love and furrowed the breasts of the unhappy sufferers.
"Vladimir!..." whispered the countess in ecstasy. Her bosom heaved, her cheeks turned crimson, her eyes burned...
A new, a terrible union was consummated!
Half an hour later the old count entered his wife's boudoir.
"Well, my darling, shall we not order a little samovar to be put on for our dear guest?" he said, patting his wife on the cheek."

Well now, I ask you, my dearest, after this — how do you find it? True, it is a little free, there is no arguing that, but then it is good. If it is good, it is good! And here, allow me, I will copy out for you one more little passage from the tale "Yermak and Zuleika."

Imagine, my dearest, that the Cossack Yermak, the wild and terrible conqueror of Siberia, is in love with Zuleika, daughter of the Siberian Tsar Kuchum, whom he has taken captive. An event straight out of the times of Ivan the Terrible, as you see. Here is the conversation of Yermak and Zuleika: "You love me, Zuleika! Oh, repeat it, repeat it!...
"I love you, Yermak," whispered Zuleika.

"Heaven and earth, I thank you! I am happy!... You have given me all, all that my troubled spirit has striven for since my boyhood. So this is where you were leading me, my guiding star; so this is why you brought me here, beyond the Stone Belt! I will show my Zuleika to the whole world, and people, those raging monsters, will not dare to accuse me! Oh, if only they could understand these secret sufferings of her tender soul, if only they were able to see a whole poem in a single tear of my Zuleika! Oh, let me wipe away this tear with kisses, let me drink it, this heavenly tear... unearthly one!

"Yermak," said Zuleika, "the world is wicked, people are unjust! They will persecute us, they will condemn us, my dear Yermak! What will a poor maiden do, who grew up amid the native snows of Siberia, in her father's yurt, in your cold, icy, soulless, selfish world? People will not understand me, my beloved, my darling!"
"Then the Cossack sabre will flash above them and whistle!" cried Yermak, his eyes wandering wildly."

And what is Yermak like now, Varenka, when he learns that his Zuleika has been stabbed! The blind old man Kuchum, taking advantage of the darkness of night, crept into Yermak's tent in his absence and stabbed his own daughter, wishing to deal a mortal blow to Yermak, who had deprived him of his sceptre and crown.
"I love to scrape iron on stone!" cried Yermak in wild frenzy, sharpening his steel knife on a shaman's stone. "I need their blood, blood! They must be sawn, sawn, sawn!!!"
And after all this Yermak, unable to survive his Zuleika, throws himself into the Irtysh, and that is the end of it.

Well, and this, for example, is just a little passage, in a humorous descriptive manner, written purely for the sake of silliness: "Do you know Ivan Prokofyevich Zheltopuz? Well, that very one who bit Prokofy Ivanovich on the leg. Ivan Prokofyevich is a man of a stubborn character, but of rare virtues; Prokofy Ivanovich, on the contrary, is extremely fond of radish with honey. That was when Pelageya Antonovna was still acquainted with him... And do you know Pelageya Antonovna? Well, that very one who always puts her skirt on inside out."

Why, it is a scream, Varenka, simply a scream! We rolled with laughter when he read it to us. That is what he is like, the Lord forgive him! However, my dearest, although it is a little fanciful and rather too playful, it is innocent, without the slightest free-thinking or liberal ideas. I must remark, my dearest, that Ratazyayev is of excellent conduct, and therefore an excellent writer, not like other writers. And really, sometimes a thought does come into one's head... well, what if I wrote something, what would happen then? Well, for example, suppose that suddenly, out of the blue, a book came out under the title "Poems by Makar Devushkin"! Well, what would you say then, my little angel? How would it seem and appear to you? And as for myself, my dearest, I will say that once my book came out, I should decidedly not dare to show myself on the Nevsky. For how would it be if everyone said, "There goes the literary author and poet Devushkin, that is Devushkin himself!" Well, what should I do then, for instance, with my boots? They are, let me remark in passing, my dearest, almost always patched, and the soles, to tell the truth, sometimes come away quite indecently. What would happen if everyone found out that the author Devushkin has patched boots! Some countess or duchess would find out, and what would she, the darling, say? She, perhaps, would not even notice; for, as I suppose, countesses do not concern themselves with boots, least of all a clerk's boots (for boots differ from boots), but they would tell her everything, my own friends would give me away. Ratazyayev would be the first to give me away; he visits Countess V.; says he is there every time, and on simple terms. He says she is such a darling, a literary lady, he says. A noose, that Ratazyayev!

But, however, enough of this subject; I write all this just so, my little angel, for mischief, to amuse you. Goodbye, my dear! I have scribbled a great deal here, but that is simply because I am in the merriest state of mind today. We all dined together today at Ratazyayev's, and so (they are rascals, my dearest!) they brought out such a Romanée... well, why write to you about that! Only mind you do not imagine something about me, Varenka. I do all this just so. I will send you books, I will certainly send them... There is a work by Paul de Kock going round here, only you, my dearest, shall not have Paul de Kock... No, no! Paul de Kock is not fit for you. They say of him, my dearest, that he drives all the critics of Petersburg to noble indignation. I am sending you a little pound of sweets — I bought them on purpose for you. Eat them, my darling, and remember me with every sweet. Only do not crunch the hard candy, but just suck it, or your little teeth will ache. And perhaps you like candied fruits too?
Write and tell me. Well, goodbye then, goodbye. Christ be with you, my dear. And I shall remain for ever
your most faithful friend,
Makar Devushkin.
§ June 27
Dear Sir, Makar Alexeyevich!

Fedora says that if I wish, some people would gladly take an interest in my situation and obtain for me a very good place in a certain household, as a governess. What do you think, my friend — should I go or not? Of course, I should then be no burden to you, and the place seems a profitable one; but, on the other hand, it is somehow frightening to go into a strange house. They are some sort of landowners. They will begin to inquire about me, to question me, to be curious — and what shall I say then? Besides, I am such a recluse, such a savage; I like to settle into a familiar corner for a long time. Somehow it is better where one is used to things: though one lives half in sorrow, it is still better. Besides, it would mean going out to service; and God knows what the duties will be; perhaps they will simply make me nurse the children. And the people are such that they are already changing their third governess in two years. So advise me, Makar Alexeyevich, for God's sake, whether to go or not? And why do you never come to see me yourself? You only show your face now and then. We almost only see each other on Sundays at church. What a recluse you are! Just like me! And yet I am almost a relation to you. You do not love me, Makar Alexeyevich, and sometimes I am very sad alone. At times, especially at dusk, I sit all, all alone. Fedora goes off somewhere. I sit and think and think, and I remember everything of the old days, the joyful and the sad, and it all passes before my eyes, all flickers as if through a mist. Familiar faces appear (I almost begin to see them awake) — I see my mother most often... And what dreams I have! I feel that my health is shaken; I am so weak; even today, when I got up from bed in the morning, I felt faint; besides, I have such a bad cough! I feel, I know, that I shall soon die. Who will bury me? Who will follow my coffin? Who will be sorry for me?... And so perhaps I shall have to die in a strange place, in a strange house, in a strange corner!... My God, how sad it is to live, Makar Alexeyevich! Why do you keep feeding me with sweets, my friend? I really do not know where you get so much money. Ah, my friend, take care of your money, for God's sake, take care of it. Fedora is selling the rug that I embroidered; they offer fifty roubles in paper money. That is very good: I thought it would be less. I shall give Fedora three roubles, and make myself a little dress, a simple one, but warmer. I shall make you a waistcoat, make it myself, and choose good material.

Fedora got me a book — "The Tales of Belkin," which I am sending you, if you wish to read it. Please, only do not soil it and do not keep it too long: the book belongs to someone else; it is a work by Pushkin. Two years ago my mother and I read these tales together, and now it was so sad to read them again. If you have any books, send them to me — only in case you did not get them from Ratazyayev. He will surely give me something of his own composition, if he has printed anything. How do you like his writings, Makar Alexeyevich? Such trifles... Well, goodbye! How I have chattered on! When I am sad, I am glad to chatter, about anything at all. It is a medicine: one feels better at once, especially if one says out everything that lies on one's heart. Goodbye, goodbye, my friend!
Yours,
V. D.
§ June 28
My dearest Varvara Alexeyevna!

Stop grieving! How is it you are not ashamed! Come, enough, my little angel; how do such thoughts come to you? You are not ill, my darling, not ill at all; you are blooming, truly blooming; a little pale, but still blooming. And what dreams and visions are these! Shame, my dear, enough; spit on those dreams, simply spit on them. Why do I sleep well? Why does nothing ever happen to me? Just look at me, my dearest. I live along, I sleep peacefully, I am perfectly healthy, a fine fellow, a pleasure to look at. Enough, enough, my darling, for shame. Mend your ways. I know that little head of yours, my dearest; the moment something comes over you, off you go dreaming and pining about something. For my sake, stop, my darling. Go among strangers? — never! No, no and no! And what is this you are thinking, what has come over you? And going out to service, besides! No indeed, my dearest, I will not allow it, I arm myself with all my strength against such an intention. I will sell my old coat and walk the streets in my shirt alone, but you shall not want with us. No, Varenka, no; I know you! It is a whim, a pure whim! And what is certain is that Fedora alone is to blame for everything: she, evidently a silly woman, put you up to it all. And do not believe her, my dearest. But perhaps you still do not know everything, my darling?... She is a silly, quarrelsome, foolish woman; she drove her own late husband out of this world. Or perhaps she angered you there somehow? No, no, my dearest, not for anything! And what shall I do then, what will be left for me to do? No, Varenka, my darling, throw this out of your head. What do you lack with us? We cannot rejoice enough in you, you love us — so live on there quietly; sew or read, or perhaps do not sew, it is all the same, only live with us. Otherwise judge for yourself, what would it look like then?... I will get you books, and then perhaps we will plan to go walking again somewhere. Only you, my dearest, stop, stop, gather your wits and do not fret over trifles! I will come to see you, and very soon, only accept from me this straight and frank confession: it is not good, my darling, it is very bad! I am, of course, an unlearned man, and I know myself that I am unlearned, that I was schooled on copper coins, but that is not what I am driving at, it is not about me here at all, but I will stand up for Ratazyayev, whatever you say. He is my friend, and therefore I will stand up for him. He writes well, very, very and once more very well. I do not agree with you and cannot possibly agree. It is written floridly, abruptly, with figures of speech, there are various thoughts; very good! Perhaps you read it without feeling, Varenka, or were not in the mood when you read it, were angry with Fedora about something, or something unpleasant happened to you there. No, read it with feeling, better, when you are content and merry and in a pleasant frame of mind, as, for instance, when you have a sweet in your mouth — that is when to read it. I do not argue (who would be against that), there are writers better than Ratazyayev, even very much better, but they are good, and Ratazyayev is good; they write well, and he writes well. He is on his own, he scribbles a little in his own way, and does very well to scribble. Well, goodbye, my dearest; I cannot write more; I must hurry, I have business. Mind you, my dearest, my bright, beloved one, calm yourself, and may the Lord be with you, and I remain
your faithful friend,
Makar Devushkin.
P. S. Thank you for the book, my dear one, we will read Pushkin too; and this evening I will certainly come to see you.
V: No, my friend, no, I cannot live among you. I have thought it over and found that I am doing very wrong in refusing such a profitable place. There I shall have at least a sure crust of bread; I shall try hard, I shall earn the kindness of strangers, I shall even try to change my character, if it is needed. Of course, it is painful and hard to live among strangers, to seek strangers' favour, to hide oneself and force oneself, but God will help me. I cannot remain a recluse all my life. Such things have happened to me before. I remember when, as a little girl, I used to go to boarding school. All Sunday at home I would frolic and jump about, sometimes my mother would scold me, and it was all nothing, all well in my heart, bright in my soul. Evening would draw near, and a deadly sadness would fall on me; at nine o'clock I had to go to school, and there everything was strange, cold, strict, the governesses so angry on Mondays, and it used to wring my soul, I wanted to cry; I would go into a corner and cry all, all alone, hiding my tears — they would say I was lazy; and I was not crying at all because I had to study. Well, what then? I grew used to it, and afterwards, when I left school, I cried again, saying goodbye to my friends. And I am doing wrong to live as a burden to you both. This thought is a torment to me. I tell you all this frankly, because I am used to being frank with you. Do I not see how Fedora gets up every day at the crack of dawn and sets about her washing, and works until late at night? — and old bones love rest. Do I not see that you are ruining yourself for me, putting your last kopeck on the edge and spending it on me? That is not for your means, my friend! You write that you will sell your last things and not leave me in need. I believe, my friend, I believe in your kind heart — but you say this now. Now you have unexpected money, you have received a reward; but afterwards what will happen, afterwards? You know yourself — I am always ill; I cannot work as you do, though my soul would be glad to, and work is not always to be had. What is left for me, then? To tear my heart with grief, looking at you both, dear souls. How can I be of the slightest use to you? And why am I so necessary to you, my friend? What good have I done you? I am only attached to you with all my soul, I love you firmly, strongly, with all my heart, but — bitter is my fate! — I know how to love and can love, but only that, and not to do good, not to repay you for your kindnesses. Do not keep me any longer, think it over and tell me your final opinion. Awaiting it, I remain

Whim, whim, Varenka, simply a whim! Leave you alone, and there you will think over with that little head of yours heaven knows what. This is not right and that is not right! And I see now that it is all a whim. What do you lack with us, my dearest, only tell me that! You are loved, you love us, we are all content and happy — what more is wanted? Well, and what will you do among strangers? You probably do not yet know what a stranger is?... No, be good enough to ask me, and I will tell you what a stranger is. I know him, my dearest, I know him well; I have happened to eat his bread. He is wicked, Varenka, wicked, so wicked that your poor little heart will not hold out, he will torment it with reproach, with blame and with ugly looks. With us you are warm and well off, as if sheltered in a little nest. And you would leave us as if without a head. Well, what shall we do without you; what shall I, an old man, do then? You are not needed by us? Not useful? How not useful? No, my dearest, judge for yourself, how are you not useful? You are very useful to me, Varenka. You have such a beneficent influence... Why, I think about you now, and I am cheerful... Sometimes I write you a letter and set out all my feelings in it, and I receive a detailed answer from you. I bought you a little wardrobe, had a hat made; at times some commission comes from you, and I do the commission... No, how are you not useful? And what shall I do alone in my old age, what shall I be good for? Perhaps you have not thought of that, Varenka; no, think of precisely that — what will he be good for without me? I am used to you, my dear one. Otherwise, what will come of it? I will go to the Neva, and that will be the end of it. Yes, really, such a thing will happen, Varenka; what is left for me to do without you! Ah, my darling, Varenka! You evidently want a carter to take me to Volkovo; and some beggarly old woman, some old slattern, to follow my coffin alone, and for them to cover me with sand there, and go away, and leave me there alone. It is a sin, a sin, my dearest! Really a sin, by God, a sin! I am sending you back your book, my dear friend Varenka, and if you, my dear friend, ask my opinion about your book, I will say that in all my life I have never happened to read such splendid books. I ask myself now, my dearest, how did I live till now such a blockhead, Lord forgive me? What did I do? What woods am I from? Why, I know nothing, my dearest, absolutely nothing! Nothing at all! I will tell you plainly, Varenka — I am an unlearned man; up to now I have read little, very little, almost nothing: I read "The Picture of Man," a clever work; I read "The Boy Who Played Little Tunes on Bells," and "The Cranes of Ibycus" — that is all, and I never read anything more. Now I have read "The Station Master" here in your book; and I will tell you, my dearest, it does happen that you live and do not know that there, right beside you, is a book in which your whole life is laid out as on your fingers. And what you never guessed before, here, when you begin to read in such a book, you gradually remember it all yourself, and find it, and guess it out. And finally, this is another reason I took to your book: some work, whatever it may be, you read and read, and sometimes, burst if you must, it is so cunning that it is as if you did not understand it. I, for example — I am dull, I am dull by nature, so I cannot read works that are too weighty; but this you read — as if you had written it yourself, as if it were, say, my own heart, such as it is, taken and turned inside out before people, and described in every detail — there! And the matter is simple, my God; why, really, I should have written it the same way; why should I not have written it? For I feel just the same, exactly as in the book, and I myself have at times been in the same situations as, for example, this Samson Vyrin, poor fellow. And how many Samson Vyrins there are walking among us, such poor wretches of the heart! And how skilfully it is all described! I nearly burst into tears, my dearest, when I read that he took to drink, the sinner, so that he lost his memory, grew embittered, and sleeps all day under his sheepskin coat, and drowns his grief in punch, and weeps piteously, wiping his eyes with a dirty coat-tail, when he remembers his strayed lamb, his daughter Dunya! No, this is natural! Do read it; it is natural! It lives! I have seen it myself — it is all living around me; take Teresa — but why go far! — take even our poor clerk — he is perhaps just such a Samson Vyrin, only with a different surname, Gorshkov. It is a common matter, my dearest, and it may happen both to you and to me. And the count who lives on the Nevsky or on the embankment, he too will be just the same, only he will seem different, because with them everything is in their own way, in the higher tone, but he too will be the same, anything may happen, and the same may happen to me. That is how it is, my dearest, and you still want to go away from us; but, Varenka, it would be a sin, it might overtake me. You may ruin both yourself and me, my dear one. Ah, my bright one, throw out of your head, for God's sake, all these free thoughts and do not torment me for nothing. Why, where could you, my weak little nestling, still unfledged, where could you feed yourself, keep yourself from perishing, defend yourself from villains! Enough, Varenka, mend your ways; do not listen to foolish counsels and slander, and read your book once more, read it attentively: it will do you good.

I spoke about "The Station Master" to Ratazyayev. He told me that it is all old, and that now books with pictures and with various descriptions have come in; I really did not quite understand what he was saying there. He concluded, however, that Pushkin is good and that he glorified holy Russia, and told me much more about him. Yes, very good, Varenka, very good; read the book once more with attention, follow my advice, and by your obedience make me, an old man, happy. Then the Lord himself will reward you, my dear one, he will certainly reward you.

Fedora brought me fifteen silver roubles today. How glad she was, poor thing, when I gave her three roubles! I am writing to you in haste. I am cutting out a waistcoat for you now — such lovely material — yellowish, with little flowers. I am sending you one book; it is all different tales; I have read some of them; read one of them called "The Overcoat." — You urge me to go to the theatre with you; will that not be too dear? Perhaps only to the gallery, if anywhere. I have not been to the theatre for a very long time, and really I do not remember when. Only I am afraid again that this undertaking will cost too much. Fedora only shakes her head. She says that you have begun to live quite beyond your means; and I see it myself; how much you have spent on me alone! Take care, my friend, that no trouble comes of it. Fedora has told me of some rumours — that you had, it seems, a quarrel with your landlady about not paying her money; I am very afraid for you. Well, goodbye; I am in a hurry. I have a little work to do; I am changing the ribbons on my hat.
P. S. Do you know, if we go to the theatre, I will wear my new little hat, and a black mantilla over my shoulders. Will that be nice?

...So, it is all about yesterday. — Yes, my dearest, in our time too a whim used to come over us. I fell in love with an actress, fell in love over head and ears, and that would still be nothing; but the oddest thing is that I hardly saw her at all, and had been in the theatre only once, and in spite of all that I fell in love. At that time there lived with me, wall to wall, some five young, excitable fellows. I fell in with them, I fell in with them in spite of myself, though I always kept within decent bounds. Well, in order not to lag behind, I too agreed with them in everything. How much they told me about this little actress! Every evening, as soon as there was a performance, the whole company — who never had a groat for anything necessary — the whole company set off to the theatre, to the gallery, and there they clapped and clapped, called and called for this actress — simply went wild! And afterwards they would not let one sleep; all night long they talked about her, each called her his Glasha, all were in love with her alone, all had one canary in their heart. They stirred me up too, defenceless as I was; I was still quite young then. I do not know myself how I found myself with them in the theatre, in the fourth tier, in the gallery. All I saw was just one little edge of the curtain, but I heard everything. The little actress, true, had a pretty little voice — ringing, nightingale-like, honeyed! We all clapped our hands raw, shouted and shouted — in a word, they very nearly laid hands on us, and one was indeed led out, true. I came home — I walk about as if in a fog! There was only one silver rouble left in my pocket, and a good ten days to go before my salary. And what do you think, my dearest? The next day, before going to work, I called in at a French perfumer's, and bought from him some scents and fragrant soap with my whole capital — I do not know myself why I bought all this then! And I did not dine at home, but kept walking past her windows. She lived on the Nevsky, on the fourth floor. I came home, rested an hour or so, and went to the Nevsky again, only to pass her windows. For a month and a half I went on like that, dangling after her; I kept hiring dashing cabmen and made detours past her windows; I wore myself out entirely, ran into debt, and then I stopped loving her: — I was tired of it! So that is what an actress is able to make of a decent man, my dearest! However, I was young, young then!...

I hasten to return to you your book, received by me on the 6th of this month, and at the same time I hasten in this letter of mine to explain myself to you. It is bad, my dearest, bad that you have put me in such an extremity. Allow me, my dearest: every station in life is appointed by the Almighty to the lot of man. One is appointed to wear a general's epaulettes, another to serve as a titular councillor; this one to command, that one to obey without complaint and in fear. This is reckoned according to a man's capacity; one is fit for one thing, another for another, and capacities are ordained by God himself. I have been in the service for nearly thirty years; I serve irreproachably, my conduct is sober, and I have never been noticed in any disorder. As a citizen, I consider myself, by my own conscience, one who has his faults, but at the same time his virtues. I am respected by my superiors, and his Excellency himself is pleased with me; and although up to now he has not shown me any particular marks of favour, I know that he is pleased. I have lived to grey hairs; I know of no great sin on my conscience. Of course, who is not sinful in small things? Everyone is sinful, and even you are sinful, my dearest! But in great offences and insolences I have never been noticed, never anything against regulations or in breach of public order, in this I have never been noticed, it has not happened; I even got a little cross — well, never mind! All this you in conscience ought to have known, my dearest, and he ought to have known it; once he took up describing, he ought to have known everything. No, I did not expect this from you, my dearest; no, Varenka! From you, of all people, I did not expect such a thing.

What! So after this one cannot even live quietly, in one's own little corner, such as it is, live without troubling the water, as the proverb says, touching no one, knowing the fear of God and oneself, so that no one touches you either, so that no one creeps into your kennel and peeps in — to see, you know, how you are getting on at home, whether, for example, you have a good waistcoat, whether you have the necessary under-garments; whether you have boots, and what they are mended with; what you eat, what you drink, what you copy?... And what is there in it, my dearest, that I, for instance, where the pavement is bad, sometimes walk on tiptoe, because I am saving my boots! Why write about another man that he sometimes goes short, that he does not drink tea? As though everyone must absolutely drink tea! Do I look into everyone's mouth to see what morsel he is chewing? Whom have I offended in that way? No, my dearest, why offend others when you are not touched yourself! Well, here is an example for you, Varvara Alexeyevna, here is what it means: you serve and serve, zealously, diligently, and — what of it! — your superiors themselves respect you (however it may be, they respect you all the same), — and then someone right under your nose, without any visible reason, out of the blue, cooks up a lampoon on you. Of course, it is true that sometimes you have something new made, you rejoice, you cannot sleep, but you rejoice, you put on new boots, for example, with such voluptuousness — that is true, I have felt it, because it is pleasant to see your foot in a fine, smart boot — that is truly described! But all the same I am genuinely astonished that Fyodor Fyodorovich let such a book pass without attention and did not stand up for himself. True, he is still a young dignitary and likes to shout at times; but why should he not shout? Why should he not give a dressing-down, if our brother needs a dressing-down. Well, let us suppose so, for example, for the sake of tone — well, for the sake of tone one may;

one must train them; one must keep them in awe; because — let it be between us, Varenka — our brother will do nothing without awe, each one only tries to be listed somewhere, to say, you know, that I am there and there, while from the work itself he sidles off sideways. And since there are different ranks, and every rank demands a dressing-down exactly corresponding to the rank, it is natural that after this the tone of the dressing-down also comes out varied by rank — it is in the order of things! And the world stands on this, my dearest, that we all set the tone one to another, that each of us scolds another. Without this precaution the world would not stand, and there would be no order. I am truly astonished that Fyodor Fyodorovich let such an insult pass without attention!

And why write such a thing? And what is it needed for? Will one of the readers make me an overcoat for it, or what? Buy me new boots? No, Varenka, he will read it and even demand a continuation. You hide sometimes, you hide, you conceal yourself in whatever you have not succeeded at, you are afraid at times to show your nose anywhere at all, because you tremble at gossip, because out of everything there is in the world they will make a lampoon on you, and now your whole civic and family life goes about in literature, everything printed, read, laughed at, gossiped over! Why, you will not be able to show yourself in the street; for it is all so proved there that our brother is now recognised by his very walk alone. Well, it would be all right if at the end he had at least mended his ways, softened something, put in, for example, after the point where they showered scraps of paper on his head: that for all this he was virtuous, a good citizen, did not deserve such treatment from his comrades, obeyed his seniors (here some example might be given), wished no one ill, believed in God and died (if he is so set on his dying) — lamented. But best of all would be not to leave him to die, poor fellow, but to arrange it so that his overcoat should be found, so that the general, learning more of his virtues, should ask for him to be transferred to his own chancery, raise him in rank and give him a good salary, so that, you see, how it would be: evil would be punished and virtue would triumph, and the clerk comrades would all be left with nothing. I, for example, would have done it so; but what is there that is special in this of his, what is good in it? Just some empty example from everyday, vile life. And how did you decide, my dear one, to send me such a book. Why, it is a malicious book, Varenka; it is simply improbable, because it cannot even happen that there should be such a clerk. Why, after such a thing one ought to complain, Varenka, to complain formally.

The latest events and your letters have frightened and shocked me and left me bewildered, and Fedora's tales have explained everything to me. But why did you have to despair so, and suddenly sink into such an abyss as the one you have sunk into, Makar Alexeyevich? Your explanations did not satisfy me at all. You see, was I not right when I insisted on taking that advantageous position they offered me? Besides, my latest adventure frightens me in earnest. You say that your love for me made you hide things from me. Even then I saw that I owed you a great deal, when you assured me that you were spending on me only your reserve money, which, you said, lay in the pawnbroker's bank for emergencies. But now that I have learned that you had no money at all, that you, having learned by chance of my wretched situation and being moved by it, resolved to spend your salary, drawing it in advance, and even sold your clothes while I was ill, now, through the discovery of all this, I am placed in such a tormenting position that to this day I do not know how to take it all, or what to think of it. Ah, Makar Alexeyevich! You should have stopped at your first kindnesses, inspired in you by compassion and kinship, and not squandered money afterwards on what was unnecessary. You betrayed our friendship, Makar Alexeyevich, because you were not frank with me; and now, when I see that your last coins went on dresses for me, on sweets, on outings, on the theatre and on books, I pay dearly for it all with regret for my unpardonable thoughtlessness (for I accepted everything from you without a care for yourself); and everything with which you wished to give me pleasure has now turned into grief for me and left behind only a useless regret. I noticed your melancholy of late, and though I myself was waiting anxiously for something, what has happened now never entered my mind. What! Could you lose heart to such a degree, Makar Alexeyevich! But what will people think of you now, what will all who know you say of you? You, whom I and everyone respected for your goodness of heart, your modesty and your good sense, you have suddenly fallen into such a loathsome vice as you were never, it seems, observed in before. What came over me when Fedora told me that you had been found in the street in a state of drunkenness and brought home to your lodging by the police! I was struck dumb with amazement, though I had expected something extraordinary, because you had vanished for four days. But did you think, Makar Alexeyevich, what your superiors would say when they learn the real reason for your absence? You say that everyone is laughing at you; that everyone has learned of our connection, and that even I am mentioned in the jeers of your neighbours. Pay no attention to that, Makar Alexeyevich, and for God's sake, calm yourself. I am also frightened by your affair with those officers; I heard of it only dimly. Explain to me what it all means. You write that you were afraid to confess to me, afraid that your confession would lose you my friendship, that you were in despair, not knowing how to help me in my illness, that you sold everything to support me and keep me out of the hospital, that you have fallen into as much debt as it is possible to fall into, and have unpleasantness every day with your landlady; but by hiding all this from me you chose the worst course. And yet now I have learned it all. You were ashamed to make me admit that I was the cause of your unhappy situation, and now you have given me twice as much grief by your conduct. All this has shocked me, Makar Alexeyevich. Ah, my friend! Misfortune is a contagious disease. The unhappy and the poor must keep away from one another, so as not to catch it still worse. I have brought you misfortunes such as you never knew before in your modest and solitary life. All this torments and crushes me.

Write to me now, quite frankly, all that has happened to you and how you came to resolve on such a deed. Set me at ease, if you can. It is not vanity that makes me write now of my peace of mind, but my friendship and love for you, which nothing will ever efface from my heart. Farewell. I await your answer with impatience. You have thought ill of me, Makar Alexeyevich.

Well now, since it is all over and everything is coming back little by little to its former state, here is what I will say to you, my dearest: you are worried about what people will think of me, and I hasten to declare to you, Varvara Alexeyevna, that my self-respect is dearer to me than anything. Wherefore, in reporting to you of my misfortunes and all these disorders, I inform you that none of the superiors knows anything yet, nor will they know, so that they will all go on feeling respect for me as before. One thing only I fear: gossip. At home our landlady shouts, but now, when with the help of your ten roubles I have paid her a part of the debt, she only grumbles, and nothing more. As for the others, they too are all right; one just must not ask them for a loan, otherwise they are all right too. And in conclusion of my explanations I will tell you, my dearest, that your respect for me I consider higher than anything in the world, and I console myself with it now in my temporary disorders. Thank God that the first blow and the first troubles are past, and that you have taken it in such a way that you do not consider me a treacherous friend and a selfish man for having kept you with me and deceived you, not being able to part with you and loving you as my little angel. I have now set to my service with zeal, and I have begun to carry out my duty well. Yevstafy Ivanovich did not so much as say a word when I passed by him yesterday. I will not hide from you, my dearest, that my debts are killing me, and so is the poor state of my wardrobe, but that again is nothing, and about that too, I beg you, do not despair, my dearest. You send me yet another fifty kopecks, Varenka, and that fifty kopecks pierced my heart. So that is how it has come to be now, that is how it is! That is, it is not I, an old fool, who am helping you, my little angel, but you, my poor little orphan, who are helping me! Fedora did well to get the money. For the time being I have no hopes at all, my dearest, of receiving any, but if any hopes should stir, I will write to you about everything in detail. But gossip, gossip troubles me most of all. Farewell, my little angel. I kiss your hand and implore you to get well. I write briefly because I am hurrying to my duties, for by diligence and zeal I want to make up for all my faults in neglecting my service; as for the further narrative of all the events and of the adventure with the officers, I put it off until evening.
Yours, respectfully and with heartfelt love,

Ah, Varenka, Varenka! Now it is precisely on your side that the sin lies, and it will stay on your conscience. With that little letter of yours you have confused me completely, bewildered me, and only now, when at leisure I have looked into the inside of my heart, do I see that I was right, perfectly right. I am not speaking of my debauch (never mind it, my dearest, never mind it!), but of the fact that I love you, and that it was not at all imprudent of me to love you, not at all imprudent. You, my dearest, know nothing; but if you only knew why it is all this, why it is that I must love you, you would not say what you do. You say all this sensible stuff only because you must, but I am sure that in your heart it is not that at all.

My dearest, I myself do not know or remember well all that happened to me with the officers. I must tell you, my little angel, that up to that time I was in a most terrible confusion. Imagine, for a whole month I had been, so to speak, holding on by a single thread. The situation was most wretched. I hid from you, and at home too, but my landlady made a great noise and outcry. That would have been nothing to me. Let the worthless woman shout, but there was this, that it was a disgrace, and, second, that she, God knows how, learned of our connection and shouted such things about it to the whole house that I was stunned and stopped my ears. But the trouble was that the others did not stop their ears, but on the contrary pricked them up. And even now, my dearest, I do not know where to go...

And so, my little angel, all this, this whole heap of every kind of misery, finished me off completely. Suddenly I hear strange things from Fedora: that an unworthy suitor had appeared at your house and insulted you with an unworthy proposal; that he had insulted you, deeply insulted you, I judge by myself, my dearest, because I too was deeply insulted. And that was when I, my little angel, went out of my wits, that was when I lost myself and was utterly undone. I, my friend Varenka, ran out in some unheard-of fury, I wanted to go to him, the sinner; I did not even know what I wanted to do, because I do not want you, my little angel, to be wronged! Well, it was sad! and at that time there was rain, slush, a dreadful gloom!... I had already wanted to turn back... It was then that I fell, my dearest. I met Yemelya, Yemelyan Ilyich, he is a clerk, that is, he was a clerk, but now he is not a clerk any more, because he has been dismissed from our department. What he is doing now I do not know, he somehow struggles along; so off we went together. Then, well, but what is it to you, Varenka, is it a cheerful thing, then, to read of the misfortunes of your friend, his calamities and the history of the temptations he endured? On the third day, in the evening, since Yemelya had egged me on, I went to him, to that officer. I asked our porter for the address. And I, my dearest, since it has come to be mentioned, had long been noticing that fine fellow; I used to watch him when he still lodged in our house. Now I see that I did an improper thing, because I was not in my proper state when I was announced to him. I, Varenka, to tell the truth, remember nothing; I remember only that he had a great many officers, or perhaps it was doubling in my eyes, God knows. I do not remember either what I said, only I know that I said a great deal in my noble indignation. Well, then they threw me out, then they threw me down the stairs, that is, it was not exactly that they threw me down, but only that they pushed me out. You know already, Varenka, how I came back; that is all. Of course, I have lowered myself and my self-respect has suffered, but then nobody knows this among outsiders, nobody except you knows it; and in that case it is all one as if it had never been. Perhaps it is so, Varenka, what do you think? All that I know for certain is that last year, in our department, Aksenty Osipovich in just the same way dared to lay hands on the person of Pyotr Petrovich, but in secret, he did it in secret. He lured him into the porter's room, I saw it all through a crack; and there he arranged matters as was needful, but in a noble manner, because nobody saw it except me; well, and I said nothing, that is, I mean to say that I announced it to nobody. Well, and after that Pyotr Petrovich and Aksenty Osipovich were all right. Pyotr Petrovich, you know, is so full of self-respect that he told nobody, so that now they bow to each other and shake hands. I do not argue, I, Varenka, do not dare argue with you, I have fallen deep and, what is most dreadful of all, lost in my own opinion of myself, but then it must have been written for me so at birth, it must be fate, and from fate you cannot run away, you know yourself. Well, there you have a detailed explanation of my misfortunes and calamities, Varenka, there, it is all such that you might as well not read it. I am a little unwell, my dearest, and have lost all playfulness of feeling. Therefore now, testifying to you my attachment, love and respect, I remain, my dear Madam, Varvara Alexeyevna,

I read both your letters, and simply gasped! Listen, my friend, either you are keeping something from me and have written me only a part of all your troubles, or... really, Makar Alexeyevich, your letters still smack of some kind of disorder... Come to me, for God's sake, come today; and listen, you know, come straight to us to dinner. I do not even know how you live there and how you have settled things with your landlady. You write nothing of all that, and seem to be keeping silent on purpose. So until we meet, my friend; be sure to look in on us today; and you would do much better if you always came to us for dinner. Fedora cooks very well. Farewell.
VI: You are glad, my dearest, that God has sent you the chance, in your turn, to repay good with good and to thank me. I believe that, Varenka, and I believe in the goodness of your angelic little heart, and I do not say it as a reproach to you, only do not reproach me, as you did then, that in my old age I have gone to the dogs. Well, there was that sin, what is to be done! If you must insist that there was some sin in it; only, my dear friend, to hear such a thing from you costs me a great deal! And do not be angry with me for saying this; my whole chest, my dearest, has been aching. Poor people are capricious, it is just so ordained by nature. I felt it before, and now I have felt it still more. He, the poor man, is exacting; he looks at God's world differently, and looks sidelong at every passer-by, and casts a troubled gaze about him, and listens to every word, wondering whether it is not about him that something is being said there. As if to say, why is he so unsightly? what exactly would he be feeling? what, for instance, would he look like from this side, and what from that side? And everyone knows, Varenka, that a poor man is worse than a rag and can get no respect from anybody, whatever they may write! those scribblers there, whatever they may write! everything will be with the poor man just as it was. And why will it be as before? Because with the poor man, in their opinion, everything must be turned inside out; he must have nothing sacred, no self-respect of any sort, no-no-no! Yemelya said the other day that they once took up a subscription for him somewhere, and for every ten-kopeck piece, so to speak, they made an official inspection of him. They thought they were giving their ten-kopeck pieces to him for nothing, but no: they paid for being shown a poor man. Nowadays, my dearest, even good deeds are somehow done in a strange way... and perhaps they were always done so, who knows! Either they do not know how to do them, or else they are great masters, one or the other. Perhaps you did not know this, well then, here you are! In other things we pass, but in this we are well informed! And why does a poor man know all this and think all such things? And why? Well, from experience! And because, for example, he knows that right beside him there is such a gentleman who goes off somewhere to a restaurant and says to himself: what, I wonder, will that wretched clerk eat today? I shall eat sauté-papillote, and he perhaps will eat porridge without butter. And what business is it of his that I shall eat porridge without butter? There are such men, Varenka, there are, who think of nothing but that. And they walk about, those indecent libellers, and look to see whether you step on the stone with your whole foot or only with your toe; that such-and-such a clerk, of such-and-such a department, a titular councillor, has bare toes sticking out of his boot, that his elbows are torn, and then they write it all down at home and print such trash... And what business is it of yours that my elbows are torn? And if you will forgive me a coarse word, Varenka, I will tell you that on this score a poor man has the very same shame as you have, let us say, as a young girl. After all, you would not undress before everybody (forgive my coarse little word); in just the same way a poor man does not like people to peep into his hovel, to see what his family relations may be, so there. And yet there was no need, Varenka, to offend me then, together with my enemies, who encroach upon the honour and self-respect of an honest man!

And in the office today I sat such a little bear, such a plucked sparrow, that I nearly burned up with shame for myself. I was ashamed, Varenka! And naturally one feels timid when bare elbows shine through the clothes and the buttons dangle on threads. And with me, as if on purpose, it was all in such disorder! One loses heart in spite of oneself. What!... Stepan Karlovich himself began today to speak to me about some business, spoke and spoke, and then, as if by chance, added: "Ah, you, my dear Makar Alexeyevich!" and did not finish the rest, what he was thinking; and I guessed everything myself and blushed so that even my bald patch blushed.
