In essence it is nothing, but all the same it is disquieting and leads to heavy reflections. Have they not found something out! And God forbid, but what if they have found out something! I confess I suspect, I strongly suspect, one little person. These villains care nothing! They will betray you! They will betray your whole private life for a farthing; they hold nothing sacred.

I know now whose doing this is: it is Ratazyayev's doing. He is acquainted with someone in our department, and surely, in the course of conversation, he passed everything on to him with additions; or perhaps he told it in his own department, and it crawled over into our department. And in our lodgings everybody knows everything down to the last detail and points a finger at your window; that I know, that they point. And when I went to dine with you yesterday, they all leaned out of their windows, and the landlady said that, you see, the devil has got himself tied up with a baby, and then she called you an improper name as well. But all this is nothing compared with the vile intention of Ratazyayev to put you and me into his literature and describe us in subtle satire; he said so himself, and good people from among our fellows told me of it. I cannot think of anything now, my dearest, and I do not know what to decide. No use hiding the sin, we have angered the Lord God, my little angel! You, my dearest, wanted to send me some book, for the sake of boredom. Oh, never mind the book, my dearest! What is a book? It is a tale of nonsense! And a novel is rubbish, written for rubbish, for idle people to read: believe me, my dearest, believe my long experience. And what is there, if they talk you round with some Shakespeare, saying, you see, there is a Shakespeare in literature, well then, Shakespeare is rubbish too, it is all sheer rubbish, and all made for the sake of one libel!

Do not worry about anything; God willing, everything will be settled. Fedora has got a heap of work for herself and for me, and we have set to the task very merrily; perhaps we shall mend everything. She suspects that all my latest troubles are not unconnected with Anna Fyodorovna; but now it is all one to me. Somehow I feel unusually cheerful today. You want to borrow money, God preserve you! You will have no end of trouble afterwards, when it comes time to pay it back. You had much better live more closely with us, come to us more often, and pay no attention to your landlady. As for the rest of your enemies and ill-wishers, I am sure you are tormenting yourself with groundless doubts, Makar Alexeyevich! You see, I told you last time that your style is extremely uneven. Well, farewell, until we meet. I expect you at our house without fail.

I hasten to tell you, my little life, that some hopes have been born in me. But allow me, my little daughter, you write, my angel, that I should not borrow? My dear, it is impossible without it; I am badly off, and with you too, who knows, something may suddenly go wrong! You are so frail; so I write to you for this reason, that borrowing is absolutely necessary. Well, so I go on.

I will remark to you, Varvara Alexeyevna, that at the office I sit next to Yemelyan Ivanovich. That is not the Yemelyan whom you know. This one, like me, is a titular councillor, and he and I are about the oldest, most rooted servants in our whole department. He is a good soul, a disinterested soul, but so uncommunicative, and always looks a perfect bear. On the other hand he is businesslike, his pen is a pure English hand, and to tell the whole truth, he writes no worse than I do, a worthy man! We have never been close, but only by custom, farewell and good day; and if at times I needed a penknife, it happened that I would ask, as it were, give me a little knife, Yemelyan Ivanovich, in a word, it was only what common courtesy requires. Well, today he says to me: Makar Alexeyevich, why, he says, are you so thoughtful? I saw that the man wishes me well, and so I opened up to him, saying, so and so, Yemelyan Ivanovich, that is, I did not tell everything, and God forbid, I never will, because I have not the heart to say it, but I opened up to him a little, that I am, you see, in straits and so on. "But you, my dear sir," says Yemelyan Ivanovich, "you should borrow; for instance, borrow from Pyotr Petrovich, he lends at interest; I have borrowed from him; and he charges a decent interest, not burdensome." Well, Varenka, my little heart leapt up. I think and think, perhaps the Lord will put it into his heart, Pyotr Petrovich, my benefactor, and he will lend me some. And I am already reckoning to myself that I would pay the landlady, and help you, and set myself to rights all round, for otherwise it is such a disgrace: it is dreadful even to sit at my place, besides the fact that our scoffers laugh, God be with them! And his Excellency too sometimes passes by our table; well, God forbid, he should cast a glance at me and notice that I am dressed improperly! And with him the main thing is cleanliness and neatness. He perhaps would say nothing, but I should die of shame, that is how it would be. Wherefore, bracing myself and hiding my shame in a pocket full of holes, I made my way to Pyotr Petrovich, full of hope and more dead than alive with expectation, both together. Well, and what, Varenka, it all ended in nothing! He was busy with something, talking with Fedosey Ivanovich. I came up to him from the side and tugged at his sleeve: Pyotr Petrovich, I said, oh, Pyotr Petrovich! He looked round, and I went on: so and so, some thirty roubles, and so forth. At first he did not understand me, and then, when I explained it all to him, he laughed, and said nothing, fell silent. I came at him again with the same. And he says to me, have you any security? And he himself buried himself in his paper, writes and does not look at me. I was a little taken aback. No, I say, Pyotr Petrovich, there is no security, and I explain to him that, you see, as soon as I get my salary, I will pay it back, I will certainly pay it back, I will consider it my first duty. Here someone called him away, I waited for him, he came back, and began to mend a pen, and as if he does not notice me. And I keep on with my own, saying, Pyotr Petrovich, is it not possible somehow? He is silent and as if he does not hear; I stood and stood, well, I think, I will try for the last time, and I tugged at his sleeve. He did not say so much as a word, mended his pen, and began to write; and I went away. They, my dearest, you see, may be worthy people all of them, but proud, very proud, what am I to them! How can we compare with them, Varenka! That is why I have written all this to you. Yemelyan Ivanovich laughed too and shook his head, but he gave me hope, the kind soul. Yemelyan Ivanovich is a worthy man. He promised to recommend me to a certain person; this person, Varenka, lives on the Vyborg side, and also lends at interest, some clerk of the fourteenth class. Yemelyan Ivanovich says that this one will certainly lend; I shall go tomorrow, my little angel, eh? What do you think? After all, it is a disaster not to borrow! The landlady all but turns me out of my lodging and refuses to give me dinner. And my boots are very bad, my dearest, and there are no buttons... and that is not all that I lack! And what if one of the superiors notices such an impropriety? It is a calamity, Varenka, a calamity, simply a calamity!

For God's sake, Makar Alexeyevich, as soon as you possibly can, borrow some money; I would not for anything ask you for help in the present circumstances, but if you only knew what my situation is! We cannot possibly stay in this lodging. The most terrible unpleasantnesses have befallen me, and if you only knew in what a state of distress and agitation I am now! Imagine, my friend: this morning there came into our room a stranger, a man in years, almost an old man, with decorations. I was amazed, not understanding what he could want with us. Fedora had gone out at that moment to the shop. He began to question me about how I live and what I do, and, without waiting for an answer, announced to me that he was the uncle of that officer; that he was very angry with his nephew for his bad conduct and for having disgraced us before the whole house; he said that his nephew was a boy and a scatterbrain and that he was ready to take me under his protection; he advised me not to listen to young men, added that he sympathised with me like a father, that he felt fatherly feelings for me and was ready to help me in everything. I blushed all over, did not know what to think, but I did not hurry to thank him. He took me by the hand by force, patted me on the cheek, said that I was very pretty and that he was extremely pleased that I have dimples in my cheeks (God knows what he said!), and finally wanted to kiss me, saying that he was already an old man (he was so loathsome!). Then Fedora came in. He was a little confused and began again to say that he felt respect for me for my modesty and good conduct and that he very much wished that I should not shun him. Then he called Fedora aside and, under some strange pretext, wanted to give her some money. Fedora, of course, did not take it. At last he made ready to go home, repeated once more all his assurances, said that he would call on me again and bring me earrings (it seems he was very confused himself); advised me to change my lodging and recommended to me a certain excellent apartment which he had in view and which would cost me nothing; said that he had grown very fond of me, because I was an honest and sensible girl, advised me to beware of depraved young men, and finally announced that he knew Anna Fyodorovna and that Anna Fyodorovna had charged him to tell me that she would visit me herself. Then I understood everything. I do not know what became of me; for the first time in my life I experienced such a situation; I was beside myself; I put him quite to shame. Fedora helped me and almost drove him out of the apartment. We decided that this is all the doing of Anna Fyodorovna: otherwise how could he know of us?

Now I turn to you, Makar Alexeyevich, and beg you for help. Do not abandon me, for God's sake, in such a position! Borrow, please, get some money, however little; we have nothing to move out of this lodging with, and to remain here is quite impossible: Fedora advises so too. We need at the very least twenty-five roubles; I will give you this money back; I will earn it; Fedora will find me more work in a few days, so that if high interest holds you back, do not look at it, and agree to everything. I will repay you everything, only, for God's sake, do not leave me without your help. It costs me a great deal to trouble you now, when you are in such circumstances, but all my hope is in you alone! Farewell, Makar Alexeyevich, think of me, and may God grant you success!

It is these unexpected blows that shake me! It is such terrible calamities that kill my spirit! Besides the fact that this rabble of various toadies and vile old fellows wants to bring you, my little angel, to a bed of sickness, besides all this, they, these toadies, want to do away with me as well. And they will do away with me, I take an oath they will! Why, even now I am readier to die than not to help you! If I do not help you, then that is my death, Varenka, a clean, real death, and if I do help you, then you will fly away from me like a little bird from its nest, which these owls, these birds of prey, have gathered to peck to death. That is what torments me, my dearest. And you, Varenka, how cruel you are! How can you? They torment you, they wrong you, you, my little chick, suffer, and on top of it you grieve that you have to trouble me, and you even promise to earn the debt, that is, to tell the truth, you will kill yourself with your weak health in order to bail me out in time. But, Varenka, only think what you are talking about! Why should you sew, why should you work, torment your poor little head with worry, spoil your pretty little eyes and ruin your health? Ah, Varenka, Varenka, you see, my dear, I am good for nothing, and I know myself that I am good for nothing, but I will make it so that I shall be good for something! I will overcome everything, I will find outside work myself, I will copy various papers for various literary men, I will go to them, I will go myself, I will force myself on them for work; because, my dearest, they are looking for good copyists, I know that they are looking, and I will not let you wear yourself out; I will not let you carry out such a ruinous intention. I, my little angel, will certainly borrow, and I will sooner die than not borrow. And you write, my dove, that I should not be frightened by high interest, and I will not be frightened, my dearest, I will not be frightened, I am frightened of nothing now. I, my dearest, will ask for forty roubles in paper money; that is not much, Varenka, what do you think? Can I be trusted with forty roubles at the first word? That is, I mean to say, do you consider me capable of inspiring at first sight probability and confidence? By my physiognomy, at the first glance, can one judge me favourably? You recall, my angel, am I capable of inspiring it? What do you think of it yourself? You know, I feel such a fear, painfully, truly I may say painfully! Of the forty roubles I set aside twenty-five for you, Varenka; two roubles for the landlady, and the rest is destined for my own spending. You see, to the landlady I ought to give more, even necessarily; but consider the whole matter, my dearest, count over all my needs, and you will see that it is quite impossible to give more, and therefore there is no need to speak of it, nor even to mention it. For a silver rouble I will buy boots; I do not know whether I shall be able to appear at the office tomorrow in my old ones. A neck-cloth too would be necessary, for the old one will soon be a year old; but since you have promised to cut out for me from your old apron not only a neck-cloth but a shirt-front, I shall think no more of the neck-cloth. So, there you are, boots and neck-cloth are provided. Now the buttons, my friend! You will agree, my little crumb, that I cannot be without buttons; and almost half of my coat-front has dropped off! I tremble when I think that his Excellency may notice such a disorder and will say, but what will he say! I, my dearest, shall not even hear what he says; for I shall die, die, die on the spot, simply take and die of shame, from the thought alone! Oh, my dearest! And then there will remain, after all necessities, a three-rouble note; so that is for living on and for half a pound of tobacco; because, my little angel, I cannot live without tobacco, and it is now the ninth day that I have not put a pipe in my mouth. I would, in all conscience, buy some and say nothing to you, but I am ashamed. There you are in trouble, you are being deprived of your last, and I here am enjoying various pleasures; so it is for that reason that I tell you all this, so that remorse may not torment you. I confess to you frankly, Varenka, I am now in an extremely wretched position, that is, nothing like it has ever happened to me before. The landlady despises me, there is no respect from anyone; terrible shortages, debts; and at the office, where even before I never had a holiday from my fellow clerks, now, my dearest, there is nothing to be said. I hide, I carefully hide everything from everybody, and hide myself, and when I go into the office, it is sidelong, sidelong, I keep away from everyone. It is only to you that I have the strength of soul to confess it... And what if he does not lend! Well, no, Varenka, it is better not to think of it and not to kill one's soul in advance with such thoughts. I write this to warn you, so that you yourself should not think of it and torment yourself with evil thoughts. Ah, my God, what will become of you then! It is true, too, that then you will not move out of this lodging, and I

will be with you, but no, I shall not come back then, I shall simply vanish somewhere, perish. Here I have scribbled on to you, and I ought to shave, it is all more decent, and decency always knows how to find its way. Well, God grant it! I will pray, and be on my way!

You at least should not despair! There is enough grief as it is. I am sending you thirty silver kopecks; more I cannot possibly manage. Buy yourself there what you need most, so as to live somehow till tomorrow. We ourselves have almost nothing left, and tomorrow I do not know what will be. It is sad, Makar Alexeyevich! However, do not be sad; it did not succeed, so what is to be done! Fedora says that it is not yet a disaster, that we can stay in this lodging for the time being, that if we moved we should gain little, and that if they want to, they will find us anywhere. Only it is somehow not good to stay here now. If I were not so sad, I would write you something.

What a strange character you have, Makar Alexeyevich! You take everything too much to heart; because of that you will always be the unhappiest of men. I read all your letters attentively and I see that in every letter you torment yourself and worry about me as you never worried about yourself. Everyone, of course, will say that you have a kind heart, but I will say that it is too kind. I give you a friend's advice, Makar Alexeyevich. I am grateful to you, very grateful for all that you have done for me, I feel all of it keenly; so judge what it is for me to see that even now, after all your misfortunes, of which I was the involuntary cause, even now you live only by my living: by my joys, my griefs, my heart! If one takes everything of another so to heart and sympathises so strongly with everything, then truly there is reason to be the unhappiest of men. Today, when you came to me after the office, I was frightened looking at you. You were so pale, scared, desperate: you had no face left, and all because you were afraid to tell me of your failure, afraid to grieve me, to frighten me, and when you saw that I almost laughed, almost everything lifted from your heart. Makar Alexeyevich! Do not be sad, do not despair, be more sensible, I ask you, I beg you for this. Well, you will see that everything will be well, everything will change for the better; otherwise it will be hard for you to live, always pining and ailing with another's grief. Farewell, my friend; I beg you, do not worry too much about me.

Well, good, my little angel, good! You have decided that it is no disaster yet that I did not get the money. Well, good, I am calm, I am happy on your account. I am even glad that you do not abandon me, an old man, and that you will stay in this lodging. And, to tell it all, my heart too was filled to overflowing with joy when I saw that you wrote so well of me in your little letter and paid the due praise to my feelings. I do not say this from pride, but because I see how you love me, when you worry so about my heart. Well, good; what is the use of talking now about my heart! The heart is a thing by itself; but here you enjoin me, my dearest, not to be faint-hearted. Yes, my little angel, I will perhaps say myself that it is not needed, this faint-heartedness; but for all that, judge for yourself, my dearest, in what boots shall I go to the office tomorrow! That is the thing, my dearest; and such a thought can ruin a man, utterly ruin him. And the main thing, my dear one, is that I do not grieve for myself, I do not suffer for myself; to me it is all the same if I had to go about in a crackling frost without an overcoat and without boots, I will bear it and endure everything, it is nothing to me; I am a simple, small man, but what will people say? My enemies, those evil tongues, what will they all start saying when you go without an overcoat? After all, you wear an overcoat for the people, and the boots too, perhaps, you wear for them. Boots in such a case, my dearest, my darling, are necessary to me for the support of my honour and good name; and in holey boots both are lost. Believe me, my dearest, believe my long experience; listen to me, an old man who knows the world and people, and not to some scribblers and smearers.

And I have not yet told you in detail, my dearest, how it all really was today, what I suffered today. I suffered, and bore so much burden of the soul in one morning, as another would not bear in a whole year. This is how it was: first of all, I set off at the crack of dawn, so as to catch him in, and still be in time for the office. The rain was such, the slush was such today! I, my sunshine, wrapped myself in my overcoat, and went on and on and kept thinking: "Lord! forgive my sins, and grant the fulfilment of my wishes." Past the church of — I went, crossed myself, repented of all my sins, and remembered that it was unworthy of me to bargain with the Lord God. I sank into myself, and did not want to look at anything; so I went on, not choosing the road. The streets were empty, and those I met were all so busy, so preoccupied, and no wonder: who would go out for a stroll at such an early hour and in such weather! A gang of dirty workmen met me; they jostled me, the peasants! Timidity came over me, I felt uneasy, and, to tell the truth, I did not even want to think about the money; come what may, come what may! Right at Voskresensky Bridge my sole came off, so that I do not know myself what I walked on. And then our scrivener Yermolayev met me, drew himself up, stands there following me with his eyes, as if asking for vodka money; ah, brother, I thought, vodka money, what vodka now! I was terribly tired, I stopped, rested a little, and dragged on further. I deliberately looked about for something to fasten my thoughts on, to distract and cheer myself; but no, I could not fasten a single thought to anything, and besides I had got so dirty that I was ashamed of myself. At last I saw from afar a wooden house, a yellow one, with a mezzanine like a belvedere, well, then, I think, so it is, just as Yemelyan Ivanovich said: Markov's house. (He is the very Markov, my dearest, who lends at interest.) I no longer remembered myself, and though I knew it was Markov's house, I still asked a watchman whose house it was, my good fellow? The watchman was such a boor, he speaks unwillingly, as if angry at somebody, drawing out his words through his teeth, and says it is, indeed, Markov's house. These watchmen are all so insensitive, but what is the watchman to me? Yet somehow the whole impression was bad and unpleasant, in a word, everything piled one upon another; from everything you draw something resembling your own situation, and it is always so. Past the house I made three turns along the street, and the more I walked the worse it became; no, I think, he will not lend, he will not for anything! And I am a stranger, and my business is delicate, and my figure is not impressive; well, I think, let fate decide; so as not to repent afterwards, they will not eat me for trying, and I quietly opened the gate. And then another trouble: a nasty, stupid yard-dog attached itself to me; it bursts its skin barking! And it is just such base, petty incidents, my dearest, that always infuriate a man and fill him with timidity, and destroy all the resolution that he has thought out beforehand; so that I went into the house more dead than alive, went in and, as bad luck would have it, did not make out what was in the dark at the threshold downstairs, stepped and stumbled over some woman, and the woman was straining milk from a pail into jugs and spilled all the milk. The stupid woman squealed and screeched, saying where are you going, my dear sir, what do you want? and began to lament about the evil one. I note this to you, my dearest, because the same thing has always happened to me in affairs of this sort; it must be written for me so; I am forever catching on something extraneous. An old witch of a Finnish landlady looked out at the noise, and I went straight to her: does Markov live here? No, she says; she stood and looked me over well. "And what is he to you?" I explain to her that, so and so, Yemelyan Ivanovich, and the rest, I say, there is a little matter of business. The old woman called her daughter, and the daughter came out too, a girl well on in years, barefooted: "Call your father; he is upstairs with the lodgers; please come in." I went in. The room was all right, pictures hang on the walls, all portraits of some generals, there is a sofa, a round table, mignonette, balsams, I think and think, should I not take myself off, enough, in good health, go away or not? and really, my dearest, I wanted to run away! I had better, I think, come tomorrow; and the weather will be better, and I will wait it out; and today, you see, the milk is spilled, and the generals look so angry... I was already at the door, but he came in, a grey-haired little man, with such thievish little eyes, in a greasy dressing-gown tied with a rope. He inquired what and how, and I said to him: so and so, here is Yemelyan Ivanovich, forty roubles, I say; the matter is such, and did not finish. I saw from his eyes that the case was lost. "No, he says, what business, I have no money; and have you some security, or what?" I began to explain that there is no security, but here is Yemelyan Ivanovich, I explain, in a word, what is needed. Having heard it all, no, he says, what Yemelyan Ivanovich! I have no money. Well, I think, so, it is all as I expected; I knew of this, I foresaw it; well, simply, Varenka, it would have been better if the earth had opened under me; such a cold, my legs went numb, shivers ran down my spine. I look at him, and he looks at me and all but says, you had better go, brother, you have nothing to do here, so that if in another case it were the same I should be quite ashamed. And what do you want the money for? (See what he asked, my dearest!) I opened my mouth, only so as not to stand there for nothing, but he did not even listen: no, he says, I have no money; I would, he says, with pleasure. I represented to him, represented, I say, that I want only a little, I say, I will repay you, I will repay on time, and that I will repay even before the time, that he may take any interest he likes and that I will, by God, repay. I, my dearest, at that moment remembered you, remembered all your misfortunes and needs, remembered your fifty kopecks; but no, he says, what interest, if only there were security! But otherwise I have no money, by God I have none; I would, he says, with pleasure, and he even swore, the robber!

Well, then, my dear one, I do not remember how I came out, how I walked through the Vyborg side, how I got to Voskresensky Bridge, I was terribly tired, chilled, shivering, and only at ten o'clock did I manage to appear at the office. I wanted to clean myself of the mud, but Snegirev, the porter, said it was not allowed, that I would spoil the brush, and the brush, he says, sir, is government property. That is how they are now, my dearest, so that among these gentlemen too I am hardly better than the rag that people wipe their feet on. For what is it that kills me, Varenka? It is not the money that kills me, but all these cares of life, all these whispers, smirks, jokes. His Excellency may somehow chance to remark upon me, oh, my dearest, my golden times have passed! Today I re-read all your letters; it is sad, my dearest! Farewell, my dear one, God keep you!

P. S. My grief, Varenka, I wanted to describe to you half in jest, but it seems the jest will not come to me. I wanted to please you. I will come to see you, my dearest, I will certainly come, tomorrow I will come.
VII: Varvara Alexeyevna! My dear, my dearest! I am lost, we are both lost, both together, irretrievably lost. My reputation, my self-respect, everything is gone! I am ruined, and you are ruined, my dearest, you, together with me, irretrievably ruined! It is I, I who have led you to ruin! They drive me away, my dearest, they despise me, they make a laughing-stock of me, and the landlady has simply begun to scold me; she shouted and shouted at me today, upbraided and upbraided me, put me lower than a chip. And in the evening at Ratazyayev's one of them began to read aloud a draft letter, which I had written to you and dropped by chance out of my pocket. My dearest mother, what a mockery they raised! They praised us and praised us, they laughed and laughed, the traitors! I went in to them and convicted Ratazyayev of treachery; I told him that he is a traitor! And Ratazyayev answered me that I am a traitor myself, that I engage in various intrigues; he says, you hid from us, you, he says, are a Lovelace; and now everyone calls me Lovelace, and I have no other name! Do you hear, my little angel, do you hear, they know everything now, they are informed of everything, and of you, my dear one, they know, and of everything that is yours, they know of everything! And what is more! Even Faldoni has joined in, he is in league with them; I sent him today to the sausage shop to fetch something; he will not go and that is all, he has business, he says! "But you are obliged," I say. "No, he says, I am not obliged, you do not pay my mistress money, so I am not obliged to you." I could not bear the insult from him, an uneducated peasant, and called him a fool; and he said to me, "I heard that from a fool." I thought he said such rudeness to me out of drunkenness, and I said, you are drunk, you peasant, you! and he said to me: "Was it you who treated me? Have you got anything to cure your own hangover; you beg ten kopecks at a time from some woman," and he added: "Ah, and you a gentleman!" That, my dearest, is what it has come to! It is shameful, Varenka, to live! Like some outcast; worse than some passportless vagabond. Heavy calamities! I am lost, simply lost! Irretrievably lost.

Dearest Makar Alexeyevich! Troubles and troubles are upon us, I do not know myself what to do! What will become of you now, and there is poor hope in me; today I burned my left hand with the iron; I dropped it by accident, and bruised and burned myself, both together. It is quite impossible to work, and Fedora has been ill for the third day already. I am in tormenting anxiety. I am sending you thirty silver kopecks; this is almost all that we have left, and, God sees, how I should like to help you now in your needs. It vexes me to tears! Farewell, my friend! You would comfort me very much if you came to us today.

Makar Alexeyevich! What is this with you? You have no fear of God, surely! You will simply drive me out of my mind. Are you not ashamed! You are ruining yourself, only think of your reputation! You are an honest, noble man, full of self-respect, and what if everyone finds out about you! You will simply have to die of shame! Or do you not pity your grey hairs? Have you no fear of God? Fedora said that she will not help you any more now, and I too will not give you money. To what you have brought me, Makar Alexeyevich! You think, surely, that it is nothing to me that you behave so badly; you do not yet know what I suffer because of you! I cannot even go along our staircase: everyone looks at me, points a finger at me and says such terrible things; yes, they say straight out that I have taken up with a drunkard. How is that to hear! When they bring you home, all the lodgers point at you with contempt: there, they say, they have brought that clerk. And I am so ashamed for you that I cannot bear it. I swear to you that I will move out of here. I will go somewhere as a maid, as a laundress, but I will not stay here. I wrote to you to come to see me, and you did not come. So my tears and entreaties are nothing to you, Makar Alexeyevich! And where did you get the money? For the Creator's sake, take care. You will be lost, lost for nothing! And what shame and disgrace! The landlady did not even want to let you in yesterday, you slept in the entry: I know all. If you knew how hard it was for me when I learned it all. Come to me, you will be cheerful with us: we will read together, we will recall old times. Fedora will tell of her pilgrimages. For my sake, my dear, do not ruin yourself and do not ruin me. For I live only for you, and for you I remain with you. And this is how you are now! Be a noble man, firm in misfortunes; remember that poverty is not a vice. And why despair: it is all temporary! God willing, everything will be set right, only you must hold yourself in check now. I am sending you a twenty-kopeck piece, buy yourself tobacco or whatever you wish, only, for God's sake, do not spend it on what is bad. Come to us, be sure to come. You will perhaps, as before, feel ashamed, but do not be ashamed: that is false shame. If only you bring sincere repentance. Hope in God. He will arrange everything for the best.

I am ashamed, my sunshine, Varvara Alexeyevna, quite ashamed. However, what is there so special in it, my dearest? Why should one not cheer one's heart a little? I do not think then about my soles, because a sole is nonsense and will always remain a plain, base, dirty sole. And boots are nonsense too! Even the Greek sages went about without boots, so why should the likes of us fuss over such an unworthy object? Why offend me, why despise me in such a case? Ah! my dearest, my dearest, what a thing to write! And tell Fedora that she is a foolish, restless, boisterous woman and, on top of that, stupid, inexpressibly stupid! As for my grey hair, in that too you are mistaken, my dear one, because I am not at all such an old man as you think. Yemelya sends his regards. You write that you grieved and wept; and I write to you that I too grieved and wept. In conclusion I wish you all health and prosperity, and as for me, I too am well and prosperous, and remain your, my little angel, friend
Dear Madam and kind friend, Varvara Alexeyevna!

I feel that I am to blame, I feel that I have offended against you, and, to my mind, there is no profit in it at all, my dearest, that I feel it all, whatever you may say. I felt all this even before my fault, but I lost heart all the same, lost heart with the consciousness of guilt. My dearest, I am not wicked and not hard-hearted; and to tear your little heart to pieces, my dove, one would have to be neither more nor less than a bloodthirsty tiger, but I have the heart of a lamb, and, as you know, I have no inclination for bloodthirstiness; consequently, my little angel, I am not altogether to blame for my fault, just as neither my heart nor my thoughts are to blame; but so, I do not know what is to blame. It is such a dark affair, my dearest! You sent me thirty silver kopecks, and then you sent a twenty-kopeck piece; my heart ached, looking at your orphan's money. You burned your own hand, you will soon be going hungry, and you write that I should buy tobacco. Well, how was I to act in such a case? Or, without any pangs of conscience, like a robber, begin to rob you, an orphan! That is when I lost heart, my dearest, that is, at first, feeling in spite of myself that I am good for nothing and that I am hardly any better than my own sole, I considered it improper to take myself for anything of importance, but on the contrary began to consider myself something improper and to some degree indecent. Well, and once I lost respect for myself, once I gave myself up to denying my good qualities and my dignity, then all is lost, then comes the fall! It is so fixed by fate, and I am not to blame for it. At first I went out a little to refresh myself. Then everything came together: nature was so tearful, and the weather cold, and rain, and Yemelya turned up there too. He, Varenka, had already pawned everything he had, everything of his had gone to its place, and when I met him he had not had a poppy-seed in his mouth for two days, so that he wanted to pawn such a thing as cannot be pawned at all, because there are no such pledges. Well, Varenka, I yielded more out of compassion for humanity than from my own inclination. That is how this sin came about, my dearest! How we wept together! We remembered you. He is very kind, he is a very kind man, and extremely sensitive. I, my dearest, feel all this myself; that is why everything like this happens to me, because I feel it all so much. I know what I owe to you, my dear! Having come to know you, I began, first, to know myself better, and I began to love you; and before you, my little angel, I was lonely and as if asleep, not living in the world. They, my villains, said that even my figure was improper, and loathed me, well, and I began to loathe myself; they said I was dull, and I really thought I was dull, but when you appeared to me, you lit up all my dark life, so that both my heart and my soul were lit up, and I found peace of mind and learned that I too am no worse than others; that only I do not shine in anything, I have no polish, no tone, but all the same I am a man, that in heart and thoughts I am a man. Well, and now, feeling that I am persecuted by fate, that, humiliated by it, I have given myself up to denying my own dignity, I, weighed down by my misfortunes, have lost heart. And since you now know everything, my dearest, I implore you with tears not to inquire any more about this matter, for my heart is breaking, and it is bitter and heavy.
Testifying to you, my dearest, my respect, I remain your faithful
VIII: I did not finish my last letter, Makar Alexeyevich, because it was hard for me to write. There are moments sometimes when I am glad to be alone, to grieve alone, to pine alone, with no one to share it, and such moments come over me more and more often. There is something in my memories that I cannot explain to myself, something that draws me so helplessly, so strongly, that for hours at a time I am numb to everything around me and forget everything, everything of the present. And there is no impression in my life now, pleasant or hard or sad, that does not remind me of something like it in my past, and most often of my childhood, my golden childhood! But I always feel heavy after such moments. I grow weaker somehow, my dreaming wears me out, and my health, as it is, is getting worse and worse.

But today a fresh, bright, shining morning, such as we rarely have here in autumn, revived me, and I welcomed it gladly. So, autumn is with us already! How I loved the autumn in the country! I was still a child, but even then I felt a great deal. I loved an autumn evening more than the morning. I remember that two steps from our house, below the hill, there was a lake. That lake — I seem to see it now — that lake was so wide, so bright, so clear, like crystal! Sometimes, if the evening was still, the lake was calm; on the trees growing along the shore not a leaf stirred, and the water was motionless, like a mirror. Fresh! Cold! The dew falls on the grass, little lights glimmer in the cottages on the shore, the herd is driven home — and that is just when I would slip quietly out of the house to look at my lake, and I would stand gazing and gazing. A bundle of brushwood burns beside the fishermen right at the water's edge, and the light pours far, far across the water. The sky is so cold and blue, and all along its edges it is streaked with red, fiery bands, and these bands grow paler and paler; the moon comes out; the air is so ringing that if a frightened little bird flutters up, or the reeds rustle in a light breeze, or a fish splashes in the water — you could hear everything. A white mist rises over the blue water, thin and transparent. The distance darkens; everything seems to drown in the haze, but close by everything is so sharply cut, as if with a chisel — the boat, the shore, the islands; some barrel, thrown away and forgotten right at the shore, barely rocks on the water; a willow branch with yellowed leaves tangles in the reeds — and a belated gull flutters up, now dips into the cold water, now flutters up again and vanishes in the mist. I would stand gazing, stand listening — it was wonderfully good to me! And I was still a child, a little child!...

I loved the autumn so — the late autumn, when the harvest is already in and all the work is done, when the evening gatherings in the cottages have begun, when everyone is already waiting for winter. Then everything grows gloomier, the sky frowns with clouds, yellow leaves lie in paths along the edges of the bare forest, and the forest turns blue, turns black — especially in the evening, when a damp fog settles and the trees loom out of the fog like giants, like ugly, terrible phantoms. Sometimes I would be late on a walk, fall behind the others, and go on alone, hurrying — and it was eerie! You tremble yourself like a leaf; any moment, you think, someone frightful will look out from behind that hollow tree; and meanwhile the wind sweeps through the forest, hums, rustles, howls so plaintively, tears a cloud of leaves from the withered branches and whirls them in the air, and after them, in a long, broad, noisy flock, with a wild piercing cry, birds fly past, so that the sky goes black and everything is covered with them. You grow frightened, and then — as if you actually heard someone — someone's voice, as if someone were whispering: "Run, run, child, don't be late; it will be terrible here in a moment, run, child!" — and horror passes through the heart, and you run and run until your breath is gone. You come running home, out of breath; at home it is noisy and merry; they hand out work to all us children: shelling peas or poppy seeds. The damp logs crackle in the stove; mother looks cheerfully on at our cheerful work; old nurse Ulyana tells of the old days, or frightening tales about wizards and the dead. We children huddle close together, and every face has a smile. And then suddenly we all fall silent

at once... hush! a noise! as if someone were knocking! It was nothing; it was old Frolovna's spinning wheel humming; how we laughed! And afterwards at night we cannot sleep for fear; such terrible dreams come. You wake up, and you dare not move, and you shiver under the blanket until dawn. In the morning you get up fresh as a flower. You look out of the window: frost has gripped the whole field; thin autumn rime hangs on the bare twigs; the lake is covered with ice as thin as a leaf; a white mist rises over the lake; merry birds are calling. The sun shines all around with bright rays, and the rays shatter the thin ice like glass. Bright, brilliant, merry! The fire crackles again in the stove; we all sit down around the samovar, and at the window our black dog Polkan, chilled through the night, looks in and wags his tail in a friendly way. A peasant drives past the windows on a brisk little horse, into the forest for firewood. Everyone is so contented, so cheerful!... Ah, what a golden childhood I had!...

And now I have burst into tears like a child, carried away by my memories. I have recalled everything so vividly, so vividly, the whole past has become so bright before me, and the present is so dim, so dark!... How will it end, how will it all end? Do you know, I have some conviction, some certainty, that I shall die this autumn. I am very, very ill. I often think that I shall die, but still I should not like to die like this — to lie in this earth here. Perhaps I shall take to my bed again, as I did then, in the spring, and I have not yet had time to recover. Even now it is very hard for me. Fedora has gone out somewhere for the whole day today, and I am sitting alone. And for some time now I have been afraid of being left alone; it keeps seeming to me that there is someone else in the room with me, that someone is speaking to me; especially when I fall to thinking about something and suddenly come to myself, so that I become frightened. That is why I have written you such a long letter; when I write, it passes. Farewell: I am ending the letter, because I have neither paper nor time. Of the money I got for my dresses and my hat, I have only one silver rouble left. You gave the landlady two silver roubles; that was very good; she will be quiet now for a while.

Do mend your own clothes somehow. Farewell; I am so tired; I do not understand why I am becoming so weak; the slightest occupation exhausts me. If work should come — how shall I work? That is just what is killing me.

I have gone through a great many impressions today, my little angel. First of all, my head ached the whole day. To refresh myself somehow, I went out for a walk along the Fontanka. The evening was so dark and damp. By five o'clock it is already growing dusk — just as it is now! There was no rain, but there was fog, no worse than good rain. Clouds moved across the sky in long, broad bands. A multitude of people were walking along the embankment, and as if on purpose the people had such dreadful, depressing faces — drunken peasants, snub-nosed Finnish women in boots and bareheaded, labourers, cab drivers, our own kind about some business or other; boys, some locksmith's apprentice in a striped smock, gaunt, sickly, his face bathed in smoked oil, with a lock in his hand; a discharged soldier, six feet tall — such was the public. It must have been the sort of hour when there could be no other public. The Fontanka, a navigable canal! So many barges that you cannot understand where they could all be fitted in. On the bridges sit women with damp gingerbread and rotten apples, and all such dirty, wet women. It is dreary walking along the Fontanka! Wet granite underfoot, on both sides tall, black, sooty houses; fog beneath your feet, fog above your head too. Such a sad, such a dark evening it was today.

When I turned into Gorokhovaya it was already quite dark and they were beginning to light the gas. I had not been on Gorokhovaya for a good while — I had not had the chance. A noisy street! What shops, what rich stores; everything simply shines and blazes, fabrics, flowers under glass, all sorts of hats with ribbons. You would think it was all laid out just for show — but no: there are people who buy all this and give it to their wives. A rich street! A great many German bakers live on Gorokhovaya; they too must be quite well-to-do people. What a number of carriages go by every minute; how does the pavement bear it all! Such splendid equipages, windows like mirrors, velvet and silk inside; the noblemen's footmen in epaulettes, with swords. I looked into every carriage, and in every one there sat ladies, so richly dressed, perhaps princesses and countesses. It must have been the hour when everyone was hurrying to the balls and assemblies. It is curious to see a princess, or any grand lady, close at hand; it must be very fine; I have never seen one — except as now, by glancing into a carriage. I thought of you there. Ah, my dear, my own! When I think of you now, my whole heart aches! Why are you so unfortunate, Varenka? My little angel! In what way are you any worse than all of them? You are good, you are lovely, you are educated; why then should such a cruel fate fall to your lot? Why does it always happen that a good person is left in desolation, while happiness comes begging to another? I know, I know, my dearest, that it is wrong to think this, that it is free-thinking; but in all sincerity, in truth, why does one man have happiness croaked over him by the raven of fate while he is still in his mother's womb, and another comes into God's world from the foundling hospital? And it happens, too, that happiness often falls to Ivanushka the Fool. "You, Ivanushka the Fool," it says, "rummage in your grandfather's sacks, drink, eat, make merry, and you, you so-and-so, just lick your lips; that is all you are good for, brother, that is what you are!" It is a sin, my dearest, it is a sin to think so, but somehow the sin creeps into the soul in spite of you. If only you too rode in a carriage like that, my own, my bright one. Generals would be catching your gracious glance, let alone our humble kind; you would be walking not in a thin old linen dress, but in silk and gold. You would not be thin and sickly as you are now, but like a little sugar figure, fresh, rosy, plump. And I should be happy then just to look at you from the street into your brightly lit windows, just to see your shadow; at the mere thought that you were happy and gay there, my pretty little bird, I should be glad myself. But now what! It is not enough that wicked people have ruined you; some worthless wretch, some good-for-nothing, insults you. Because his coat sits on him like a peacock, because he looks at you through a gold lorgnette, the shameless fellow, he gets away with everything, and we must listen indulgently even to his indecent talk! Enough, is that how it should be, my dears! And why is it all so? It is because you are an orphan, because you are defenceless, because you have no strong friend to give you decent support. And what kind of man is that, what kind of people are they, to whom insulting an orphan is nothing? They are rubbish, not people, simply rubbish; they only count as people, but in fact they do not exist, of that I am sure. That is what they are, these people! And in my opinion, my dear, that organ-grinder I met today on Gorokhovaya inspires more respect than they do. He goes about all day and toils, waiting for some stale, worthless kopeck to live on, but he is his own master, he feeds himself. He does not want to beg for alms; instead, for

people's pleasure he works like a wound-up machine — here, he says, is what I can do, I will bring you pleasure. A beggar, a beggar he is, true, the same beggar still; but a noble beggar; he is tired, he is frozen, but he keeps working, in his own way, but still he works. And there are many honest people, my dearest, who earn a little, according to the measure and usefulness of their labour, but bow to no one and beg bread of no one. And I am just the same as this organ-grinder — that is, not that, not at all like him, but in my own sense, in the noble sense, the gentleman's sense, just the same as he is; I work as far as my strength goes, with what I can, as they say. More than that is not in me; well, there is no judging what is not there.

I started on that organ-grinder, my dearest, because it happened that today I felt my poverty doubly. I stopped to look at the organ-grinder. Such thoughts were coming into my head — so, to distract myself, I stopped. I stood there, cab drivers were standing there, some girl, and a little girl as well, all so dirty. The organ-grinder had set himself up in front of somebody's windows. I notice a little fellow, a boy of about ten; he would have been pretty, but he looked so sick, so sickly, in just a shirt and something else, almost barefoot, standing with his mouth open, listening to the music — childhood! He was gazing at how the German's puppets dance, and his own hands and feet were numb, and he was shivering and gnawing the end of his sleeve. I notice that he has a little paper in his hand. A gentleman passed by and threw the organ-grinder some small coin; the coin fell straight into that box with the little fence where a Frenchman is shown dancing with ladies. As soon as the coin clinked, my boy started, looked timidly around and, it seems, took me for the one who had given the money. He ran up to me, his little hands trembling, his little voice trembling, held out the paper to me and said: a note! I unfolded the note — well, what, it is the usual thing: my benefactors, the mother of the children is dying, three children are starving, so help us now, and when I die, then, for not forgetting my little ones now, I shall not forget you in the other world, my benefactors. Well, what of it; it is plain, it is the way of life, and what could I give them? Well, and I gave him nothing. And how sorry I was! A poor boy, blue with cold, perhaps hungry too, and he is not lying, upon my word, he is not lying; I know about these things. Only it is bad that these wretched mothers do not look after their children, and send them half-naked with notes in such cold. She may be a stupid woman, with no character; and perhaps there is no one to look after her, so she sits with her legs tucked under her, and perhaps she really is ill. Well, one should apply to the proper place; but then, perhaps she is simply a swindler, and sends the hungry, sickly child on purpose to deceive people, and makes him ill. And what will the poor boy learn with these notes? Only his heart is hardened; he goes, he runs, he begs. People pass by, but they have no time. Their hearts are of stone; their words are cruel. "Away! Get out! Go on with you!" That is what he hears from everyone, and the child's heart hardens, and the poor, frightened boy shivers in vain in the cold, like a nestling fallen from a broken nest. His hands and feet are freezing; his breath is short. Look, he is already coughing; it will not be long before the sickness crawls into his chest like a foul reptile, and then, you see, death is already standing over him, in some stinking corner, without care, without help — and that is his whole life! That is how life can be! Oh, Varenka, it is torment to hear "for Christ's sake" and to pass by and give nothing, to tell him: "God will provide." Some "for Christ's sake" is still not so bad. (And there are different kinds of "for Christ's sake" too, my dearest.) Some is long, drawn-out, habitual, learned by rote, plain beggar's talk; it is not so tormenting not to give to that; this is a long-standing beggar, an old one, a beggar by trade, you think, he is used to it, he will get by and knows how to get by. But some "for Christ's sake" is unaccustomed, rough, terrible — like today, when I had just taken the note from the boy, and a man was standing there by the fence, not asking everyone, and he says to me: "Give a groat, sir, for Christ's sake!" — and in such an abrupt, rough voice that I shuddered with some dreadful feeling, and did not give the groat: I had none. And then, rich people do not like the poor to complain aloud about their hard lot — they say they disturb them, they are importunate! And poverty is always importunate — perhaps their hungry groans keep them from sleeping!

To tell you the truth, my own, I began to describe all this to you partly to ease my heart, but more to show you a sample of the good style of my compositions. For you will surely admit yourself, my dearest, that my style has lately been forming. But now such melancholy has come over me that I have begun to sympathize with my own thoughts to the depths of my soul, and although I know myself, my dearest, that you do not get far by this sympathy, still in a way you do justice to yourself. And truly, my own, one often belittles oneself without any reason, thinks nothing of oneself, and ranks oneself lower than some chip of wood. And if I may use a comparison, perhaps this comes from my being frightened and hunted down myself, just like that poor little boy who begged alms of me. Now I shall speak to you, for example, in a figure, my dearest; just listen to me: it happens to me, my own, early in the morning, hurrying to the office, to stop and gaze at the city, how it awakens there, rises, smokes, seethes, thunders — and then sometimes before such a sight you shrink so, as if someone had given your curious nose a flick, and you trudge along your way quieter than water, lower than grass, and give up with a wave of the hand! Now look at what is going on inside those black, sooty, big, solid houses, look into it, and then judge for yourself whether it was right to rank myself so senselessly and fall into unworthy confusion. Notice, Varenka, that I am speaking in a figure, not in the literal sense. Well, let us see what there is in those houses. There, in some smoky corner, in some damp kennel which, out of necessity, is counted as lodgings, some workman has woken from sleep; and in his sleep, let us say, he dreamed all night of boots, which yesterday he happened to cut wrongly, as if just such trash should be what a man dreams of! Well, but he is a workman, he is a cobbler: it is forgivable that he thinks of one subject only. He has children squealing there and a hungry wife; and it is not only cobblers, my dear, who get up like that sometimes. That would be nothing, and not worth writing about, but here is the circumstance that comes out of it, my dearest: right there, in the same house, a floor above or below, in gilded halls, the richest person may also have dreamed of the same boots in the night — that is, boots of another sort, of another style, but boots all the same; for in the sense I mean here, my dearest, all of us, my own, turn out to be a little bit cobblers. And that would be nothing either, but it is bad that there is no one near this richest person, no one to whisper in his ear: "Enough, enough of thinking of such things, of thinking only of yourself, of living only for yourself; you are not a cobbler, your children are healthy and your wife asks for nothing; look around, do you not see a more noble object for your cares than your own boots!" That is what I wanted to say to you in a figure, Varenka. It may be too bold a thought, my own, but the thought comes sometimes, and then it bursts from the heart in a hot word in spite of you. And so there was no reason to value myself at a groat, frightened by one noise and thunder! Let me finish, my dearest, since you may think that I am speaking slander to you, or that it is just some fit of the spleen come over me, or that I have copied it out of some book? No, my dearest, put that out of your mind — it is not so: I abhor slander, no spleen has come over me, and I have copied nothing out of any book — so there!

I came home in a sad frame of mind, sat down at the table, heated my little kettle, and got ready to drink a glass or two of tea. Suddenly I see Gorshkov coming in to me, our poor lodger. I had already noticed in the morning that he kept slinking about among the tenants and wanted to come up to me. And in passing I will say, my dearest, that their way of living is incomparably worse than mine. Why, a wife, children! So that if I were Gorshkov I do not know what I should do in his place! Well, so my Gorshkov came in, bowed, a tear, as always, festering on his eyelashes, shuffling his feet, and unable to say a word. I seated him on a chair, a broken one, true, but there was no other. I offered him tea. He apologized, apologized at length, but finally took the glass. He wanted to drink it without sugar, began apologizing again when I began to insist that he must take sugar, argued a long time, refusing, finally put the very smallest piece in his glass and began assuring me that the tea was extraordinarily sweet. Ah, to what abasement poverty brings people! "Well, how is it, my good man?" I said to him. "Why, it is this and that, my benefactor Makar Alexeyevich, show God's mercy, give help to an unfortunate family; children and a wife, nothing to eat; and how is it for the father, for me?" he says. I was about to speak, but he interrupted me: "I am afraid of everyone here, Makar Alexeyevich, that is, not afraid, but, you know, ashamed; they are all so proud and haughty. I would not trouble you, my dear sir and benefactor," he says, "for I know you have had unpleasantness yourself, I know that you cannot give much, but lend me something, anything; and I have dared to ask you," he says, "because I know your kind heart, I know you have been in want yourself, that you are even now suffering troubles — and that is why your heart feels compassion." And he ended by saying: forgive my boldness and my impropriety, Makar Alexeyevich. I answer him that I would be glad with all my soul, but that I have nothing, absolutely nothing. "My dear sir, Makar Alexeyevich," he says to me, "I do not ask much, but it is this and that" (here he turned quite red) "my wife, my children, we are hungry — even some ten-kopeck piece." Well, then my own heart ached. How they outdo me, I think! And all I had left was twenty kopecks, and I was counting on them: I meant to spend them tomorrow on my most pressing needs. "No, my dear fellow, I cannot; it is this and that," I say. "My dear sir, Makar Alexeyevich, whatever you like," he says, "even ten little kopecks." Well, I took out of the drawer and gave him my twenty kopecks, my dearest — a good deed all the same! Ah, poverty! I fell into talk with him: but how is it, my good man, I ask, that you are so in need, and yet in such need you rent a room at five silver roubles? He explained to me that he had taken it half a year ago and paid the money in advance for three months; and then circumstances came together so that he, poor man, could go neither this way nor that. He had been waiting for his case to be finished by this time. And his case is an unpleasant one. He is, you see, Varenka, answerable before the court for something. He is at law with some merchant who cheated on a contract with the treasury; the fraud was discovered, the merchant was brought to trial, and he dragged Gorshkov into his robbers' business, Gorshkov having happened to be involved there somehow too. And in truth Gorshkov is guilty only of negligence, of carelessness and of an unforgivable oversight of the interests of the treasury. The case has been going on for several years: all sorts of obstacles keep meeting Gorshkov. "Of the dishonour laid on me," Gorshkov tells me, "I am innocent, quite innocent, innocent of fraud and robbery." The case has stained him a little; he was dismissed from the service, and although they did not find him gravely guilty, until he is completely cleared he cannot to this day recover from the merchant some considerable sum of money due to him, which the merchant disputes before the court. I believe him, but the court does not take his word; the case is one of such hooks and knots that you could not untangle it in a hundred years. They have hardly begun to untangle it when the merchant adds another hook and another hook. I take a sincere interest in Gorshkov, my own, I feel for him. A man without a post; because he is unreliable he is not taken on anywhere; what stores he had have been eaten up; the case is tangled; and meanwhile one had to live; and meanwhile, out of the blue, quite inopportunely, a child was born — well, there is the expense; the son fell ill — expense, died — expense; his wife is sick; he is unwell with some chronic illness: in a word, he has suffered, suffered fully. However, he says he expects a favourable decision in his case any day now and that there is no longer any doubt of it. I am sorry, sorry, very sorry for him, my dearest! I was kind to him. He is a lost, entangled man; he seeks protection, so I was kind to him. Well, farewell, my dearest, Christ be with you, be well. My dear one! When I think of you, it is as if I were applying medicine to my aching soul, and though I suffer for you, even suffering for you is easy for me.

I write to you beside myself. I am all in a flutter over a dreadful event. My head is spinning round and round. I feel that everything around me is spinning. Ah, my own, what I shall tell you now! We had no foreboding of this. No, I do not believe that I had none; I foresaw it all. My heart heard it all beforehand! Why, only the other day I even saw something like it in a dream.

Here is what happened! I shall tell you without style, just as the Lord puts it on my soul. I went to the office today. I arrived, I sit, I write. And you must know, my dearest, that I was writing yesterday too. Well, so yesterday Timofei Ivanovich comes up to me and in person deigns to instruct me that — here, he says, is a needed paper, an urgent one. Copy it, Makar Alexeyevich, he says, cleanly, quickly and carefully: it goes up for signature today. I must tell you, my little angel, that yesterday I was not myself, I did not want to look at anything; such sadness, such melancholy came over me! My heart was cold, my soul was dark; in my memory there was only you, my poor bright one. Well, so I set about copying; I copied it clean, well, only I do not know how to say it more exactly to you, whether the unclean one himself led me astray, or whether it was decreed by some secret fate, or whether it simply had to happen so — only I skipped a whole line; the sense that came out, the Lord knows what it was, in fact none came out at all. The paper was late yesterday and was presented to his Excellency for signature only today. I, as if nothing had happened, appear today at the usual hour and settle myself side by side with Yemelyan Ivanovich. I must remark, my own, that lately I have become twice as shy and ashamed as before. Recently I have not even looked at anyone. If someone's chair so much as creaks, I am more dead than alive. Just so today, I huddled, I kept quiet, I sat like a hedgehog, so that Yefim Akimovich (such a teaser as there never was in the world before him) said aloud to everyone: why, Makar Alexeyevich, do you sit so — oo-oo-oo? and made such a grimace that everyone around him and me simply rolled with laughter, and of course at my expense. And they went on and on! I pressed back my ears and shut my eyes, and sat without stirring. That is my way; so they leave off sooner. Suddenly I hear a noise, a running about, a bustle; I hear — do my ears deceive me? — they are calling me, demanding me, calling Devushkin. My heart trembled in my breast, and I do not know myself what I was afraid of; I only know that I was more frightened than I have ever been in my life. I grew fast to my chair — and as if nothing had happened, as if it were not I. But now they begin again, nearer and nearer. Now it is right at my ear: Devushkin! Devushkin! where is Devushkin? I raise my eyes: before me stands Yevstafy Ivanovich; he says: "Makar Alexeyevich, to his Excellency, quickly! What trouble you have made with that paper!" That was all he said, but enough, was it not, my dearest, enough was said? I went dead, I turned to ice, I lost my senses, I go — well, simply more dead than alive I set off. They lead me through one room, through another room, through a third room, into the study — I stood before him! I cannot give you a positive account of what I was thinking then. I see his Excellency standing, and all of them round him. I think I did not bow; I forgot. I was so dumbfounded that my lips trembled and my legs trembled. And there was reason, my dearest. In the first place, I was ashamed; I glanced to the right into the mirror, and simply what I saw there was enough to drive one mad. And in the second place, I had always behaved as if I did not exist in the world at all. So that his Excellency was hardly aware of my existence. Perhaps they had heard, in passing, that in their department there is a Devushkin, but they had never entered into closer dealings with him.

He began angrily: "How is this, sir! What are you thinking of? An important paper, needed in a hurry, and you spoil it. And how can you" — here his Excellency turned to Yevstafy Ivanovich. I only hear the sounds of the words reaching me: "Negligence! Carelessness! You land us in trouble!" I opened my mouth for something. I wanted to beg forgiveness, but could not; to run away — I did not dare attempt it, and then... then, my dearest, such a thing happened that even now I can scarcely hold the pen for shame. My button — the devil take it — the button that was hanging on its little thread — suddenly broke off, sprang away, began to hop (I must have caught it by accident), jingled, rolled, and straight, straight, the accursed thing, to the feet of his Excellency, and this in the middle of the general silence! That was my whole justification, my whole excuse, my whole answer, all that I had meant to say to his Excellency! The consequences were terrible! His Excellency at once turned his attention to my figure and my costume. I remembered what I had seen in the mirror: I rushed to catch the button! A foolishness came over me! I bent down, I want to take the button — it rolls, it spins, I cannot catch it; in short, I distinguished myself in dexterity as well. Then I feel that my last strength is leaving me, that all, all is lost! My whole reputation is lost, the whole man is ruined! And then, in both my ears, out of nowhere, both Teresa and Faldoni begin ringing. At last I caught the button, got up, drew myself straight, and if I was a fool, I should have stood quietly, hands at my sides! But no: I began fitting the button to the torn threads, as if it would stick that way; and I am even smiling, I am even smiling. His Excellency turned away at first, then looked at me again — I hear him say to Yevstafy Ivanovich: "How is this?... look at the state he is in!... how he!... what he!..." Ah, my own, what is there — how he? What he? He distinguished himself! I hear Yevstafy Ivanovich say: "Never noticed, never noticed in anything, of exemplary conduct, sufficient salary, according to his rank..." "Well, relieve him somehow," says his Excellency. "Give him an advance..." "But he has drawn, they say, he has drawn, drawn so much in advance for so long a time. The circumstances, no doubt, are such, but his conduct is good, and he has never been noticed, never noticed." I, my little angel, burned, I burned in hellfire! I was dying! "Well," says his Excellency aloud, "copy it again quickly; Devushkin, come here, copy it again without a mistake; and listen..." Then his Excellency turned to the others, gave various orders, and they all dispersed. As soon as they had dispersed, his Excellency hurriedly takes out a pocketbook and from it a hundred-rouble note. "Here," he says, "what I can; reckon it as you like..." — and thrust it into my hand. I, my angel, started; my whole soul shook; I do not know what was happening to me; I wanted to seize his little hand. And he turned all red, my dear one, and — here I do not depart by a hair from the truth, my own — he took my unworthy hand and shook it, just took it and shook it, as if I were his equal, as if I were just such a general as himself. "Go," he says, "what I can... Make no mistakes, and now we are quits."

Now, my dearest, here is what I have decided: I ask you and Fedora, and if I had children I would command them too, to pray to God, that is, so: not to pray for their own father, but for his Excellency daily and forever! I will say more, my dearest, and I say it solemnly — listen to me well, my dearest — I swear that however I perished of anguish of soul in the cruel days of our misfortune, looking at you, at your sufferings, and at myself, at my humiliation and my incapacity, in spite of all that, I swear to you that the hundred roubles are not so dear to me as the fact that his Excellency himself deigned to shake my unworthy hand, the hand of a straw, a drunkard! By that he gave me back to myself. By that act he resurrected my spirit, made life sweeter to me for ever, and I am firmly convinced that, sinful as I am before the Almighty, my prayer for the happiness and prosperity of his Excellency will reach his throne!...

My dearest! I am now in terrible disorder of soul, in terrible agitation! My heart beats, it wants to leap out of my breast. And I myself am somehow weak all over. I am sending you forty-five roubles in paper money, I give twenty roubles to the landlady, I keep thirty-five for myself: with twenty I shall mend my clothes, and fifteen I shall keep for living. Only now all these morning impressions have shaken my whole being. I shall lie down. I am, however, at peace, very much at peace. Only my soul aches, and I can hear down there in its depths my soul trembling, quivering, stirring. I shall come to see you; but now I am simply drunk with all these sensations... God sees everything, my dearest, my dove, my priceless one!

I am inexpressibly glad of your good fortune, and I know how to value the virtues of your superior, my friend. So now you will rest from your grief! But only, for God's sake, do not waste your money again. Live quietly, as modestly as you can, and from this very day begin always to put aside something, so that misfortunes may not catch you suddenly again. Please, for God's sake, do not worry about us. Fedora and I shall manage somehow. Why did you send us so much money, Makar Alexeyevich? We do not need it at all. We are content with what we have. It is true that we shall soon need money for moving from this lodging, but Fedora hopes to get an old, long-standing debt from someone. I am keeping, however, twenty roubles for urgent needs. The rest I am sending back to you. Please take care of your money, Makar Alexeyevich. Farewell. Live peacefully now, be well and cheerful. I would write you more, but I feel terribly tired; yesterday I did not get out of bed the whole day. You did well to promise to come. Do visit me, please, Makar Alexeyevich.

I implore you, my own, do not part from me now, now, when I am perfectly happy and content with everything. My dear one! Do not listen to Fedora, and I shall do whatever you please; I shall behave well, out of respect alone for his Excellency I shall behave well and punctually; we shall again write each other happy letters, we shall confide to each other our thoughts, our joys, our cares, if there are any cares; we shall live together, in harmony and happiness. We shall take up literature... My little angel! In my fate everything has changed, and all has changed for the better. The landlady has grown more agreeable, Teresa wiser, even Faldoni himself has become somehow brisk. I have made peace with Ratazyayev. I went to him myself, in my joy. He is really a good fellow, my dearest, and all the bad things they said about him were nonsense. I have discovered now that it was all a vile slander. He never even thought of describing us: he told me so himself. He read me his new work. And as for his calling me a Lovelace that time: that was not abuse or any improper name: he explained it to me. The word is taken literally from the foreign tongue and means a brisk fellow, and to put it more prettily, more literarily, it means a lad — not to be trifled with — there! and not anything of that kind at all. It was an innocent joke, my little angel. It was I, the ignoramus, who foolishly took offence. But I have already apologized to him... And the weather is so remarkable today, Varenka, so fine. True, in the morning there was a little drizzle, as if sifted through a sieve. No matter! The air has become a little fresher for it. I went to buy boots and bought wonderful boots. I strolled along the Nevsky. I read the "Bee." Yes! I am forgetting to tell you the main thing.

This morning I got into a talk with Yemelyan Ivanovich and Aksenty Mikhailovich about his Excellency. Yes, Varenka, he did not treat only me so kindly. He has not been a benefactor to me alone, and he is known throughout the world for the goodness of his heart. From many places praises are sent up in his honour and tears of gratitude are shed. An orphan girl was brought up in his house. He deigned to settle her: he married her to a well-known man, a clerk who was employed on special commissions under his Excellency himself. He placed the son of a widow in some office, and he has shown many other kindnesses besides. I thought it my duty, my dearest, to lay my mite there too, and I told everyone aloud of his Excellency's action; I told them everything and concealed nothing. I put my shame in my pocket. What shame is there here, what pride at such a time! Right out loud — let the deeds of his Excellency be glorious! I spoke with feeling, I spoke with fire, and I did not blush; on the contrary, I was proud that I had such a thing to tell. I told it all (only about you I prudently kept silent, my dearest), and about my landlady, and about Faldoni, and about Ratazyayev, and about the boots, and about Markov — I told it all. A few of them were smirking there; yes, true, they were all smirking. Only in my figure, no doubt, they found something funny, or about my boots — precisely about my boots. But with any bad intention they could not have done it. It is so, youth, or because they are rich men, but with a bad, with a malicious intention they could by no means have laughed at my speech. That is, anything against his Excellency — that they could by no means have done. Is it not so, Varenka?

I still cannot somehow collect myself, my dearest. All these events have so confused me! Have you firewood? Do not catch cold, Varenka; it does not take long to catch cold. Oh, my dearest, you kill me with your sad thoughts. I am praying to God, how I pray to Him for you, my dearest! For example, have you woollen stockings, or some other warmer clothing. Take care, my dear one. If you need anything there, then for the Creator's sake, do not offend an old man. Just come straight to me. The bad times are past now. Do not worry about me. Ahead everything is so bright, so good!

And it was a sad time, Varenka! Well, no matter, it is past! When the years go by, we shall sigh even over this time. I remember my young years. Ah, yes! Sometimes not a kopeck. Cold, hungry, but merry, and that is all. In the morning you walk along the Nevsky, meet a pretty little face, and you are happy for the whole day. A glorious, glorious time it was, my dearest! It is good to live in the world, Varenka! Especially in Petersburg. Yesterday, with tears in my eyes, I repented before the Lord God, that the Lord might forgive me all my sins in that sad time: murmuring, liberal thoughts, debauchery and gambling. I remembered you with tenderness in my prayer. You alone, my little angel, strengthened me, you alone comforted me, sent me on my way with good advice and instruction. That, my dearest, I can never forget. I have kissed all your little notes today, my dear one! Well, farewell, my dearest. They say there is some clothing for sale somewhere near here. So I shall just look in a little. Farewell then, my little angel. Farewell.

I am in terrible agitation. Listen to what has happened to us. I have a presentiment of something fatal. Judge for yourself, my priceless friend: Mr. Bykov is in Petersburg. Fedora met him. He was driving, ordered the droshky to stop, came up to Fedora himself, and began to inquire where she lives. She at first would not say. Then he said, smiling, that he knew who was living with her. (Evidently Anna Fyodorovna told him everything.) Then Fedora could not bear it, and right there in the street began to reproach him, to rebuke him, told him that he is an immoral man, that he is the cause of all my misfortunes. He answered that when a man has not a kopeck, of course he is unhappy. Fedora told him that I could have managed to live by my work, could have married, or else found some situation, and that now my happiness is lost for ever, that I am moreover ill and shall soon die. To this he remarked that I am still too young, that I still have things fermenting in my head, and that our virtues too have grown tarnished (his words). Fedora and I thought that he did not know our lodging, when suddenly yesterday, just as I had gone out to the Gostiny Dvor for shopping, he walked into our room; it seems he did not want to find me at home. He questioned Fedora a long time about our way of life; he examined everything we have; he looked at my work, and finally asked: "And what clerk is that who is acquainted with you?" Just at that moment you were crossing the yard; Fedora pointed you out to him; he looked and smiled; Fedora begged him to leave, told him that I was already unwell from troubles and that seeing him in our home would be very disagreeable to me.
