He said nothing; he said that he had come just so, with nothing to do, and wanted to give Fedora twenty-five roubles; she, of course, did not take it. What could this mean? Why did he come to us? I cannot understand how he knows everything about us! I am lost in conjectures. Fedora says that Aksinya, her sister-in-law, who comes to see us, is acquainted with the laundress Nastasya, and Nastasya's cousin is a watchman in the department where an acquaintance of Anna Fyodorovna's nephew serves, so perhaps the gossip crept over somehow? However, it is quite possible that Fedora is mistaken; we do not know what to think. Is it possible that he will come to us again! The very thought terrifies me! When Fedora told me all this yesterday, I was so frightened that I almost fainted with fear. What more do they want? I do not want to know them now! What business have they with me, poor me! Ah! in what fear I am now; I keep thinking that Bykov will walk in this very minute. What will become of me! What else has fate in store for me? For Christ's sake, come to me at once, Makar Alexeyevich. Come, for God's sake, come.

Today something happened in our lodgings that was terribly sad, quite inexplicable and quite unexpected. Our poor Gorshkov (you must take note of this, my dearest) has been completely cleared. The decision, you see, came out long ago, but today he went to hear the final ruling. The affair ended very happily for him. Whatever blame there was on him for negligence and carelessness — he was wholly absolved of it all. They ordered that a considerable sum of money be recovered from the merchant in his favour, so that his circumstances are greatly improved, and his honour is rid of the stain, and everything is better — in one word, his wish was fulfilled in the fullest possible way. He came home today at three o'clock. He had no face left on him, he was pale as a sheet, his lips were trembling, and yet he was smiling — he embraced his wife and children. We all went to him in a crowd to congratulate him. He was very much moved by what we had done, bowed on all sides, and shook each of us by the hand several times over. It even seemed to me that he had grown taller and straighter, and that there was not a single tear left in his eyes. Such a state of agitation he was in, poor man. He could not stand still for two minutes; he picked up everything that came to hand, then threw it down again, smiled and bowed without stopping, sat down, got up, sat down again, said God knows what — he says: "My honour, my honour, my good name, my children" — and how he said it! He even wept. We too, most of us, shed tears. Ratazyayev, evidently wanting to cheer him up, said: "What good is honour, my dear fellow, when there is nothing to eat? Money, my dear fellow, money is the main thing; that is what you should thank God for!" — and with that he clapped him on the shoulder. It seemed to me that Gorshkov took offence, that is, he did not exactly express displeasure, but only looked at Ratazyayev somehow strangely and took his hand off his shoulder. And before, my dearest, that would not have happened! However, characters are of all sorts. I, for instance, would not have shown myself proud on such a joyful occasion; for what is it, my dear, that makes one sometimes make an extra bow and show humility, if not a fit of kindness of soul and too great a softness of heart... but, however, it is not about me that we are speaking! "Yes," he says, "money is good too; thank God, thank God!" — and then all the time we were with him he kept repeating: "Thank God, thank God!.." His wife ordered a more delicate and more plentiful dinner. Our landlady herself cooked for them. Our landlady is, in some ways, a kind woman. And before dinner Gorshkov could not sit still. He went into everyone's rooms, whether they called him or not. He would simply walk in, smile, sit down on a chair, say something, and sometimes say nothing — and go away. He even took cards in his hands at the midshipman's; they sat him down to make a fourth. He played and played, muddled something in the game, made three or four moves, and threw it up. "No," he says, "you see, I am just so, I am, he says, just so," — and left them. He met me in the corridor, took me by both hands, looked me straight in the eyes, but so strangely; pressed my hand and went away, still smiling, but somehow heavily, oddly smiling, like a dead man. His wife wept for joy; everything was so cheerful with them, like a holiday. They dined quickly. Then after dinner he says to his wife: "Listen, my dear, I shall lie down a little," — and went to the bed. He called his little daughter to him, laid his hand on her head, and for a long, long time stroked the child's head. Then he turned again to his wife: "And what of Petenka? Our Petya, he says, Petenka?.." His wife crossed herself, and answered that he is dead, after all. "Yes, yes, I know, I know everything, Petenka is now in the heavenly kingdom." His wife sees that he is not himself, that the event has shaken him completely, and says to him: "You should go to sleep, my dear." — "Yes, good, I will in a moment... just a little," — here he turned away, lay for a little while, then turned back, wanted to say something. His wife did not catch it, and asked him: "What, my friend?" But he did not answer. She waited a little — well, she thinks, he has fallen asleep, and went out for an hour to the landlady. After an hour she came back — she sees her husband has not woken yet and lies there, not stirring. She thought he was asleep, sat down, and began to work at something. She tells how she worked for about half an hour and became so sunk in thought that she does not even remember what she was thinking about, she says only that she forgot about her husband. But suddenly she came to herself from some anxious feeling, and the deathly silence in the room struck her first of all. She looked at the bed and sees that her husband is lying all in one position. She went up to him, pulled off the blanket, and looks — and he is already cold as ice — dead, my dearest, Gorshkov is dead, died suddenly, as if struck down by thunder! And why he died — God knows. It has so overwhelmed me, Varenka, that I cannot come to my senses even now. I somehow cannot believe that a man could die so simply. Such a poor fellow, such a luckless wretch, this Gorshkov! Ah, what a fate, what a fate! His wife is in tears, so frightened. The little girl has squeezed herself into some corner. There is such a commotion going on there; there will be a medical inquiry... I cannot tell you for certain. Only it is a pity, oh, what a pity! It is sad to think that this is really how it is, that you know neither the day nor the hour... You perish like this, for nothing...

I hasten to inform you, my friend, that Ratazyayev has found me work with a certain author. Someone came to him and brought him such a thick manuscript — thank God, there is a lot of work. Only it is so illegibly written that I do not know how to set about it; they want it quickly. It is all written about something that one seems not to understand... We have agreed on forty kopecks a sheet. I write all this to you, my dear, because now there will be some outside money. Well, and now goodbye, my dearest. I am going straight to work.
I have not written to you for three days now, my friend, and I have had many, many cares and a great deal of anxiety.

The day before yesterday Mr. Bykov came to see me. I was alone; Fedora had gone somewhere. I opened the door to him and was so frightened when I saw him that I could not move from the spot. I felt that I had turned pale. He came in, as usual, with loud laughter, took a chair and sat down. For a long time I could not collect myself; at last I sat down in a corner with my work. He soon stopped laughing. It seems my appearance struck him. I have grown so thin lately; my cheeks and eyes are sunken, I was as pale as a handkerchief... indeed, anyone who knew me a year ago would hardly recognise me. He looked at me long and fixedly, and at last grew cheerful again. He said something; I do not remember what I answered him, and he laughed again. He sat with me a whole hour; talked to me for a long time; asked me about one thing and another. At last, before leaving, he took me by the hand and said (I am writing to you word for word): "Varvara Alexeyevna! Between ourselves, Anna Fyodorovna, your relation, and my close acquaintance and friend, is a most vile woman." (Here he called her by another, indecent word.) "She led your cousin astray from the path, and ruined you. For my part, I too proved a scoundrel in this affair, but then, what of it, it is the way of the world." Here he burst into laughter with all his might. Then he remarked that he was no master of fine speaking, and that the main thing, which needed to be explained and which the duties of honour commanded him not to keep silent about, he had already declared, and that he would now proceed briefly to the rest. Then he announced to me that he seeks my hand, that he considers it his duty to restore my honour, that he is rich, that after the wedding he will take me away to his village in the steppe, where he wants to hunt hares; that he will never come to Petersburg again, because Petersburg is foul, that he has here in Petersburg, as he himself expressed it, a good-for-nothing nephew, whom he has sworn to disinherit, and precisely for this reason, that is, wishing to have lawful heirs, he seeks my hand, that this is the chief reason for his proposal. Then he remarked that I live very poorly, that it is no wonder I am ill, living in such a hovel, predicted certain death for me if I remained like this even one more month, said that lodgings in Petersburg are nasty, and, finally, whether I did not need anything?

I was so struck by his proposal that, I do not know why, I wept. He took my tears for gratitude and told me that he had always been sure that I was a kind, sensitive and educated young lady, but that he had not decided on this step until he had found out in full detail about my present conduct. Here he asked about you, said that he had heard everything, that you were a man of honourable principles, that for his part he did not wish to be in your debt, and would five hundred roubles be enough for you for all that you have done for me? And when I explained to him that you had done for me what no money could ever repay, he told me that it was all nonsense, that it was all novels, that I was still young and read poetry, that novels ruin young girls, that books only spoil morals, and that he cannot bear any books; he advised me to live as many years as he has, and only then speak about people; "then," he added, "you will know people too." Then he told me to think carefully about his proposals, that it would be most unpleasant to him if I took such an important step without thinking, he added that thoughtlessness and infatuation ruin inexperienced youth, but that he extremely desires a favourable answer from me, and that, finally, in the opposite case, he will be forced to marry a merchant's daughter in Moscow, because, he says, I have sworn to disinherit the good-for-nothing nephew. He left five hundred roubles on my embroidery frame by force, for sweets, as he said; said that in the country I would grow fat as a flat cake, that I would live with him like a cheese in butter, that he has an awful lot of business on his hands just now, that he had dragged about all day on affairs and that now, between business, he had dropped in on me. Then he went away. I thought for a long time, I thought over a great deal, I tormented myself with thinking, my friend, and at last I decided. My friend, I shall marry him, I must agree to his proposal. If anyone can save me from my disgrace, restore my good name to me, and avert poverty, privation and misfortune from me in the future, it is he alone. What more can I expect from the future, what more can I ask of fate? Fedora says that one must not lose one's happiness; she says, what, in that case, is to be called happiness? I, at least, find no other way for myself, my priceless friend. What am I to do? I have already ruined all my health by work; I cannot work continually. To go into service in people's houses? I should waste away from misery, and besides, I should please nobody. I am sickly by nature and therefore shall always be a burden on other people's hands. Of course, even now I am not going to paradise, but what am I to do, my friend, what am I to do? What have I to choose from?

I did not ask you for advice. I wanted to think it over alone. The decision which you have just read is unchangeable, and I shall announce it to Mr. Bykov immediately, who, as it is, is hurrying me for a final decision. He said that his affairs do not wait, that he must go, and that they cannot be put off for trifles. God knows whether I shall be happy; my fate is in His holy, inscrutable power, but I have decided. They say that Mr. Bykov is a kind man; he will respect me; perhaps I too shall respect him. What more can one expect from our marriage?

I am informing you of everything, Makar Alexeyevich. I am sure you will understand all my misery. Do not turn me from my intention. Your efforts will be in vain. Weigh in your own heart everything that compelled me to act so. I was very anxious at first, but now I am calmer. What lies ahead, I do not know. What will be, will be; as God sends!..
Mr. Bykov has come; I am throwing down the letter unfinished. I wanted to tell you so much more. Bykov is here already!

I hasten to answer you, my dearest; I hasten to declare to you that I am astounded. All this is somehow not right... Yesterday we buried Gorshkov. Yes, that is so, Varenka, that is so; Mr. Bykov acted nobly; only here, you see, my dear, that is how you agree. Of course, everything is God's will; that is so, it must certainly be so, that is, God's will must certainly be in it; and the providence of the Heavenly Creator is, of course, both good and inscrutable, and fates too, and they are the same. Fedora also takes an interest in you. Of course, you will be happy now, my dearest, you will live in comfort, my little dove, my bright one, my beloved, my little angel — only here, you see, Varenka, how can it be so quickly?.. Yes, business... Mr. Bykov has business — of course, who has none, and he too may have some... I saw him as he was coming out from you. A fine-looking, fine-looking man; even a very fine-looking man indeed. Only all this is somehow not right, the point is not exactly that he is a fine-looking man, and I, too, am now somehow not myself. Only here, how shall we write letters to each other now? I, I, how shall I be left alone? I, my little angel, am weighing it all, weighing it all, as you wrote to me there, I am weighing it all in my heart, these reasons. I was just finishing copying the twentieth sheet, and in the meantime these events have come upon me! My dearest, here you are going away, so you have various purchases to make, little shoes of all kinds, a dress, and as it happens I have a shop I know in Gorokhovaya; you remember how I used to describe it to you. But no! How can you, my dearest, what are you saying! You cannot go now, it is quite impossible, utterly impossible. You have big purchases to make, and a carriage to get. Besides, the weather is bad now; just look how the rain is pouring as from a bucket, and such a wet rain, and then... and then you will be cold, my little angel; your little heart will be cold! Here you are afraid of a stranger, and you are going. And on whom shall I be left here alone? And here Fedora says that great happiness awaits you... but she is a violent woman and wishes to ruin me. Will you go to the all-night vigil today, my dearest? I would go to look at you. It is true, my dearest, perfectly true, that you are an educated, virtuous and sensitive young lady, only let him rather marry the merchant's daughter! What do you think, my dearest? Let him rather marry the merchant's daughter! I shall run in to you, my Varenka, as soon as it gets dark, for an hour. It gets dark early now, so I shall run in. I shall certainly come to you today, my dearest, for a little hour. Now you are expecting Bykov, but when he goes away, then... Wait, my dearest, I shall run in...
IX: Mr. Bykov said that I must absolutely have three dozen shirts of Holland linen. So we must find seamstresses as soon as possible for two dozen of them, and we have very little time. Mr. Bykov is angry, says there is a terrible lot of fuss with these rags. Our wedding is in five days, and on the day after the wedding we leave. Mr. Bykov is in a hurry, says that no great time should be wasted on nonsense. I am worn out with the bustle and can scarcely stand on my feet. There is a terrible heap of business, and really it would be better if none of it were needed. And besides: we are short of blonde lace and of lace trimming, so we must buy some more, because Mr. Bykov says that he does not want his wife to go about like a cook, and that I must absolutely "wipe the noses of all the country ladies." That is what he says himself. So, Makar Alexeyevich, please apply to Madame Chiffon in Gorokhovaya and ask her, first, to send seamstresses to us, and second, to take the trouble to call herself. I am ill today. In our new lodgings it is so cold and the disorder is terrible. Mr. Bykov's aunt is barely breathing from old age. I am afraid she will die before our departure, but Mr. Bykov says it is nothing, she will revive. In our house the disorder is terrible. Mr. Bykov does not live with us, so the servants all run away, God knows where. It happens that Fedora alone waits on us; and Mr. Bykov's valet, who looks after everything, has been missing, nobody knows where, for the third day now. Mr. Bykov calls every morning, is angry about everything, and yesterday beat the steward of the house, for which he had unpleasantness with the police... There was nobody to send my letter to you by. I am writing by the city post. Yes! I nearly forgot the most important thing. Tell Madame Chiffon that she must absolutely change the blonde lace, in accordance with yesterday's sample, and that she must come herself to show me the new selection. And tell her also that I have changed my mind about the canezou; that it must be embroidered with the crochet hook. And another thing: the letters for the monograms on the handkerchiefs are to be embroidered in tambour stitch; do you hear? in tambour stitch, and not in satin stitch. Mind you do not forget that it is tambour stitch! And I nearly forgot something else! Tell her, for God's sake, that the leaves on the pelerine are to be sewn raised, and the tendrils and stems in cordonnet, and then the collar is to be trimmed with lace or a broad flounce. Please pass it on, Makar Alexeyevich.

P. S. I am so ashamed that I keep tormenting you with my commissions. The day before yesterday, too, you ran about the whole morning. But what is to be done! In our house there is no order whatever, and I myself am unwell. So do not be vexed with me, Makar Alexeyevich. Such misery! Ah, what will become of it, my friend, my dear, my kind Makar Alexeyevich! I am afraid even to look into my future. I have a sort of foreboding about everything, and I live as though in some kind of daze.
P. S. For God's sake, my friend, do not forget anything of what I have just told you. I am always afraid that you may somehow make a mistake. Remember, then, tambour stitch, and not satin stitch.

I have carried out all your commissions with care. Madame Chiffon says that she had already thought herself of trimming in tambour stitch; that it is more proper, or something, I do not know, I did not quite take it in. And then, you wrote there about a flounce, so she spoke about the flounce too. Only I, my dearest, have forgotten what she said to me about the flounce. I only remember she said a great deal; such a nasty woman! What was it now? Well, she will tell you everything herself. I, my dearest, am quite worn out. Today I did not go to the office either. Only you, my dear, are despairing for nothing. For your peace of mind I am ready to run round all the shops. You write that you are afraid to look into the future. But today at seven o'clock you will learn everything. Madame Chiffon will come to you herself. So do not despair; hope, my dearest; perhaps everything will turn out for the best — there. So that, I keep on about this accursed flounce — ah, this flounce of mine — flounce! I would run in to you, my angel, I would run in, I would certainly run in; I have already twice come up to the gate of your house. But Bykov is always, that is, I mean to say, that Mr. Bykov is always so angry, so that, well, it is not quite... Well, but what of it!

For God's sake, run at once to the jeweller. Tell him that the earrings with pearls and emeralds are not to be made. Mr. Bykov says that it is too rich, that the price bites. He is angry; says that it is already costing him enough as it is and that we are robbing him, and yesterday he said that if he had known and foreseen such expenses beforehand, he would not have got himself involved. He says that as soon as we are married we shall leave at once, that there will be no guests and that I need not hope to whirl about and dance, for the holidays are still far off. That is how he talks! And God sees whether I need all this! It was Mr. Bykov himself who ordered everything. And I dare not answer him anything: he is so hot-tempered. What will become of me!

I — that is, the jeweller says it is all right; but I wished first of all to say about myself that I have fallen ill and cannot get up from my bed. Now, just when the troublesome, needful time has come, the colds have fallen upon me, the enemy take them! I also inform you that, to complete my misfortunes, his Excellency has been pleased to be strict, and was very angry and shouted at Yemelya Ivanovich, and at the end was quite worn out, poor dear. So I am informing you of everything. And I wished to write you something more, only I am afraid of troubling you. For I, my dearest, am a stupid, simple man, I write whatever comes into my head, and so perhaps you will think something there, something such — well, but what of it!

I saw Fedora today, my dear. She says that you are to be married tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow you leave, and that Mr. Bykov is already hiring horses. About his Excellency I have already informed you, my dearest. And another thing: I have checked the bills from the shop in Gorokhovaya; everything is correct, only very expensive. But why is Mr. Bykov angry with you? Well, be happy, my dearest! I am glad; yes, I shall be glad if you are happy. I would come to the church, my dearest, but I cannot, my back is aching. And so, about the letters: who now, my dearest, will carry them between us? Yes! You have done a kindness to Fedora, my dear! That was a good deed you did, my friend; you did very well. A good deed! And for every good deed the Lord will bless you. Good deeds do not remain without reward, and virtue will always be crowned with the crown of God's justice, sooner or later. My dearest! I would like to write you so much, I would write every hour, every minute, I would write and write! I still have one of your books left, Belkin's Tales, so you know, my dearest, do not take it back from me, give it to me, my dear. It is not that I so much want to read it. But you yourself know, my dearest, winter is coming; the evenings will be long; it will be sad, and so I could read. I, my dearest, shall move from my lodging into your old one and shall rent it from Fedora. I will not part with this honest woman for anything now; besides, she is so hard-working. Yesterday I examined your empty lodging in detail. There, as your little embroidery frame was, with the work on it, so it has stayed untouched: it stands in the corner. I looked at your embroidery. There are still scraps of various kinds lying about. You had begun to wind threads on one little letter of mine. In the little table I found a sheet of paper, and on the paper was written: "Dear Sir, Makar Alexeyevich, I hasten" — and nothing more. Evidently someone interrupted you at the most interesting place. In the corner behind the little screen your little bed stands... My dear one!!! Well, goodbye, goodbye; for God's sake, answer me something to this little letter as soon as you can.

It is all over! My lot is cast; I do not know what it is, but I submit to the will of the Lord. Tomorrow we leave. I am saying goodbye to you for the last time, my priceless one, my friend, my benefactor, my dear one! Do not grieve over me, live happily, remember me, and may God's blessing descend upon you! I shall remember you often in my thoughts, in my prayers. — So this time is over! I shall carry little that is pleasant into my new life from the memories of the past; the more precious will be the memory of you, the more precious will you be to my heart. You are my only friend; you alone here loved me. For I saw everything, I knew how you loved me! One smile of mine made you happy, one line of my letter. Now you will have to get used to being without me! How will you stay here alone! With whom will you stay here, my kind, priceless, only friend! I leave you the book, the embroidery frame, the begun letter; when you look at those begun lines, then in your thoughts read on further everything that you would like to hear or read from me, everything that I might have written to you; and what would I not write now! Remember your poor Varenka, who loved you so dearly. All your letters are left in Fedora's chest of drawers, in the top drawer. You write that you are ill, and Mr. Bykov will not let me go anywhere today. I shall write to you, my friend, I promise, but God alone knows what may happen. And so let us part now for ever, my friend, my dear, my own, for ever!.. Oh, how I would embrace you now! Goodbye, my friend, goodbye, goodbye. Live happily; be well. My prayer for you will be unceasing. Oh! How sad I am, how it weighs upon my whole soul. Mr. Bykov is calling me. Yours, ever loving you
P. S. My soul is so full, so full now of tears...
Tears crowd upon me, tear me. Goodbye.

My dearest, Varenka, my dear, my priceless one! They are taking you away, you are going! Now it would be better if they tore the heart from my breast than took you from me! How can you do this! — Here you are weeping, and you are going?! Here I have just received a little letter from you, all spotted with tears. So, you do not want to go; so, you are being carried off by force, so, you are sorry for me, so, you love me! But how, with whom will you be now? There your little heart will be sad, sick and cold. Misery will suck it dry, grief will tear it in two. You will die there, they will lay you in the damp earth there; and there will be nobody there even to weep for you! Mr. Bykov will go on hunting hares... Ah, my dearest, my dearest! why did you resolve on this, how could you resolve on such a step? What have you done, what have you done, what have you done to yourself! They will bring you to your coffin there; they will wear you out there, my little angel. For you, my dearest, are as weak as a little feather! And where was I? What was I, fool that I am, gaping at here! I see the child is wayward, the child simply has a headache! Instead of simply dealing with it — no, a fool of fools, I think nothing and see nothing, as if I were in the right, as if the matter did not concern me; and I even ran about after a flounce!.. No, Varenka, I shall get up; by tomorrow, perhaps, I shall be well, and so I shall get up!.. I, my dearest, shall throw myself under the wheels; I will not let you go away! But no, what is this in fact? By what right is all this done? I shall go with you; I shall run after your carriage if you do not take me, and I shall run with all my might until the breath goes out of me. But do you only know what there is, where you are going, my dearest? Perhaps you do not know it, so ask me! There is the steppe, my dear, there is the steppe, the bare steppe; bare as my palm! There walk heartless peasant women and uneducated peasant men, drunkards walk. There the leaves have now fallen from the trees, there are rains, there is cold — and you are going there! Well, Mr. Bykov has something to do there: he will be with his hares; but you, what will you do? Do you want to be a lady of the manor, my dearest? But, my little cherub! Just look at yourself, do you look like a lady of the manor?.. But how can such a thing be, Varenka! To whom shall I write letters, my dearest? Yes! just take it into consideration, my dearest — I mean, to whom will he write letters? Whom shall I call my dearest; whom shall I call by that sweet name? Where shall I find you afterwards, my little angel? I shall die, Varenka, I shall certainly die; my heart will not bear such a misfortune! I loved you as the light of God, I loved you as my own daughter, I loved everything in you, my dearest, my own! and I myself lived only for you alone! I worked, and wrote papers, and walked, and strolled, and committed my observations to paper in the form of friendly letters, all because you, my dearest, lived here, opposite, close by. Perhaps you did not even know it, but all of this was exactly so! Yes, listen, my dearest, consider, my dear little one, how can it be that you should go away from us? My own, you cannot go, it is impossible; simply, decidedly there is no possibility at all! Look, it is raining, and you are weak, you will catch cold. Your carriage will get wet; it will certainly get wet. As soon as you drive out beyond the toll-gate, it will break down; it will break down on purpose. For here in Petersburg they make carriages abominably! I know all these carriage-makers; they only care to make a pretty shape, some kind of toy, but not sturdy! I swear they make them flimsy! I, my dearest, shall throw myself on my knees before Mr. Bykov; I shall prove it to him, I shall prove everything! And you, my dearest, prove it too; prove it to him with reason! Say that you are staying and that you cannot go!.. Ah, why did he not marry the merchant's daughter in Moscow? Let him marry her there! A merchant's daughter suits him better, she would suit him much better; I know why that is! And I would keep you here with me. But what is he to you, my dearest, this Bykov? How has he suddenly become dear to you? Perhaps it is because he keeps buying you flounces, perhaps it is because of that! But what is a flounce? why a flounce? It is nonsense, my dearest! Here the question is of human life, and it, my dearest, is a rag — a flounce; it, my dearest, the flounce, is a scrap of cloth. Why, I myself, as soon as I get my pay, will buy you flounces; I will buy them for you, my dearest; I have a shop I know there; only let me wait for my pay, my little cherub, Varenka! Ah, Lord, Lord! So you really are leaving for the steppe with Mr. Bykov, leaving for ever! Ah, my dearest!.. No, you must write to me again, write me another little letter about everything, and when you have gone, write from there too. Otherwise, my heavenly angel, this will be the last letter; and it cannot possibly be that this letter should be the last. Why, how is it, so suddenly, just so, certainly the last! But no, I shall write, and you write too... For my style is just now forming... Ah, my dear, what is style! For I do not even know now what I am writing, I do not know at all, I know nothing, and I do not read it over, and I do not correct the style, but write only to write, only to write you as much as possible... My dear, my own, my dearest!
